SPRING. Gently hurried And buried The winter has passed to its natural doom; All its boldness' And coldness, Its winds bleak and dreary. are gone with its gloom, As exiles to tenant a summer-long tomb! Zephyrs sighing Are flying, With musical voices borne swiftly along. Birds are viinging And singing All tuneful with gladness, a spring-wooing song; And sweet are the birds to the woodlands that throng!

Sunl,ght gleaming Is streaming, In bright flowing rivers, embracing the earth! Universal Rehearsal Of symphony hails the fair spring at her birth. Whose advent is greeted will paramount mirth. Welcome, dear Spring! We will fling All care to the winds in this moment supreme. Vir, will treasure The pleasure Of blessings as lasting and deep as they seem, With spring-tide abroad like a beautiful dream! Warrington, March 27th, 1882. BENJ. SAWDON.

WHAT IS A GENTLEMAN? What is a gentleman? Is it a thing Decked with a scarf-pin, a chain, and a ring, Dressed in a suit of immaculate style, Sporting an eye-glass, a lisp, and a smile? Talking of operas, concerts, and balls, Evening assemblies and afternoon calls, sunning himself at "At Homes" and bazaars, Whistling mazurkas, and smoking cigars? What is a gentleman? Say, is it one Boasting of conquests and deeds he has done? One who unblushingly glories to speak Things which should call up a flush to his cheek? One, who, whilst railing at actions unjust, Robs some young heart of its pureness and trust; Scorns to steal money. or jewels, or wealth, Thinks it no crime to take honour by stealth? What is a gentleman? Is it not one Knowing instinctively what he should shun, Speaking no word that cm injure or pain, Spreading no scandal and deep'ning no stain? One who knows how to put each at his ease, Striving instinctively always to please; One who can tell, by a glance at your cheek, When to be silent and when he should speak? What is a gentleman? Is it not one Honestly a .eatin the bread he has won, Living in uprightness, fearing his God, Leaving no stain on the path he has trod, Caring not whether his coat may be old, Prizing sincerity far above gold, Reeking not whether his hand may be hard, Stretching it boldly to grasp its reward? What is a gentleman? Say, is it birth Makes a man noble, or adds to his worth? Is there a family tree to be had Spreading enough to conceal what is bad? Seek out the man who has God for his Guide, Nothing to blush for, and nothing to hide; Be he a noble, or be he in trade, This is the gentleman Nature has made. —Andrew's American Queen. •

So do the operations of most people who gat below low-water mark, as they end in the Bankruptcy Court. CAUGHT A TARTAR.—The RO7. Ralph Erskine, one of the fathers of the secession from the Kirk of Scotland, paid a visit to his venerable brother, Ebenezer, at Abernethy. " Oh ! man," said the latter, "bat ye come in gude time ; I've a diet of examination to-day, and ye mann tak it, as I have matters o' life and death to settle at Perth." " With all my heart," quoth Ralph. " Noo, Billy," says Ebenezer. " ye'll find a' my folk easy to examine but aria, and him I reckon ye had better no meddle wi'. He has an auld, fashions, Scotch way of answering ae question by putting another; and maybe he'll affront ye.' "Affront me!" quoth the indignant theologian; "do ye think he can foil me wi' my am n natural tools?" " Aweel," said his brother, " I'se gie ye fair warning; ye had better no CA' him up." The recusant was one Walter Simpson, the smith of the parish. The gifted Ralph, indignant to the last degree at the bare idea of such an illiterate clown cnopping divinity with him, de- termined to gravel him at once with a grind, leading, un- answerable question. Accordingly, after putting a variety of preliminary interrogatories to the senior clodhoppers, he all at once, with a loud voice, cried out, " Walter Sintpeon !" " Here, sir," says Walter, "are ye wanting me ?" " Atten- tion, sir! Now, Walter, can you tell toe how long Adam stood in a state of innocence 9" " he got a wife," replied the anvil hammerer, in an instant; "bat can ye tell me, sir, hoo lang he stood after ?" "sit down, Walter'," said the discomfited divine. Tas AFRICA:Ls' EXPLORER IN HIS EVENING TENT.—We are delightfully situated on a small island in the middle of the river. Here we heve formed our camp to secure our- selves from molestation. The island is well supplied with large shady trees, though it is very narrow—so narrow that my tent stretches nearly right across, and three steps from the door bring me to deep water in which I have my daily bath. The men have scattered themselves over the rest of the available space and are making the woods re-echo with their loud laughter as the story goes round; while every now and then the song resounds sharp and clear in this, night air. They are all in a very jolly mood round the ruddy camp fires, for antelope is abundant and some days' rest in prospect. As for myself, I have lit my lamp, discussed my cup of coffee, and made every preparation for commenc- ing my correspondence. Yet I feel tempted by my surround- ings to linger and dream. A certain delicious feeling of com- fort and safety invites me to sit by the rushing river and, with feet elevated in American fashion, to gaze at the stars, become sentimental, and on the swift wings of fancy hurry far away from Africa and At rich joys. My reverie, how- ever, is soon rudely broken. Through the otherwise dreamy elements of the night comes a sound which only too pointedly reminds me where I am. A lion has caught the scent of our antelope's meat, and stands amid the shades of the opposite bank vainly longing to join the feast. Just as I am getting most sentimental a savage roar resounds through the forest, making me start and shiver as if cold water were being poured down my back, and producing a creeping sen- sation at the roots of my hair. The interruption is a rather abrupt reminder that I must be practical. Therefore let us • to business !—Joseph Thomson, in "Good Words" for March. CRITICISED Eacii Ornnit's WORIC.—One day an editor, hard at work, trying to devise a plan to make his delinquent subscribers pay their dues, was called upon by a shoemaker, who dropped in to give the editcr some valuable hints on running a newspaper. The editor, overjoyed at the oppor- tunity, gave the man his best cane-seat chair, honoured him with a fresh cigar, and listened attentively to what he had to say. Quoth the shoemaker, as he lit the weed: "Your paper needs a hundred improved features. You do not grasp the topics of the day by the right handle; you don't set the locals in the right kind of type; your telegraph news is too thin, even the per itself is poorly manufac- tured, not thick enough and too chalky white; you dcn't run enough matter, and what you dc run ain't of the right sort; your idea about protective tariff is infernally foolish, and your stand in the Conkling matter was bad. I tell you these things because I want to see you succeed. I tell you as a friend. I don't take your paper myself. but I see it once in a while; and as a paper is a public affair, I suppose I have as good a right to criticise as anybody. If a man wonts to give me advice, I let him; I'm glad to have him, in fact." "That's exactly it," said the editor, kindly ; "I always had a dim idea of my shortcomings, but never had them so clearly and convincingly set forth as by you. It is impossible to express my gratitude for the trouble you have taken not only to find out these facts, but to point them out also. Some people, knowieg all these things, perhaps nearly as well as you, are mean enough to keep them to themselves. Your suggestions come in a most appropriate time. Ihave wanted someone to lean on, as it were, for some weeks. Keep your eye on the paper, and when you see a weak spot, come up." The ehoemaker left, happy to know that his suggestions had been received with such a Chris- tian spirit. Next day, just as he was finishing a boot, the editor came in, and picking up the mate, remarked :—" I want to tell you how that boot strikes me. In the first place, the leather is poor; the stitches in the sole are wide apart, and the uppers too near the edge. Those uppers will go to pieces in two weeks. It's all wrong, my friend, put- ting poor leather in the heels Red smoothing it over with grease and lampblack. Everybody complains of your boots; they don't last; the legs are too short, the toes too narrow, and the instep too high. How you can have the gall to charge 12 dole. for such boots beats me. Now, I tell you this because I like to see you succeed. Of course, I don't know any more about shoemaking than you do about a newspaper, but still I take an interest in you because you are so well disposed towards me. In fact, I—" Here the exasperated cobbler grabbed a lepetene, and the editor gained the street, followed by old knivee, pincers, hammers, and awls, lean after him by the wrathful cobbler, who, on regaining his seat, swore by the nine gods that no imper- tinent, lop-eared idiot should ever come round trying to teach him his trade.—Cherokee Courant. At the next Chicago fat stock show prizes are to be offered as follows :—Early maturity; animal showing the greatest average gain per day since birth, entries to be ac- companied by affidavit giving exact age. Cost of produc- tion; entries to be accompanied with a verified statement, giving itemised cost of production, the exact age, breeding of the animal, the weight, as well as the market value of the several kinds of food consumed year by year from date of birth until the animal is exhibited. ' I PRESERVED POTATOES.—Economist writes to US :—" a e list now, while potatoes are so abundant everywhere, the follow- ing plan of preserving them for cattle food is worth making widely known: They most be well boiled, drained, and allowed to dry thoroughly. They should then be mashed, and well mixed through with a little salt, and afterwards tightly pressed down in any kind of vessel. Potatoes treated in this way will remain in good condition for many menthe." MAIZE FOR FODDER.—Mr. Thos. Harris, of the American Land Office, 16, Borough, S.E. writes :—"Maize for fodder may be sown from the middle of May to the middle of Jane; it may de both earlier and Liter, but the young plants will not stand the late fepsts,lnd the crops should have the chance of three months of warm weather. It may be either drilled or planted; but in either case the rows should be 2 feet apart and the plants 8 inches. If planted, two pecks will be sufficient to the acre; if drilled, a bushel or more will be needed, and the plants will require thinning." CARBOLIC Actle IN FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—Mr. Mark Charrock, farm bailiff to Messrs. Greenwood and Roberts, Ra.dholme Leund, Clitheroe, states that he has found great benefit from the use of carbolic acid in cases of , foot-and-mouth disease. The disease broke out in a herd of 83 cattle, of which 13 were affected when the experiments wite Celvert's No. 5 carbolic acid applied by means of Cal- vert's "Vaporiser." A farther outbreak occurred two days afterwards, but from that time the spread of the disease was arrested, ai3d the whole of the affected animals speedily recovered. The success in this case was so marked, both with regard to checking the spread of the disease and curing it, that an extensieee trial of this remedy will pro- bably be made. CANON BAGOT ON THE SETTING OF MILE.—" All milk," says the Canon, "coming into the dairy should be strained through a fine wire strainer. The object of setting milk is to get all the cream from it. Undoubtedly the Swedishor Schwartz is the best, because the cream is obtained in twelve hours, leaving the milk perfectly sweet. The American cooley system is much the same, using cold water instead of ice. Bat all these deep setting systems are unsuitable for Ireland, because ice is too dear, water cold enough is next ti impossible to get, and last, though not least, the ap- pliances for these systems are very expensive. Until the setting of milk is swept away by the mechanical separator, we must continue the old-fashioned way of shallow pane. There is a rule in setting milk which it is well always to bear in mind, namely, the lower the temperature of a dairy the lower the setting ought to be, and the higher the tem- perature the shallower the setting, so that, following out this rule, milk may be set from 81n. deep in winter to Lin. in summer. The careful following out of this rule will do much to counteract the inconvenience often felt from the want of a stove or heating apparatus in a dairy. Milk should always be skimmed before it has turned the least sour. The separator—a machine which mechanically sepa- rates cream from milk—is fast coming to the front, and in a year or two, in its improved form, will.proba.bly be used in all large dairies. The principle of all separators is that milk revolving at a high speed throws up the cream to the top. Already great improvements have been made, and it has been conclusively proved that the whole of the cream has been separated, leaving none in the milk." THE WINTER OF 1881-82.—As the winter of 1881-82 is now over (taking December, January, and February as the three winter months), it may be interesting to compare it with some of its predecessors; and this comparison will show it to have been one of the mildest winters of recent years. Its mean temperature has been higber than that of any winter during the twenty years' observations, except- ing those of 1863 and 1869, and was 107 degrees higher than that of the exceptionally cold winter of 187879. The following table will show more clearly than aty written description the relation, in the matter of temperature and rainfall, which the winter just closed bears to previous years:— Mean Rain- Winter Temp. fall. Rainy Averages for of degrees. Inch days. five years. 1862-63 1863-64 1864-65 1865-66 1866-67 1867-68 1863-69 1869-70 1870-71 1871-72 1872-73 1873-74 1874-75 1875-76 1876-77 1877-78 1878-79 1879-80 35 36-44 degrees. Average 1880 81 1881-82 The results of the twenty years' observations show very clearly that on the average the winters have been gradually becoming colder, as will be seen in the last column of the above table; the average winter temperature for the five years ending 1867 (3952 deg.) having steadily fallen to 36 44 deg for an equal period ending 1882, notwithstand- ing the remarkably mild winter which has just closed. In the matter of rainfall it will be seen that the last five-year period has been considerably the driest, owing in a great measure to the severe frost of recent winters. The average winter temperature for the twenty years is 38 57 deg., and the average ramfall is 6 925 inches; the mean temperature of the winter of 1881-82 was, therefore, 2-63 deg. above the average and the rainfall was -625 of an inch below the mein value for the winter season.—Thos. G. Been, Carlisle. NORMANDY BUTTER.—Mr. Barter recently gave an ad- dress on this subject. He said :—I saw the whole process of churning and butter making at a farmer's near Bayeaux, 1 who had obtained several gold medals for his butter, and the I bronze medal at the Paris Exhibition of 1876. The farm 1 CC:MI:A.9 of about 160 acres of excellent land, the rent being £4 an acre. Seventy cows are kept, all of the C3tentin breed. The churn was turned by horse power at the rate of sixty revolutions a minute. The churning tcok forty minutes, and was stopped the Ament the butter came in small grains. Two-thirds of the buttermilk was then re- moved, and spring water poured in by a pipe, as before de- scribed. It was then turned slowly for thirty revolutions, two-thirds of the milk and water being again taken out, and I more water poured in. The two first washings were reserved for the pigs. The same operation was then repeated till the water came away quite clear. It took in all eight washings, the number of revolutions being reduced each time. By not removing all the buttermilk or water, the particles of butter are kept separate, so that they ere much more completely I washed and the grains preserved. After the last webbing the churn was half filled with water, and rocked gently . backwards and forwards to collect the butter, which was re- moved in lamps of about 41b. It was not worked at all, . I but each lump was slightly pressed with the hands in a 1 basin of water, then taken out and gently pitted with a , wooden spoon to remove the water, and place ffle on a little I round table covered with a clean, new cloth, which was branded with the name of the farmer and the medals he had obtained; five or six lumps were placed one over the other, and flattened and shaped with the spoon, the only imple- ment used. The butter was then neatly pinned up, and the weight marked on it, so that there is no tare or deduction of any kind; each package weighs about 251 b., and is placed in a small package lined with reed, which costs about 45. A carrier from the railway company calls around to the farmers to take the packages to the station; the entire cost , to Paris, including carriage, tolls, factor, &c., is about 25. a pound. The butter sent in this way direct to Paris is all consigned to factors, and sold ber auction at the Halles central; that which I saw made fetched 2s. 9d. a pound. , At another farm I visited the proprietor had got 3s. a pound the week before, and often gets 4s. 3d. in winter. The Nor- j mandev butter we get in England is in reality only second or third quality. All the farmers and dealers I spoke to on the subject said the best butter was never sent to England, as the English would not give the price for it. I visited the weekly butter market at Isigny. It began at 10 a.m. The women stood in lines, each with her basket before her, the lumps of butter, varying in weight from about 101 b. to 701 b., were each made up in a clean cloth. The buyers go round with a small woolen knife, and examine it very carefully, taste and smell it, and often break off large pieces to sea the grain. They write on the lump of butter the price they offer. If not accepted, it is blotted out by passing the knife ever it; but if agreed to, the quality and private mark of the buyer is put on it, and the women take it to the depot, where it is weighed, paid for, and the quality again checked. Each description is placed separately in very large baskets, lined witblinen. At one depot I saw it divided into let, • 2nd, 3rd, and 4th quality; the prices were—let, is. 7de; 2nd, is. 4d. ; 3rd, is. 3d. The butter for Paris was despatched the same day by the 2 p.m. train in a special waggon arranged with shelves. Aril the butter is sold per- fectly fresh, the supply averaging about 35,0001 b. a week. I would say, in conclusion, that as good butter can and has , been made in the south of Ireland as anywhere in the world, and I hope I have shown clearly that the art of dairying in , its practical bearing, and the manufacture of butter of the highest quality is not, after all such a very difficult sub- ject. Scrupulous cleanliness and close attention to detail is the great secret of success.
He who respects his work so highly and does it so rever- ently that he cares little what the world thinks of it, is the man about whom the world comes at last to think a great deal.

div.head: . TIM EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882.
div.p: . TIM EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882.
SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

A scidntific expedition to Persia is being despatched from Austria under the command of Dr. J. C. Polak, formerly physician to the Shah. The expedition will proceed vid Odessa, Poti, Tiflis, Baku, and Rescht, to Hamadan, the ancient Ecbatana. The expedition is to return in about six months.

M. Merey, who is travelling in Italy, has 4ccomplished a feat which will be serviceable in connection with the study of the mechanism of flight in birds. He has taken, by means of a revolving lens, a series of instantaneous photo. graphs of birds on the wing. He claims to have rendered visible actions lasting only one five-hundredth part of a second.

Movements of the ground seem to be now going on in the Jura, says Nature. M. Girardot has lately pointed out that villages which were invisible from each other at the begin- ning of the century, and even thirty or forty years ago, are now visible. First, the roofs appeared; then, in part, the walls. Such is the case with the villages of Doucier and Marigny, near Lake Chalain. Important changes have been observed even within ten years. Professor Shs.ler, of Harvard University, attributes the rigid climate of the northern portion of America to the rising of the land at Behring's Straits, which intercepts the warm ocean current from Japan, turn;ng it towards Oregon and California. This rising is thought to have ceased, and it will probably be followed by a subsidence. Professor Shaler proposes to. clear away three small islands in the narrowest part of the Straits, and some obstructing reefs along shore, so that the Japanese Gulf stream might carry its warming influence further north. Mr. W. Markownikoff, of Moscow, has been investigating the so.called desaggregation of tin. Some tin cans kept in one of the Government buildings during cold weather showed blisters, then boles, and finally fell to powder. This phenomenon has been several times observed. A very re. markable case was reported by Oademans and Walz. A good commercial tin was, during its transport from Rotter- dam to Moscow in a very cold winter, changed into a gray powder. Mr. Markownikoff finds that the process of change having commenced cannot be stopped by removing the cans to a warm room. The destruction, however, ceased if the spots were cut out. He thinks that more or leas rapid cooling predisposes the metal to desaggregation that it is favoured by a low temperature, and is accelerated by vibra. tion. ' At the last meeting of the Anthropological Institute, Mr. J. E. Price read a "Note on the Aggri Beads," which are occasionally dug up in the Gold Coast territory, and sell for more than their weight in gold, being amongst the most valued of royal jewels. They have been found in various parts of England, some of those exhibited having been ob- tained from Cnlchester, where they were found associated with human remains, while others were discovered during the recent alterations at Leadenhall Market. „Mr. Price thought that the appearance of these beads in England might be accounted for by the fact that when the Romans occupied the country they brought with thenfmany African slaves, who wore necklaces with Aggri beads, and that when these slaves died their necklaces were buried with them. Near Mandeeley, on the coast of Norfolk, says the Academy, there occurs a deposit called the "Arctic Fresh- water Bed," discovered a short time ago by Mr. A. Nathorst. This formation is of considerable geological interest, inas- much as it is supposed to offer the earliest indications of the advent of arctic conditions in that area. Mr. Clement Reid, of the Geological Survey, has obtained from this bed a few teeth and bones, which are the first vertebrate remains yet unearthed from the deposit. Mr. E. T. Newton, of the Museum of Practical Geology, refers them to the pouched marmot (or Spermophilus). Remains of the Sivermophilus of any age are so exceedingly rare in this country that the discovery is welcome to British geologists; but it is es- pecially interesting as showing that the pouched marmot lived in East Anglia at the beginning of the glacial period, and prior to the deposition of the till, or lower boulder clay. MOUNTAINEERING IN NEW ZEALAND.—It has been left to an American subject to be the first man other than a Maori to scale the precipices and examine the crater of Tongariro. It is satisfactory, in the interests of science and exploration, to learn that Herr Emil Boss, accompanied by several mem- bers of the English Alpine Club, has reached Melbourne en route for New Zealand, where they propose to attempt the ascent of all the principal peaks and to explore the giant glaciers surrounding Mount Cook. They are attended by Kauffmann a well-known Swiss guide, and, as their leader has ascended all the great peaks of S witzerland, and also visited the Andes and Himalayas, he may be considered to have ample experience to qualify him for the task before him. After finishing their work in New Zealand, the party propose to visit New Guinea for the purpose of exploration, included in which is probably an ascent of the famous Mount Owen Stanley.—The Colonies and India. NEw PROCESS FOR:TEMPERING STEEL.—At the last meeting of the French Academie des Sciences, M. Dumas gave an account of a new process for tempering steel in- vented by aM. Clemenceau. M. Dumas introduced the communication by stating that recent experiments on the causes of th.e conversion of iron into steel have indicated the possibility of the impregnation of the carbon with iron vapour and the impregnation of the metallic mass with the vapour of carbon. M. Dumas considers that this inter- change may explain the new properties acquired by the con- verted iron, which he attributes to the substance being thus rendered less porous and more homogeneous. M. Clenaen- ceau's tempering process consists in taking a bar of steel, heating it to redness, enclosing it in a box which it exactly fills, and then submitting it to enormous hydraulic pressure. The steel is allowed to cool under these conditions. When withdrawn it proves to be very highly tempered and suit- able for making magnets, which have a remarkable degree of resistance. This steel is now being used in the manufac- ture of telephones, and it makes excellent and very fine tools. The compression can be regulated so as to give any required degree of temper to the steel. DEAFNESS IN RAILWAY OFFICIALS.—The Lancet says that Professor S. Moos, of Heidelberg, influenced, we pre- sume, by the important results which have resulted from the attention of experts being directed to the colour percep- tion of railway officials and others whose actions are guided by coloured signals, has communicated to the Zeitschrift far Ohrenheilkunde the results of his obsavations and read- ing in regard to the causes and effects of deafness in railway officials, to which, he points out, railway accidents may not unfrequently be attributed. Dr. Jacoby found that in the course of ten years and a half no less than 20 out of a total number of 80 engine-drivers applied to him for affections of the organ of hearing; of these five had unilateral affections of the labyrinth, and 15 lesions of the middle ear. Dr. Hartman, again, has found that the surrounding conditions have to be taken into consideration, drivers having some- times to work their way through violent storms of wind, over ground that is hard frozen, and through long tunnels, and that under these conditions hardness of hearing, which, however, is often only transitory, is apt to be established. Professor Moos refers to the Canonbury railway accident, and to a singular case in which the engine and tender with a luggage van entered the station at Provins, in France, alone the train having been unfortunately omitted to be coupled to the engine before starting, indicating, as Pro. feesor Moos remarks, that both engine.driver and stoker mast have failed to miss the rumble of the ordinary train, owing to some defect of hearing. He records other cases, and he thinks that the hearing of drivers should be tested as carefully as their vision. _ -

OLD LONDoN WALL—.& very curious and interesting relic is being destroyed and carted away. Half way up Ludgate-hill there runs towards the river a narrow alley known as St. Martin's-court, and here recently remained one of' the four fragments of old London Wall. It is now in process of demolition, and it could only be wished that builders in these days would turn out work equally good. It consists of great lumps of stone, held together by mortar as binding as Portland cement. There were, according to Peter Cunningham in the year 1850, but four fragments then in existence of the wall which formerly encircled the city of London---" one in the churchyard of St. Giles, Cripple- gate ; a second in St. Martin's-court, off Ludgate-hilf; a third in the Old Bailey, concealed. behind houses; and a fourth behind the houses in Trinity-square, on the west side of a vacant plot of ground in George-street, Tower-hill.° Those who take the least interest in the antiquities of Lon- don cannot visit this old relic too soon. At the same time they may be, perhaps, with advantage reminded that the neighbourhood of Ludgate-hill is rich in historical associa- tions. Lud Gate, which was taken down a hundred and twenty years ago, was one of the four city gates. Its cellars were used as a prison. Outside it lay a bridge over the Fleet, which was once a navigable river running down Far- ringdon-street, and which still runs underground, discharg- ing itself at the northern end of Blackfriars Bridge. What is now Lq,dgate-hill was once known as Bowyer-row—the City gate being actually defended by archers, and it being, consequently, convenient that bowyers should ply their trade in the immediate neighbourhood.—Observer.

was no light consideration. If a poor man died naturally,or of an incurable disease, it was to his family and friends a misfortune, but nothing more; but if he died of a complaint which was curable, and if his death was attributable to the absence of care which might have been given, but which he could not afford to pay for, then a feeling was aroused which was not favourable to the social good, or the good understanding between different classes. From that point of view our hospitals, convalescent homes, and all in- stitutions of the same kind, were not merely safeguards against bodily disease—they were a security against a class of moral diseases dangerous to the State, and diseases of which one common symptom was the decay of patriotic feeling and the jealousies and antagonisms of classes.

admiration till the shadows of evening had long closed in, was in private life the most gentle, the most genial, the most affable, the most unassuming, the most playful of friendt. Such was the effect of Carran's pleasantry that even on ordinary occasions servants in attendance at the table were compelled to break forth in laughter. He had a favourite black servant who lived with him for many years, and to whom for his great fidelity Mr. Curran was very much attached. This poor fellow was observed for a few days to be oppressed with gloom and sadness, the cause of which was not directly inquired into. One.morning whilst in this state he came up anxiously to his master, and with apparent regret and an air of much dejection, requested to be discharged. Mr. Curran told him he was very mach concerned to lose the services of so faithful a person, that he had a strong regard for him, and on inquiring into the reason of his desire to leave him' the black replied—" It is impossible for me to remain longer with you, massa.." "Why, my good fellow, we will see all care taken of you." "No, massa, I cannot live longer with you. lam losing. my health with you—you make me laugh too mach." Some of Curran's best speeches have not been handed down to us, and even some of those which we possess are but impetfectly reported. But we can still be warmed by their feeling and warned by their wisdom. Though these speeches were delivered on behalf of men who had dared to resist "the powers that be," there is in them no popular seduction —no blazonry of revolt, no attempt to colour political con- vulsions into national virtues—none of the charletan which gives place to shadows and passes off the courage to over- throw under the stamp of patriotism. No man more anxiously threw the flashes of his genius down the dark path where heated brains and desperate hearts rushed to their ruin than Curran. And this, in a word, is his claim to our es- teem, and affection, and admiration, that Laving by his talents raised himself from a bumble condition to a station of high trust, amid innumerable temptations, he held himself erect in servile times, and has left an example of political honour upon which the most scrutinising malice cannot de- tect a stain.

div.head: LORD DERBY ON HOSPITAIS.
div.p: LORD DERBY ON HOSPITAIS.

On Saturday the hospital at Bur, which has been erected at a cost of £13,000, was opened by Lord Derby. In the morning a procession, in which the various trades and bene- fit societies were represented, together with the mayors and corporations of Bury and Heywood, the members of the local boards within the union, and other public bodies, accompanied his lordship to the hospital.—Lord Derby, be- fore declaring the hospital open, said that the great atten- tion paid to health and disease and sanitary matters was due, for the most part, to the devoted efforts of obscure and self- sacrificing men. Those questions had obtained a hold on the public mind such as they never had before, and we not only talked about them, but thought about them. We might not be always successful or judicious in our experiments, but at any rate we were not indifferent. We recognised the fact that there was no better test of a true civilization of a country than its death-rate, and there was no such evidence, and, at the same time, no such cause of true national well- being as the health of the population. What they were then doing concerned them not only locally, but socially and irrationally, for a hospital was one of the most effectual ways in which the richer classes could help the poor, with- out the suspicion of jobbing or the possibility of abuse. In our civilization and in our country, without a cordial feeling between the richer and poorer classes, not only could we not look for any permanent prosperity in the future, but we could feel no real security in the present. His lordship then formally declared the hospital opened.—ln the after- noon a didner was held in the Phillips Hall.!--Lord Derby in proposing "Success to the Bury Dispensary Hospital," pointed out that in a state of civilization like ours, old and highly artificial, involving enormous disparities of fortune— in a country like ours, where there were many rich and arm many very poor, those who were well off ought to re- gard it as a special piece of good fortune that they had the opportunity of using some part of their wealth in assisting their poorer neighbours in this way, and that to his mind

div.head: ILLUSTRIOUS IRISHIIEN.
div.p: ILLUSTRIOUS IRISHIIEN.

No. XIII.—JOHN PHILPOT CURRAN. Let him but stand, in spite of power, A watchman on the lonely tower, His thrilling trump will rouse the land When fraud or danger is at hand, By him, as by the beacon light, The Pilot must keep course aright.— TV. Scott.

Up to the present we have not referred to Curran's Parlia- mentary career. The reason is obvious. It was less memorable than his career at the Bar. In the Law Courts his lot was cast. There he had no compeers, and there he exerted all his energies in the advocacy of right. But in the House of Commons he was somewhat reluctant to urge him- self to exertions rendered less imperious by the crowd of able men who fought the battle of the Opposition. His speeches in the House were seldom marked with the excel- lencies which distinguished his professional eloquence. They were desultory and irregular, and as one has well said, "lively bursts and sketches conceived more in the wanton- ness of fancy than the serious exertion of his mind, keen strokes of satire, flying shafts of wit, instead of profound reasoning." Yet his Parliamentary career, if not very brilliant, was at least eminently consistent and disinterested. He made his maiden speech in favour of Flood's Reform Bill, and he took part in almost every subsequent effort to purify the Parliament, to emancipate the Catholics, to re- duce the pensions, to ameliorate the civil code, and to pre- vent the introduction of military law. He laboured with special earnestness, though without success, to assimilate the law of treason in Ireland to that of England, by which two witnesses were necessary for a capital conviction, and if he had succeeded he would have prevented some of the worst judicial scandals of his age. In the 'House, as at the Bar, his voice was always heard denouncing political profli- gacy and corruption, and advocating those measures which would, if passed, have ameliorated the condition of his un- happy country. Upon the death of Mr. Pitt, the political party with whom Curran had so long been acting, having come into office, he was appointed Master of the Rolls and a member of the Privy Council. With this appointment he was dissatisfied at the time. Indeed he was never reconciled to the office. In a letter to Grattan on his appointment he says :—" When the Party with which I had acted so fairly had, after so long a proscription, come at last to their natural place, I did not expect to have been stuck into a window a spectator of the procession." Whatever might have been the dignity or the emoluments of the effice, it had no political conse- quence, and therefore to him who had acted such a part in the history of his country it seemed rather like a compensa- tion for former services than a means of taking that honour- able share, to which he felt himself entitled in an Adminis- tration that promised such benefits to Ireland. We need not, therefore, be surprised that he never became entirely reconciled to this appointment. One incident in Carran's closing years is worth recording, illustrating, as it does, his courage and chivalrous devotion. When the Catholic Board was declared to be an unlawful assembly it was resolved, while abstaining from assembling the Catholic Board, to hold an aggregate meeting of Catho- lies. This meeting assembled on the 11th of Jane, 1814. As O'Connell was addressing the meeting an interruption at a side door caused him to turn round. In a moment there was silence. Then a cheer was heard from the people out- side. Suddenly the immortal name of Curran rang through the edifice. Many a stout arm was extended to help the dying patriot as he feebly advanced to the front of the stage where the Catholic leaders stood. The excitement was almost too much for him. He sank into a chair, and for a few moments covered his face with his hands. An eye• witness of the scene says:—" I never shall forget the sharp penetrating glance he threw over the assembly when he seemed to rally from the transient debility which at first oppressed him, and the fixed regard he cast upon O'Connell when he resumed his address." His appearance among the Catholics at the moment when everything seemed to look black and menacing to their hopes, when tyrant power de- nounced and oppressed them, when false or fekewarm friends betrayed or fell from them, not only touched their hearts and gratified them, but rekindled in their soul fresh spirit and energy. Their memories went back to the days of '9B, when with a patriot's words of flame the dauntless advocate of the United Irishmen, in his zeal for his lost clients, struggled against despair, never once shrinking from the face of threatening, or the many perils which gathered around him. The hero then was the hero still, and we need not wonder that the Catholics looked upon him on this occa- sion with feelings of homage and devotion. In the spring of 1817 Curran began to sink rapidly. While dining with his friend Thomas Moore he suffered a slight paralytic attacktin one of his hands. He also imperi- enced frequent oppressions in the chest. His medical ad- visers recommended him to visit the mild climate of the South of Europe. Preparatory to following this advice he passed over to Dublin to Arrange his affairs. His friends perceived by his altered looks that the end was not far off. Of this he was not insensible himself. As he walked through the grounds of his country seat with Mr:M`Nally, he spoke of the impending event with tranquility and resignation.

I melt (said he) and am not Of stronger earth than others. "I wish it was all over." On the day of his departure for England, after having parted in the ordinary way from another of his friends he returned suddenly, grasped his hand. saying in an affectionate but firm tone, "You will never behold me more." Upon his arrival at Cheltenham he was revisited by paralytic symptoms. He called upon a physician and asked him to declare explicitly whether it indi- cated any disposition to palsy. The physician assured him that there was no indication of the,kind. Then said Curran, "I suppose I am. to consider what has lately happened as a runaway knock, and not a notice to quit." He removed to London, intending to prosecute his journey to the South of France But on the Bth of October he was attacked by apo- plexy, and at nine o'clock on the 14th of October, 1817, in the 68th year of his age, he expired. His remains were privately interred in London in one of the vaults of Pad- dington Church. The man whose career we have thus sketched was in truth an Illustrious Irishman. No man loved his country more passionately than Curran loved Ireland. His love of Ireland was of no vulgar or fickle kind, originating in inter est, vanity' or ambition. Ireland was the choice of his youth, and was from the first to the last regarded by him, not so much with the feelings of a patriot) as with the ro- mantic idolatry of a lover. To her his heart was contracted "for better or for worse"—to her "what he had to give he gave," confederating all his most cherished projects with her wayward fortunes, and surrendering to her service all the resources of his genius in the successive stages of her pride, her hopes, her struggles, and her despair. We have been reminded by some of his biographers that he loved England too. We doubt it not. But he loved Ireland better, and he seemed to have thought, in the words of the poet— Though England's our father and Ireland our mother, Yet one side we know is much surer than t'other.

And he was an Illustrious Irishman, too. Seldom has Ireland produced a patriot of more brilliant and varied talents. Rising from a position of the deepest humility, he early attracted public attention as a wit of almost the highest order, and an orator who might compare with the greatest of his countrymen. A member of a profession where all promotion depended on the Government, and was then given from political motives, he was never guilty of aban- doning a principle or swerving from a public -duty. He exhibited the most chivalrous courage in one of the worst periods of judicial intimidation, and the most perfect disin- terestedness in one of the worst periods of judicial corrup- tion. Before his sarcasm and invective corrupt Judges and perjured witnesses often trembled and winced. Fitzgibbon quarrelled with Curran at the Bar, and the appearance of the Advocate in Court always excited some mark of spleen, sure to be retaliated with tenfold scorn. One day the Chancellor happened to be followed by a favourite mas- tiff into Court, and while Curran was pleading his Lordship carelessly turned away and began to pat the dog. Curran instantly stopped. There was a sudden silence. The Chan- cellor looked surprised, and haughtily exclaimed "Go on, sir !" "My lord," said Curran, "I beg a thousand pardons; I thought your Lordships were in consultation." On one occasion Lord Clonmel was so pressed by the argument, the eloquence, and the wit bf Mr. Curran, that he lost temper and called upon the Sheriff to be ready to take any one into arrest, who would be found so contemptuously presumine. to fly in the face of the Court. Mr. Curran, perceiving the twittering of a swallow actively in pursuit of flies (for like Nero's Court, so, in the presence of this Imperious Judge, scarcely a fly was to be found), in his turn called on the Sheriff to take that swallow into arrest, for it was guilty of contempt, as it had contemptuously pressed a fly in the face of the Court. The ridicule of this, and the peals of laughter which ensued, closenhe scene. In sterner moods he was grander. The hammer Came down with a heavy thud, for the smith was in earnest. His cross-examinations were the delight of everyone but their subject. His wild wit and eccentric allusions his knowledge of native habits, and his keen insight into human nature made him trium- phant in the presence of an Irish jury, and he was never more resistless than when he seemed to give way to the sportive spirit of the moment, and never nearer the detection of knavery than when he and the knave seemed to laugh together. It was then that suddenly turning on him he tore off the disguise, and in language more searching than the scourge tortured the naked perjurer into truth. A fellow of this kind was once hunted by Curran to the very verge 'of confession when he suddenly refused to answer, and on the Judges demanding the reason, he replied "he did not know what he said, the little gentleman (Curran) put him into such a doldrum." "What's that ?" asked the Judge. "Oh, my lord," replied Carran, "a doldrum is a complaint com- mon to gentlemen of the witnesa's family. It is a confusion of the head arising from a corruption of the heart.' And yet this man before whose sarcasm perjured witnesses so often trembled—under the lash of whose wit corrupt Judges at times quivered—this man on whose burning eloquence crowded and sometimes hostile Courts hung breathless in

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.
In opening the commision of assize at Galway, on Monday, the Lord Chief Justice alluded to the fact that in only 83 instances out of 360 offences had persons been made amenable.

Mr. Parnell has declined to write, unless under very ex- ceptional circumstances, letters from Kilmainham, on the ground that he objects to imposing on the Governor of the jail the unpleasant duty of reading his private letters. Early on Monday morning a six-inch metal shell was thrown into the residence of Messrs. Lucas Brothers, Dun- many, near Letterkenny. An explosion followed, demolish- ing two rooms. The inmates fortunately escaped, being in distant apartments. At Rathdowney, in Queen's County, on Saturday, the Rev. Thomas Frehan, Roman Catholic curate, was called upon to find sureties for his good behavior owing to his having made an inflammatory speech. The rev, gentleman refused to give bail, and he wAs conveyed to the county prison. It is stated by a Parsonstown correspondent that on Saturday night a desperate affray took place at Cloghan, King's county, between soldiers and a number of emergency men. An altercation took place, when it is alleged the emergency men discharged their revolvers at the soldiers, and fired several bullets in the latters' hut. Several persons have been arrested.

A report reached Athlone on Monday that the residence of Mr. John Ross Mahon, J.P., in county Roscommon, has been blown up with dynamite. The explosion occurred at three lo'clock on Sunday morning, the front and side walls being blown down, and the house made a complete wreck. Fortu- nately the family escaped without injury. A party of " Moonlighters " attacked the dwelling-house of James Cuddy,-farmer, at Newtown, county Kilkenny, at half-past three on Monday morning. Several shots were fired, the bullets lodging in the bedpost, but Cuddy escaped injury. Two men, named Long and Delaney, have been arrested on suspicion and remanded, rrending further inquiries. A report comes from Thurles, in Tipperary, of a party of " Moonlighters " being fired upon by the police, who, having received information of an intended midnight visit to the house of an obnoxious farmer, were lying in wait. One of the lawless band fell wounded—it is believed mortally—and was identified as a resident of the neighbourhood. There has been a meeting—extending over four days—of the Irish Roman Catholic hierarchy. The proceedings were, of course, private. It is stated in a Dublin paper that, among other things, the state of the country was under con- sideration, but that the prelates were unable under present critical circumstances to frame an address to the people. A committee was, 11 wever, appointed to consider the question. Mr. P. Egan admits that the sum received from the Irieh- American organisations up to February 17 reaches a total of £106,000, for "general Land League purposes." He wishes the Permanent Committee of the late Fenian Convention at Chicago to institute an audit of his accounts. Mr. R. Pigott would be a valuable member of such a body. He alleges that Mr. Egan is drawing £4,000 a year from the fund. , About one o'clock on Monday morning, a dreadful outrage was committed at Drumany, county Donegal. A regular military bombshell was thrown into a bedroom on the ground floor of the house of a farmer named Henry Lucas, which shattered the window of the parlour to pieces, arnd blew up through two storeys above, doing great damage. Fortunately no members of the family were sleeping in that part of the house, and no liNces were lost. The Government have made arrangements for the ap- pointment of three additional Sub-Commissions to deal with I the long list of cases waiting, for adjudication under the Irish Land Act in Tyrone, Armagh, and a group of smaller counties where claims for reohiction of rent have accumu- lated. These Extra Commissions will begin their work immediately after Easter, and continue regular sittings until the August holidays. A report reached Dublin on Saturday night of the at- tempted murder of a gamekeeper. It appears that a game- keeper named Boyle, in the employment of Lord Ventry, was travelling in a train between Gortatlea and Tralee, county Kerry, when a man named Keane, in the same cotp- partment, drew a revolver and discharged three shots at him, one taking effect., Boyle, in great agony, stated that the cause was that he had, at the request of some ladies' opened the carriage windows. Keane was arrested at Castleisland Railway Station. Boyle is stated to be in a serious condition. At the Cork assizes, on Monday,- forty-six young men, described as mostly farmers' sons and labourers, were indicted for treason-felony, and also for various offences alleged to have been committed by them as members of the barbarous gang known as " Moonlighters," Council for the Crown produced an affidavit, made by a sub-inspector of constabu- lary, to the effect that if the trials were deferred to the Summer Assizes important evidence would be brought forward, and Mr. Baron Dowse made an order for postpone- ment accordingly. On Saturday, the Rev. Thomas Feehan, Roman Catholic , curate of Rathdowney, Queen's county, was ordered to find sureties of the peace because of an inflammatory harangue he had delivered. It pow appears that on Thursday last his Bishop, Dr. Moran, "under the peculiar circumstances that had arisen," withdrew from him the faculties beheld except the faculty of offering the Holy Sacrifice, and further ordered from that day the Rev, gentleman's connection with the parish of Rathdowney shall cease. Father Feehan, in communicating the fact to the press, says that Dr. Moran could never have taken this step if he had not been grossly deceived and misled.

LETTER FROM MR. PARNELL. The Lord Mayor of Dublin has received the ,subjoined letter from Mr. Parnell, M.P.:—" Kilmainham Prison, March 25th, 1882. My dear Lord Mayor,-:-Will you be so kind as to add my name to the list of shareholders in the Irish Exhibition Company. It has given me the greatest pleasure to see the progress made by you towards the successful holding of an Exhibi- tion of Irish Manufactures this year, and I trust that the year 'B2 may be signalised by the result. I regret that it has not been in my power to render any practical help in your movement for the revival of home manufactures, but I do not the less anxiously watch and sympathise with the exertions of your company. The task you have set your- selves of holding the exhibition this year is one, no doubt, of great difficulty; but, nevertheless, it is better to make the attempt than to postpone the undertaking to a less favour- able time.—My dear Lord Mayor, Tours very truly, Cras. S. PARNELF. The Right lion. the Lord Mayor of Dublin."

TRADE NOTES. Following the notice of Friday last, all the employes at the Park End and New Fancy collieries, Forest of Dean, went out on strike on Monday. The Clyde shipwrights, on Monday, began work at an advance of 4d. per hour on their pay, which is now 71-d. per hour.

The mia and East Lothian Coalminers' Association have issued a notice to the various collieries that on and after Wednesday, the sth day of April, the wages of all miners will be reduced 14 per cent., and a proportionate reduc- tion will .be made on the wages of all other workers below ground. The Providence Weaving Shed, Church, which contains 500 looms, has been stopped since last Friday week, but a notice has been posted that work will be resumed as soon as a dispute between the tenant, Mr. Walsh, and the owner, Mr. Lonsdale, has been settled. The trial, which affects the lease is pending in London. The operative potters employed by Mr. Woolf, M.P., at Knottingley, Yorkshire, after striking for 26 weeks against a reduction of 10 per cent., have, through the instrumentality of Air. Owen, chairman of the Staffordshire Potteries Opera- tives' Confederation, settled their dispute, the terms of ths settlement in some instances being of the nature of a com- promise, A large number of answers have been received in reply to the circular of the Oldham Limited Liability Association and the Oldham Master Cotton Spinners', &,c., Association, and from what can be learned there is a strong disposition in many quarters to go upon short time. several largo limited companies have given in their adhesion to the movement, and it is thought that the consent of the requi- site two-thirds for a stoppage for a week at Easter will be obtained. , Representatives of Fife and Clackmannan miners on Mon- day afternoon had a conference with coalmasters at Dunferm- line respecting the reduction of 121. per cent. in wages recently notified. The coalmasters urged that the decline in the iron trade and the exceptional mildness of the winter compelled them to enforce the reduction. The conference closed with the masters' refusal to withdraw the notice. At a meeting of the council of the Amalgamated Associa- tion of Operative Cotton Spinners, on Sunday, a resolution was passed concurring in the determination of the work- people of Messrs. Stpethurst and Son, Chorley, not to resume work unless the employers agree to calculate the wages earned from the indicated length of yarn spun, and de- ciding, in the event of the threatened lock-out b:ing per- sisted in, to take all the members in the Chorley district on the funds of the association.

Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., attended a meeting of trade society representives held on Saturday afternoon, in Man- chester, in order to make preliminary arrangements for the holding of the Trade Union Congress next September. The hon. member in his address dwelt upon the measures designed for the benefit of the working classes which the Parlia- mentary Committee had promoted. He pointed out the defects in the Employers' Liability Act, which he said it was proposed to remedy, and declared that a number of useful bills, including Mr. Hugh Mason's Boiler Explosions Bill, would before this time have passed into law had it not been for "an intolerable despotism, misnamed liberty, which prevented Parliament from carrying out the wishes of the people." The meeting subsequently appointed a strong committee to make arrangements for the Congress. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE: Manchester, Wednesday. —The coal trade of this district continues extremely dull, with all descriptions of fuel except the best qualities of slack more or less a drug in the market, and the pits as a rule not working more than three to four days a week. Burgy and the common sorts of firing slack are plentiful, but best slacks are getting rather scarce. The quoted prices remain without material alteration. Coals from outside districts, especially from Derbyshire, and also from Yorkshire, are, however, being pushed in this market at very low figures. At the pit mouth the average quoted prices remain at about 88 6(1 to 9s for best coals, 63 up to 78 for second qualities, 5s to 58 Bei for common coal, 48 (11 to 5s for burgy, 3s 9d to 4s 3d for good slack, and about 3s to 3s 3d for inferior sorts. Shipping continues very quiet, and there are heavy stocks lying at both Garston and Liverpool, which are offered at exceedingly low figures. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE: Manchester, Wednesday. —The iron market here has been very quiet all through the week, and so far as prices have been tested by the limited amount of business doing they have shown a tendency in the favour of buyers. Lancashire makers of pig iron are more open to offers, and would now sell readily at 48s to 49s less 2 for delivery equal to Manchester. .For district brands very low figures are in some cases being quoted, and although makers are holding out for higher prices there are sellers of Lincolnshire iron at under 478 per ton less 2; delivered here, and of Derbyshire at about is. per ten more. Finished iron makers are easier to deal with, and although the quotations of the leading manufacturers who are still kept well employed on old orders remain at £7 per ton for bars delivered into the Manchester district, £6 17s 6cl would now have to be taken to secure new business, and some of the local makers are now quoting £0 15s per ton. The engineer- ing trades continue generally well supplied with work, and in the branches connected with marine work there is still plenty of activity. THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.,--The 3farlr-lane Express says :—" Duriug the past week there has been a short Spell of winterly weather, and high winds have pre- vailed, but the temperature again became mild towards the close of the week, a warm and soaking rain having occurred on Saturday evening, followed by a heavy gale. This rain- fall will be of great service to the spring crops, and gener- ally acceptable on the fallows. Wheat will also benefit by it. All crops continue to look wonderfully well and full of promise. Most of the provincial markets have been sparingly supplied with English wheat, and prices for finest samples ha fe been generally reported as sixpence to a shilling higher during the early days of the week; but quietness has ' characterised those held later. In London, sellers have been unable to realise any improvement. Flour has become more , difficult of sale, and in some instances less money has been accepted to effect sales. The season for malting barley may, now be considered closed, but there is not much difference. to note with regard to value. Malt is easier to buy, and oats, beans, and peas are without change. Foreign wheat off stands showed some advantage to sellers in the early part of the week in London, but on Friday Monday's rates were not generally obtainable."

MR. TENNYSON AND THE TEETOTALLERS.—Referring to a protest by the Good Tsmplare against the Poet Laureate's recent "Ode," Mr. Hellen Tennyson writes:—" My father begs to thank the Committee of the Executive of the Grand Lodge of England of Good Templars for their resolution. No one honours more highly the good work done by them than my father. I must, however, ask you to remember that the common cup has in all ages been a sacred symbol of unity, and that my father has only used the word drink in re- ference to this symbol. I much regret that it should have been otherwise understood." A GREAT CITY OF CLIFF DWELLERS.—During the past season a remarkable discovery of an ancient cliff city, sixty miles long, was made by Mr. James Stephenson, the leader of the 4rchreelogical Exploring Expedition to Mexico and Arizona, under the direction of the Smithsonian Institution. Mr. Stephenson tells the Neto York Tribune that for sixty miles along the face of a winding cliff, except where the elements had put them away, the canyon walls had been carved out like swallows' nests, and the cave dwellings ex- tended two, three, four, and sometimes five rows, one atove another. Mr. Stephenson examined this deserted city dur- ing several days, personally visiting portions distant forty- five miles from each other, and discovering with his glass that the excavations extended fifteen or twenty miles further on. By far the greater number are inaccessible, but many of the old paths, worn many inches deep by the feet of the ancients who dwelt there, are intact, and by them the ex- plorer mounted to the old dwellings. There wits a marked similatity in the form and construction of these excava- tions. There was only one aperture, which served for door, window, and chimney. The single room had an oval roof, which bore the grooves made by the flinty adzes or axes of the excavators. The method of digging or carving out these caves was disclosed by the form and direction of the grooves, which were usually parallel to each other, and several inches apart, while between, as shown by the rough surface of the stone, the remaining substance had been broken off. There were fire-places at the rear, but no place of exit for the smoke except the single aperture in front. Many of the dwellings had side or rear excavations of small size, within some of which corn-cobs and beans were found, evidently left by chance inhabitants of a later period. Near the roof of many of the caves there were mortises, projecting from which in some instances there were dis- covered the decayed ends of wooden sleepers. These were of a kind of wood not recognisable as a present growth of the locality, and unknown to the explorers. Specimens were brought away to be examined and classi- fied by naturalists. In the sides of some dwellings there were found small recesses, evidently used' as cupboards for the household utensils of the family. The substance of the cliff was tuffs., a volcanic ash, quite soft, and easily worked by the rude implements of the old builders. Upon the top of the Mesa, or table-land, above these caves, there were found large circular structures, now in ruins, but with walls to the height of 10 or 12 feet still standing. They were evidently places of worship. They were built of square stones of nearly uniform size, about 20 in. in length by 6 in. in width and 4 in. in thickness, cut from the cliff. Measurements were made of two of these structures, one of which was 100 feet and the other 200 feet in diameter, and might have held from 1,000 to 2,000 people. The in- ference that these ''ere places of worship is drawn from the fact that the Pueblos of the present day, who are fire and sun worshippers, have similar temples. No remains of altars were found, which fact is doubtless to be explained by the exposed situation and soft materialsprobably used in the construction of such furniture. The southern end of this cave city, which seemed to have been the most densely popu- ,ated, presented many evidences of art and industry. This locality is more broken, and offers a better chance for sue- cessf al resistance to the assaults of an enemy. There were found many animal forms carved out of stone. In one place there were two life-sized mountain lions, animals which are still peculiar to that region. There are also to be seen many smaller animal forms, so much worn away that it cannot be determined what they were designed to represent. Upon standing walls in this neighbourhood are many hieroglyphics, which, from their resemblance to the picture writing of the living Pueblos, may, Mr. Stephenson thinks, be partially, if not entirely, deciphered. The great aae of this city is proved by the vast accumulation of debris from the upper portion of the cliff which covers its base. In places where mountain brooks have cut their way through, the existence of one, and sometimes two, rows of cave dwellings below the surface of the debris is disclosed. Mr. Stephenson thinks that several centuries have passed since this dead city was in its prima.

div.head: TREASONABLE MANIFESTO.
div.p: A TREASONABLE MANIFESTO.

The following placard was posted throughout Dublin on Tuesday night, but was quickly torn down by the police : "Men of Dublin, a Whig Government which has placed the liberty of our oppressed people at the mercy of a few dis- reputable adventurers, and has made truth a crime in Ire- land, is now preparing to silence the voice of your represen- tives even in an alien House of Commons. This is in order that fresh scourges and heavier fetters may be forged more easily, swiftly, and silently for our crushed and bleeding country, that the wheels of the British Juggernaut may be oiled for its more convenient passage over the lives and rights of the Irish people. Let the electors of Dublin be no more deceived by false-tongued Brooks and Lyons, who have become the willing henchmen of the Government in its oppression of the people. Do the people of Dublin intend to let Brooks and Lyons vote to silence Parnell, Dillon, Sexton, Redmond, Healy, and the rest of the bravest men who have dared all English power in defence of their country? Electors of Dublin, let Mesrs. Brooks and Lyons know y•Ou are watching them next Thursday."

div.head: ANOTHER MURDER IN DUBLIN.
div.p: ANOTHER MURDER IN DUBLIN.

Another murder was committed in Dublin on Tuesday. About one o'clock in the afternoon, three men, M‘Mahon, Martin, and Brophy, went into Mrs. Dunlop's public-house, Dorset-street, and after ordering drink and sitting down in a room a few minutes, a shot was fired, immediately upon which Brophy ran out. Tie was followed and brought back, when it was found that M‘Mahon had been shot through the heart. On the floor was a six-chambered revolver fully charged. The police were called in, and on searching I Brophy found another revolver, five chambers of which were loaded, and the sixth evidently just disc.harged. M'Mahon died within five minutes after his removal. Martin, in whose possession was found a quantity of ammunition, was also apprehended, and his house In Fontenoy-street being searched, a number of rifles, bayonets, revolvers, and cartridges Were discovered. The police thereupon arrested Martin's father, twg brothers, and another man, who were in the house at the time. The Martins are compositors, but Brophy refuses to give any information about himself: The tragedy has created the greatest excitement in the city, it ,being the third in close succession attributed to Fenianism. The prisoners have been taken before the magistrates and remanded.
Women are not cruel by nature. We never heard of one thoughtless enough to step on a mouse.

One hundred .thousand Austrian troops will shortly be sent to the Balkan provinces. The Daily NeWS Vienna correspondent learns from St. Petersburg that nine soldiers of the Presbraschen regiment were arrested on Sunday, on a charge of Nihilism. Arrangements between the various cable companies are now nearly complete, by which the price of messages to America will be raised to two shillings per word. The Morning Post says recent trustworthy reports from St. Petersburg affirm that General Scobeleff has been com- pletely banished from the court, and the banquet in his honour has been abandoned. A Daily News Maritzburg telegram states that the people in Zululand are dissatisfied, and desire a settlement either by the return of Cetewayo or other means. There are com- plaints of John Dunn's conduct. An extensive smuggling conspiracy has been discovered on the part of some of the city and Federal officials at San Francisco to defraud the "United States Government, by means of opium smuggling. An explosion occurred in the granulating room of the Vulcan Po•vder Factory at San Francisco, on Tuesday. Eleven persons were killed, including six Chinese, and four others were dangerously wounded. Swarms of locusts have appeared at Larnaca, and energetic measures have been adopted to destroy them. Sir R. Bid- dulph, who is personally superintending the operations, has left for the scene of the devastation. An official print at Vienna states that the trial of Mr. Evans, ,a correspondent at Ragusa, and his fellow-pri- sobers—' a literary man named Gopevics and a citizen named Alexic "—will take place next month" before a jury. General Garibaldi landed at Palermo on Tuesday amidst the acclamations of A great concourse of people. The journals declare that nothing will be done to give to the celebration of the anniversary of the " Vespers " the appearance 4:2f a de- monstration against France. The trial of the Albanians charged with causing the death of Captain Selby will commence next week. Mr. Consul Wrench, in refutation of the argument of thQ defence that the captain's party provoked attack by trespassing, has pointed out that no law on trespass exists in Turkey. A despatch from Richmond (Virginia) announces that a great fire has occurred there, destroying the Petersburg Railroad Bridge, three tobacco factories, six tobacco stem manufactories, the Tredegar and Vulcan Ironworks, several flour mills, some kaoline works, and twenty dwelling- houses. Three persons were killed. The loss is estimated at $500,000.

The Russian official press makes a point of stating that no fewer than three regiments, of which the German Em- peror is honorary colonel, telegraphed their "warmest con- gratulations" to His Majesty on his birthday. Moreover, the further and more reassuring intelligence is published that at the Gatschina dinner the members of the German Embassy were present. THE ALLEGED BRITISH MISSION TO THE VATICAN.— The Rome Fanfulla states that Mr. Errington has hastily left Rome, haviing been summoned to London by the British Government. It adds that he is expected to return shortly, in order to resume negotiations with the Vatican, which the same journal declares are not unconnected with the eleva- tion of Dr. M'Cabe to the cardinalate. It is affirmed in a telegram from Constantinople that, notwithstanding appearances, the relations between Germany and Turkey have become less cordial. From the same source we learn that M. Tissot has reported to the French Government a serious diminution of French influence in the East, and recommended that his successor at Constantinople should be instructed to take steps with a view to the culti- vation of a more friendly feeling on the part of the Sultan towards France. Sergeant Mason, who was recently sentenced to a long term of imprisonment for attempting to shoot President. Garfield's assassin, is found to have been wrongfully con- victed. The United States Judge Advocate-General has made the discovery that the proceedings of the court•martial in Mason's case are invalid, and that he is unlawfully im- prisoned. It has been stated that at the time the sergeant fired his prisoner was so placed that he could not have possibly been touched by the bullet which was meant to put an end to his existence. On some such technical objec- tion as this Mason's trial for attempted murder has been in- validated, and he is now likely to escape with a very light punishment. DEATH OF AN OTTOMAN STATESMAN.—Ruchdi Pasha, the great Ottoman statesman, formerly Grand Vizier of Turkey, is dead. He is not known to any„of our English works which profess to give an account of the career of dis- tinguished contemporaries, but he was a man worthy of more than passing notice. Born of poor parents, he went through a process of intellectual training which gained for him in geography, mathematics, and physics the reputation of one of the greatest scholars of the country. He was also a linguist of fame and ability. We know him, perhaps, best as the Turkish plenipotentiary at the conference held in London in 1870, but for many years he has held a leading place amongst the diplomatists of Europe. LIFEBOAT DISASTER AT HONFLEIIR : Loss OF 19 LIVES. —A. lamentable disaster was, on Sunday morning, witnessed from Honfleur. A lifeboat whiclialready during the morn- ing had brought safely into port the crew of a schooner in distress, again went out in response to a signal from a sloop. The vessel was reached and the crew taken into the boat, but just as the men were taking to their oars a tremendous sea broke over the boat, entirely submerging it. On its re- appearance it was empty, and none of the occupants have since been seen. These consisted of the thirteen men who manned the lifeboat and the six sailors belonging to the sloop. 1. THE ITALIAN BUDGET.—The Italian Budget was sub- mitted to the Chamber of Deputies by Signor Magliani on Saturday. It appears that the surplus of the final estimates for 1882. which was to have been 21,500,000 lire is reduced to 17,000,000 by increased expenditure, of which 12,000,000 is set down for army purposes. M. Magliani explained that his programme was not to issue any more rents, except such as had been authorised for railway works, for which it was hoped that provision would soon be made out of the general funds, and to reduce the floating debt as much as possible. He added.the assurance that the forced currency would be abolished as soon as the Treasury had obtained a sufficient metallic reserve to withdraw the paper money from circula- tion, and the Government would do all in their power to lessen the distnrbance which must naturally accompany the change to a free currency. ATTACK ON CAPTAIN BOSA.NQUET.—A telegrain received through Reuter's Agency from Rome, states that the cir- cumstances ot a recent attack, near Cagliari, upon Captain Bosanquet, commanding Her Majesty's ironclad Northum- berland, are as follow :—At nightfall on the 22nd instant Captain Bosanquet, while walking alone in an unfrequented locality about five and a half miles from Cagliari, was at- tacked by an individual who presented a revolver at his breast. Captain Bosanquet seized the man's arm imme- diately, thus diverting the direction of the weapon, which ; was discharged without doing him any injury. A struggle ensued, during which Captain Bosanquet and and his as- sailant fell to the ground. The latter, however, succeeded in snatching from Captain Bosanquet's person his watch, a sovereign in gold, and a few pieces of silver, and afterwards made his escape. He was, however, arrested by the Italian gendarmes on the followin day, still in possession of the Nv at ch. He was found to be a young man of 22, named D'Aquila from Palermo, where he followed the trade of a barber. 'Captain Bosanquet was in plain clothes at the time of the assault. Before leaving Cagliari Captain Bosarquet sent a letter to the Journal L'avenire, expressing his thanks for the activity displayed by the authorities and the sym- pathetic feeling manifested by the inhabitants. But for the bad weather a popular demonstration would have been made in honour of the British squadron. AFGHANISTAN AND CENTRAL ASIA. The Times Gundakanduff correspoadent says :—lnforma- t ion collected from merchants as well as from news-writers leads me to the conclusion that Ameer Abdurrah4m is rapidly extending his influence and consolidating his power in Afghanistan. He has become more conciliatory, and is now

div.p: said the Chairman of the South-Eastern Railway Committee had been warned that the Government claimed the bed of the sea belcw low water mark, and for three miles beyond, and that they would use every power at their disposal in such manner as the general intel ests of the country might seem to require. THE CLOSURE.—Mr. BRIGHT resumed the debate on the Closure resolutions. He said the rule was more moderate and less stringent than he would have himself suggested, and argued that it guarded the rights of minorities better than a two-thirds majority. Large minorities could take care of themselves. He said the House was paralysed, and it was equally the interest of both parties to free Parlia- ment from the obstruction and tyranny of a small number of members who despised English opinion, and openly sought to degrade Parliament. The right hon. gentleman was followed by Col. STANLEY. He feared the resolution before the House had been dictated not merely against ob- struction but against legitimate debate, and he predicted that if the French institution, the closure, were imported it would be used as it was in France, and business would not really be advanced. Mr. O'SHAUGHNESSY supported the closure in the interests of Ireland; while Mr. NEWDEGATE looked upon the proposal as a direct attack by Mr. Chamber- lain and the caucus upon parliamentary government. The debate was continued by Sir R. Bletmerhassett, Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Mr. Mitchell Henry, and Mr. Sexton. The last-named gentleman made an impassioned and bitter attack on Mr. Bright, at the same time warning the House that, closure or no closure, the Irish party with whom he was associated would "permeate" the business of Parlia- ment in every department. As for obstruction he defiantly declared that the House had only as vet seen the fringe of Irish activity.—Shortly after twelve o'clock Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE addressed the House, and objected to the con- ditions under which the debate was conducted. The threat of a final dissolution or the resignation of the Government he regarded as an undue interference with freedom of discussion, and as furnishing a bad omen as to the uses to which the closure would be put.— The debate was wound up by Mr. Gladstone, after which the •SPEAKER put the question that the words of the proposed rule, which Mr. Marriott proposed to leave out shall stand part of the question, and at five minutes past two o'clock the House was cleared for a division. The tellers for the ayes were the Government whips, and for the noes Mr. -Marriott and Mr. Cowen. The numbers were : For Mr. Gladstone's motion 3lB • For the amendment
Majority for the Government 39 The announcement was received with tremendous cheering from the Liberal side of the House. •
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
