div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 1, 1882.

moving the tribes to elect heads or representatives, his object being to acquire information regarding the feelings of the people and to be able to communicate through such heads his own instructions. It will be recollected that the Ameer Shere All kept such representatives with him as a consultative body, and they gave him great strength. The Ameer probably awaits the arrival of the British agent, Mahomed Afzul Khan, before leaving Herat or Turkestan. Many of Ayoub's followers are returning to Afghanistan. The Mohmand Khan of Lalpura has at last gone to Cabul, and he will probably be followed by the Badshah of Kunar. The caravan trade by the Harnai route from Sibi towirds Quetta and Candahar last week was valued at nearly 30,000 rupees, and passed in perfect safety. The correspondent of the same journal at Calcutta says: —A number of rumours from Cabul have reached Lahore during the past week, and have been published by the Civil and Military Gazette. If these stories are true Herat is in a state of almost open insurrection, and the Ameer's author- ity in other parts of the country is becoming daily less. Mysterious hints, tco, are given of the arrival in Maimena of supposed Russian emissaries, who are, said to have been well received by the Governor • but no confirmation of these reports has been received by Government, nor is there any authentic news of Ayoub's arrival at Teheran. Little is known as to what is actually passing at Herat. No doubt the situation is critical, and it is quite possible a revolt may break out there, but probably no overt act of rebellion has yet occurred. Afzul Khan, who has been appointed British Agent at Cabul, goes to Simla for instructions before start- ing. He will then proceed to Cabul via Peshawur, accom- panied by an escort of one jemader, three duffadars, and 12 troopers, The Ameer is making preparations to receive him. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. _ _

A Paris telegram says:—A Vienna telegram published here states that England and France have communicated to the Powers identieal instructions, which have been forwarded to their agents in Egypt, with a view to obtain an amend- ment of the financial law lately voted by the Chambsr of Notables. The English and French diplomatic agents are instructed to request that revenues assigned for the service of the international debt and not included in the budget voted by the chamber shall be specified and guaranteed. It is added that all the Powers view these instructions favour- ably. A Cairo telegram of Tuesday's date says :—Sensational rumours have been current on the Alexandria Bourse, point- ing to the possible deposition or abdication of the Khedive, but they receive no credence in well-informed quarters, where it is represented that the assurances contained in the joint notes of England. and France guaranteeing the maintenance of his Highnes on the Throne are sufficient to deprive such reports of all value. It is understood in deplomatic circles that the negotiations with regard to Egypt which are now proceeding between the Great Powers are limited for the preseat to the discussion of clause 34 of the Organic Law, by which the service of the Egyptian Debt is alone declared to be exempt from the control of the Chamber of Notables. The English and French Govern- ments have, it is believed, proposed that the clause should be more definitely worded, and that the exemption shouid be made to apply expressly to the budgets of all provinces and administrations, the revenues of which are specially assigned to the service of the debt. RUSSIAN VOLUNTEERS FOR HERZEGOVINA. A St. Petersburg telegram says :—The Gobs publishes a letter from Odessa according to which the first detachment of volunteers, the greater part of whom are Herzegovinians, left there on the 20th inst. for Herzegovina, under the com- mand of Colonel Jovanovitch and Major Aldieff. The letter says that those of the party who have sufficient means will pay the expenses of their journey. The members of the Odessa Slavophile Committee are actively engaged in collecting donations for the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina who have been compelled to leave their homes.
Al ISGEL EA_NEOTTS.

Private Brown, Ist Lincolnshire Regiment, Aldershot, has been sentenced to five year's penal servitude for insubordina- tion towards a superior officer, and Private Doras, 2ad Sutherland Highlanders, to two years for the same offence. Three men were suffocated on Monday in a coal pit at Bitton, near Bristol. The pit; belonging to Messrs. Bain, was on Saturday night discovered to be on fire, and three men named Cook (father and son) and Walters, upon de- scendinz an old shaft on Monday morning to suppress it, were suffocated.

A very serious stabbing case was investigated at Shef- field on Monday. The prisoner, a man named Black, quarrelled with a Peter Quinn in a public house. He then left, but waited about till Quinn had left, and be then stabbed him several times, turning round the knife whilst it was in the wound. He was committed for trial.

In the churchyard of Manghold, near Ramsey, Isle of Man, there was a subsidence of land, which laid bare frag- ments of coffins and a quantity of human remains. Mines have been worked at some distance beneath the surface, and it is supposed that the propping timbers have given way. An address expressing the regret of the community in the Isle of Man was presented on Tuesday to Sir H. B. Loch on his retirement from the governorship of the island, to which his Excellency responded. He attributed the progress of the island rather to the constitutional sys- tem under which it was governed, than to anything that he had done.

Most unexpected tidings of the safety of a long missing crew have reached Liverpool. The Fleetwood schooner Richard Swarbrick left the Mersey at the beginning of August last, for Plymouth, and vessel and crew were after- wards unheard of till Monday. It appears that the schooner sank in the Channel, but the men escaped and were picked up by an Austrian barque. They are now in Jamaica. A very attractive fancy fair was on Tuesday opened at St. George's Hall—which has been transformed for the occasion into the appearance of a Chinese mart—in aid of the reduction of the debt on the Lancashire Independent College, Whalley Range. The Mayor of Liverpool, Pro- fessor Scott, and Mr. Clarke Aspinall took part in the ceremony. A correspondent learns from an official of a leading rail- way company that the terms of an arrangement for the adoption of a parcels pest were concluded between the rail- way companies and the Post Office authorities nearly two years ago, but were not ratified by the Treasury. The delay in resuming the negotiations was mainly due to the death of one of the principal officials of the Post Office. The railway cempanies have only now received the new propo- sals, the terms of which differ from those originally agreed upon, and they will give early and full consideration thereto. A. RAID ON GAMBLERS.—Twenty-one men from villages surrounding Bradford were before the Bradford West Riding magistrates, on Monday, on a charge of gambling on Sun- day. The men were part of a gang numbering over .100, who held regularly organised meetings for gambling, and upon whom a large body of police made a raid on Sunday. Twenty-one captures were made, and one man, who jumped into the canal, was almost drowned. Sentences of two and three months' imprisonment were passed. AN ENGLISH TENANT FARMERS' MANIFESTO.—FoIIowing closely upon a similar demonstration in Cardiganshire, a " manifesto " has been issued to the tenant farmers of Car- marthenshire. It sets forth that rents are generally from 10 to 15 per cent. too high; that a variety of circumstances had combined to reduce the vast majority of -tenant farmers to the verge of bankruptcy; that no person should take a hold- ing the tenant of which has given notice to his landlord for reduction in rent, for repairs or improvements, nor any hold- ing from which a tenant is expelled by reason of game; and that no tenant farmer shoulu attend, bid, or take any land offered for rent or public sale.—Pall Gazette. The World says the approaching marriage of the Duke of Westminster with his own cousin has put the gossiping quidnuncs into a flutter of excitement. The future bride is the Hen. Katherine Cavendish, youngest daughter of Lord and Lady Chestam, and sister of the second Countess of Leicester and of Lady Lyttleton. She is 24 years of age,, while the Duke has attained his 59th year. The brother of the bride recently married Lady Beatrice Grosvenor, youngest daughter of the Duke and of the late beautiful and popular Duchess of Westminster, so that by this union the Duke will find himself brother-in-law to his daughter and his son-in-law. An extraordinary scene was witnessed on Monday in the well-known chapel in Tavistock-place, in which Archdeacon Dunbar was lately accustomed to conduct his ministrations. The chancel had been cleared for a prize fight between two well-known pugilists, ropes and stakes being fixed, while all the customary professional paraphernalia was called into requisition. The combat, which was characterised by inci- dents of considerable brutality, went on for some time before the police forced the doors and arrested one of the princi- pals, together with twelve men charged with aiding and abetting, all of whom have been brought up at liow-street and remanded.

BRITISH COLONIES ..iND THE TRADE WITH FRANCE.— Representations having been made by the Executive Coun- cil of the British and Colonial Union to the Earl of Kimber- ley on the subject of the exclusion of British colonies from participation in the most-favoured-nation treatment in the recent Anglo-French commercial convention, his Lordship's Secretary has replied to the following effect:—" His Lord- ship is informed that the French Government declines to consider the claim of the British colonies to share in the most favoured nation treatment, on the grounds—first, of the great diversity and frequent changes in some of the colonial tariffs; second, of the high duties chargeable on French goods upon their introduction into some of the colonies; and third, on account of the Customs autonomy of some of the colonies, and the inability of Her Majesty's Government to bind them."

The Princess Louise, Mr., Mrs., and the Misses Gladstone, visited Harrow on Saturday, and were received with cheers by the students, headed by their volunteer corps. After taking lunch with the head master (Dr. Butler), they pro- ceeded to the speech room, where the boys sang their school hymns. Mr. Gladstone, in acknowledging the welcome, said the first 12 or 13 years of his official life were passed under the leadership of three distinguished Harrow men— Sir Robert Peel, Lord Aberdeen, and Lord Palmerston. He urged the boys to avail themselves earnestly of the oppor- tunities they now enjoyed, the value of which they would never know until they became things of the past. The Princess Louise, through Dr. Butler, expressed her high ap- preciation of the welcome offered to her. PATRONAGE IN THE CHURCH.—Mr. LeathatE'S bill to prohibit the common sale of patronage in the Church of England was printed on Tuesday. The preamble states that great scandals have arisen and the interests of religion and of the Church of England have been injuriously affected by the common sale of patronage, and it is expedient to render next presentations and advowsons of benefices inalienable except under certain conditions, and to make other amend- ments in the law relating to ecclesiastical patronage. It proposes that the sale of any limited interest in advowsons shall be void, except in the case of any marriage settlement and in certain other cases. It proposes to make the aliena- tion of the fee simple of advowsons also void, with certain exceptions. It gives power to patrons to transfer advowsons to Queen Anne's Bounty, and for the value of an advowson to be charged on the benefice. The governors of Queen Anne's Bounty may be compelled to purchase the fee simple of an advowson, but no lesser interest, and for this purpose they are to have borrowing powers in connection with the Treasury. CONFERENCE OF LATTER DAY SAINTS.—The half-yearly conference of the Church of the Latter Day Saints in Man- chester was held in the Hulme Town Hall on Sunday. There were three services held during the day, and each was largely attended. At the morning service the statistical re- port was read by Elder Brown' president of the conference, and it showed that there were 463 members and officers in the Manchester cotiference, and that during the year 85 had been baptised, 73 had emigrated,, seven had been excom- municated, and five had died. Several elders afterwards addressed the meeting. At the afternoon service addresses were delivered by Bishop Whitney and by Elder Stayner, editor of the Milennial Star, the official organ of the Mormon European Mission. Several strangers were present at the meeting, and one person who attempted to interrupt the proceedings was promptly ejected. In the evening the conference was addressed by Apostle Carrington, the presi- dent of the European Mission. CHARGE AGAINST A CLERGYMAN.—An extraordinary affair Is reported from Worksop. About Christmas the Rev. A. Willis, a Church of England clergyman, became princi- pal of the Worksop school, and on several occasions offici- ated at the local churches. Mr. Forrest, a leading tradesman in the town, dissatisfied with the chastisement of 'bis boy, who was a pupil. under Mr. Willis, made enquiries, and as- certained that the rev, gentleman had previously lived at , Farnham, Surrey, where, it was asserted, his transactions had been of a questionable character. Mr. Forrest obtained a quantity of evidence, and contemplated the exposure of Mr. Willis, but in the meantime the Surrey police authori- ties, having ascertained the whereabouts of the rev, gentle- man, forwarded a warrant charging him with having obtained money under false pretences to the local police superintendent, by whom he was apprehended on Saturday. SALTATION ARMY RIOT AT CHESTER. On Sunday a , serious collision occurred between a body f the Chester Salvation Army and the Irish population of the district known as Boughton, into which the Salvation Army had not previously penetrated. The officers of the Army gave in- timakion to the police before marching that they were going into Boughton, the Irish quarter, in order to beat up their converts, and several constables were instructed to *serve order. The members of the Army left the Pavilion Rink, their head-quarters, at ten o'clock in the morning. In the meantime the Catholic population, having heard of their coming, turned out en masse armed with cudgels and stones, and carrying flags of various kinds. The police advised the Salvationists not to proceed in view of the threatening aspect of affairs, but they did so nevertheless. The Irish received them with shouts and a volley of rubbish, threatening them with further violence if they proceeded. The Army en- deavoured to proceed, when a fierce fight ensued, and the Salvationists, who were unarmed, were roughly handled. Stones and bricks vere thrown, and sticks were freely used. The police did all that was possible to prevent the violence of the mob. Miss Captain lllconbridg,e, in command of, the Salvation Army at Chester, was struck by a stone on the temple and had to be carried into a neighbouring house, where she was attended to by Dr. Roberts. Sergeant Price, of the Chester police' received a heavy blow on the mouth with a stone. Several ether persons received severe injuries before the riot terminated. In the afternoon the Irish again congregated and were marching about a thousand strong to storm the Rink, when Mr. Fenwick, the chief constable of Chester, stopped the ringleaders, and after a brief parley happily succeeded in inducing them to return.
Two children were on Wednesday burnt to death in a house in Hampstead-road, London. The Steamer Assyrian A.l.march left the Thames on Satur- day for New York with Jumbo on board.
The Right Hon. W. E. Baxter, after a tour of scveral months.in India, has resumed his place in Parliament.
A violent gale swept over the greater part of the country during Saturday and Sunday, doing much damage, hut the loss of only one life is reported.
The memorial praying .for the reprieve of Dr. Lamson on the ground of his alleged insanity was presented to the Home Secretary on Wednesday. _ . _
There was a prize fieht for 115 a side at Strawberry Hill, London, on Wednesday, of which the police knew nothing. Another, arranged for Surbiton, was watched, and could not come off.

Mr. Samuel Morley's action in the Bradlaugh case has been condemned by the Bristol Radical Association, and in consequence of their action the hon. member intends to meet his constituents for the purpose of eliciting their opinions on the subject. A man named Jackson, described as a phrenologist and minister of a sect called the Gospel Band, has been corn-1 mated for trial at Nottingham, charged with criminall3i assaulting a girl attending Ws chapel. There are several charges pending against the prisoner, all of them of a shock- ing character, The experiment of sixpenny books is next to be tried with two editions where the interest is artistic. There have already been so many cheap editions of Washington Irving that we may assume that Messrs. Macmillan and Co., in their promised sixpenny issues of "Old Christmas" and " Bracebridge Hall," are thinking mainly of the more than 100 original illustrations designed by Mr. Randolph Calde- cott, and engraved by Mr. J. D. Cooper. THE FINCHLEY MURDER —John Baker, professional " burglar, was again brought up at Highgate Police Coart, on Thursday, on the charge of murdering Enoch Clarke, whose' body was found in a wood at Finchley. Evidence was given which clearly connected the prisoner with several burglaries in Finchley and the neighbourhood, and several of his corn-1 panions testified that he had gone out with Clarke and returned alone, and had accounted for Clarke's absence by stating that he had been apprehended by a patrol. The case was adjourned. In giving judgment at Liverpool, on Thursday, at the close of the inquiry as to the loss of the steamer Ballina, the Wreck Commissioner passed a severe censure upon Mr. C. Pollexfen, the managing owner of the vessel. Mr. Rothery found that the vessel was overladen when she started on her last voyage, and that Mr. Polloxfen was greatly to blame both for the loss of the vessel and of the lives of those on board, as he had ample warning from the first that the ship was an unsuitable one. He was ordered to pay £l5O towards the costs of the inquiry. THE WORKINGTON MYSTERY. The youth Harrison, charged with the murder of Lucy Sands, was brought be- fore the magistrates at Workington on Saturday, and again remanded. One witness said that on the day the body was found he remarked to the prisoner that it was strange it should have lain so long on the public road, to which the , prisoner replied, with a wink, "I knew the body was lying there a long time since. I knew from the first." Another witness spoke to the prisoner having three weeks after the girl was missed stated that he knew where she was, that "she was all right, and be knew all about her ;" and a third witness deposed to having been told by Harrison that he thought Sands had gone to Preston. On Wednesday night a public meeting, under the patron- age of the National Patriotic Association, was held in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester. Sir Robt. Peel, after denounc- ing the foreign policy of the Government, said the present Ministry could not rule Ireland by constitutional means, and 80 they set to work to gag and coerce the nation. Mr. Gladstone sought to ride roughshod over the liberties of the people. He could not control the independence of the House of Lords, and he tried to insult it; he .could not con- trol the liberties of the House of Commons, so he sought to gag it. Resolutions condemning the policy of the Govern- ment at home and abroad were passed. FALL PROM A THEATRE GALLERY.—ShortIy after ten on Monday night an accident, which it is feared, may prove fatal, occurred at the Prince of Wales Theatre, Birmingham. Mr. Wilson Barrett's company had commenced an engage- ment in "Proof," and there was a very large audience, especially in the gallery, which was crowded. Towards the close of the performance, Thomas Pope, aged 27, cooper, Holiday-street, who was at the back of the stage gallery, endeavoured to get a seat, hut in the attempt met with opposition, and the result was that he rolled over the heads of the closely-packed audience and thence over the gallery ledge, falling against the next tier—the boxes. Pope re- ceived very serious injuries, and was taken to the Queen's Hospital.

On Saturday afternoon a free library for Ashton-under- Lyne was opened by Mrs. Ely Andrew, wife of the Mayor of that borough. The library contains at present 3,900 volumes, and of this number upwards of 2,000 have been purchased by means of a bequest of £570 made by the late Mr. G. Heginbottom. Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., has also presented 1,000 volumes, and the Earl and Countess of Stamford and Warrington have promised to contribute 100 volumes each. At a public meeting which was held after the opening ceremony an address commemorative of the event was presented to Mrs. Andrew. Resolutions were also passed recording the deep sense of the inhabitants of Ashton- under-Lyne of the generosity of the late Mr. Heginbottom, tendering thanks to Mr. Hugh Mason and other donors of books, and In the committee who had carried out the work of forming the library. THE PECULIAR PEOPLE.—On Saturday, in the Court for Crofin Cases Reserved, the case of the Queen v. Morby was heard. In this case the prisoner was convicted before Mr. Justice Hawkins, at the Central Criminal Court, of the man- slaughter of his child, a boy of the age of eight, who re- sided with his parents at Woolwich, the charge against him being that he, being one of a sect known as the "Peculiar People," did not provide his son with medical care but trusted in prayer and anointment, in accordance, as alleged by the prisoner, with the epistle of St. James, v. 14. The jary found the prisoner guilty of "manslaughter," and Mr. Justice Hawkins thereupon reserved these questions for the opinion of this court—First, was there any evidence that the life of the child would have been prolonged for any period of time, however short, if the prisoner had callectin and pro- vided medical aid, or in other words, was the death accelera- ted by his breach of duty? and secondly, whether, assuming the death was thus caused, was the prisoner guilty of man- slaughter !—Tho court quashed the conviction. THE RECENT DARING BURGLARY AT CORWE.N% The story of the recent daring burglary at a farmer's residence, near Corwen, has had a somewhat singular sequel. The money which was %stolen, amounting to over £2,000, has been discovered in an out-building in the farm premises, having, it is believed, been placed there by the thief or thieves since the offer of a £lO reward. Taffy in this case may have been a welshman, but it is pretty evident that he was no thief. No enterprising burglar or cracksman would dream of giving up his plunder in such a manner, especially when it is remembered that the great bulk of it was in gold, and, therefore, not traceable. It is more likely that some practical joke has been played on the owner, of the money, who could never be brought to put his savings into a bank, having no confidence in such institutions. By this time probably Mr. Evans has seen reason to conclude that there are worse places than banks wherein to deposit one's for- tune.

THE MURDER OF A Bo Y AT SEA.—The hearing of a case against Osmond Otto Brand and Frederick Rycroft, skipper and third hand on board the smack Rising Sun, charged with the murder of the apprentice, William Pepper, on the high seas, on the 20th December last, was concluded on Tuesday before the Hull stipendiary. Evidence was given showing that, on the sth of January, Brand reported to the Hull police that while they were on fishing ground 120 miles off Spurn Point, Pepper was knocked off the smack by the foresail.—Joseph Pepper, father of the murdered lad, said the same story was told to him as to the Hull police. Brand, when he told him, stood him a glass of grog.—Ser- geant Harvey said the rest of the crew denied that the lad had been ill-treated.—The Chief-constable said the witness Drench first told him of the affair, and when his statement was read over to Brand at the police office the latter replied, "It's false. There's others in it besides me." After some formal evidence, the case for the prosecution was closed. Both prisoners were committed for trial on the capital charge. An endeavour is being made to remove the case to the Central Criminal Court for trial. MiS6ING Giuns.—No information has yet been received as to the whereabonts of Mary Seward, aged fourteen years, who has been missing since April 13th of last year, and Eliza Carter, aged thirteen years, who left her home on the 18th of last January, and has not since been heard orby her friends, his remarkable that both gitls resided in West- road, West Ham—Seward at No. 98, and Carter at No. 25 and it has been ascertained that in the eastern part of the metropolis, including West Ham and Leytonstone, a suspi- cious gang of foreigners have been going about, no one can say on what business. The conclusion arrived at by parties engaged in the work of tracing the whereabouts of the mis- sing girls is that they have been abducted by the foreign agents of an infamous trade to the Continent, and that their fate will never be known. A reward of £25 has been offered by Government for information respecting Eliza Carter, but in addition to that a benevolent lady has now guaranteed a further sum of £5O for the discovery of the girl. Govern- ment has offered a reward of £25 in the case of Mary Seward, and her afflicted father has added £lO to that sum. The police authorities at West Ham have done their best in these distressing cases; but there is a feeling that the in- quiries have been too much localised, and that sufficient publicity has not been given to the facts. THE ROYAL MARRlAGE.—According to the most recent arrangements, the marriage of Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, with the Princess Helen of Waldeck-Pyrmont will be celebrated at St. George's Chapel, Windsor, on Thursday, April 27. The Princess is expected to leave for England on or about the 18th of April, and will remain at Windsor Castle as the guest of Her Majesty until the day of the ceremony. The bridesmaids will be Lady Gertrude Russell, youngest daughter of the Duke -of Bedford' Lady Mary Campbell, sixth daughter of the Duke of Argyll : Lady Seymour, third daughter of the Marquis of Conyngham ; Lady Alexandrina Louisa Mande Vane Tempest, only daughter of the Marquis of Lonhnderry ; Lady Florence Beatrice Anson, eldest daughter of the Earl of Lichfield ; Lady Eva Sarah Louisa Granville, only daughter of the Earl of Warwick; Lady Anne Catherine Sybil Lindsay, sister of the Earl of Crawford and B dcarres ; and Lady Florence Mary Bootle Wilbraham, second daughter of the Earl of Latham. The Archbishop of Canterbury will per- formsthe ceremony, assisted by the Bishops of London, Oxford, Worcester, and Winchester. It is expected that the best men of the Royal bridegroom will be the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Connaught. The bride will be given away by her father.

Mr. Shell, formerly member for Athlone, is likely to iveorne the popular candkiate for county Meath. It is stated that six warrants are out agninst Iriob mem- bers of Parliament, none of ‘vhom will visi;. Ireland du! int; the Easter recess.

Ihe :umnal Oxford and Cambridge chess match was played on Thursday, in London—seven players on each side—with this result—Cambridge, 7 ; Oxford, 51. The Duke of Albany is stilr confined to his room at Men- tone, and it is said that some of the preparations for his marriage on April 27th have been countermanded. . The Freeman's Journal understands that Dr. Nulty, Roman Catholic Bishop of Meath, has refused to attend the Lords' Committee to give evidence on the working of the Land Act.
The townspeople of Tavistock, the birthplace of Sir Francis Drake, have determined to erect a statue to Drake's memory. The Duke of Bedford has himself offered to pre- sent the statue to the town.

It is stated that Mr. Irvines entire staff at present em- ployed at the Lyceum Theatre, reaches the extraordinary number, considering the size of the house and the plays put upon the stage, of 600. Mr. David Jones is to play his old character of Perkin Middlewick in "Our Boys" at the Strand Theatre, Loudon, on May Ist, which wid he his 1,363 rd appearance in the character.

Mr. Thomas Watson, of Horse Carrs, Rochdale, is about t) present to the Committee of the Rochdale Infirmary, for the purposes of that institution, more commodious premises than they now hold. The value of the gift is about £5,000. The inquest on the young man M'Mahon, the victim of the most recent murder in Dublin, was concluded mf Thurs.: day. The verdict of the jury was to the effect that they had no evidence to show by whom the deceased was shot. The town clerk of Oldham has been instructed by two committees of that body to make inquiries with a view to the council insuring its outdoor servants against accident, so as to meet claims under the Employers' Liability Act. Mr. John Bright, having been requested by the Good Templars to support "local option" and a stringent Sun- day closing law for England, writes that the demands are in advance public opinion, and the Government is not likely to submit them to Parliament.

The charges preferred against a number of persons for assaulting and otherwise ill-treating members of the Salva- tion Army at Chester, a few days ago, were heared before the magistrates of that city on Thursday, but on the appli. cation of the prisoners' solicitor the cases were adjourned till to-day. Mr. Dillon, M.P., has, through the medical officar of Kil- mainhain gaol, made "a formal protest against being detained in prison." He says he is in much worse health than when be was arrested in October. It is stated that Mr. Forster has intimated that the Lord Lieutenant declines to discharge Mr. Dillon. At the Central Criminal Court on Thursday, James Casey, aged 20, confectioner, was again put upon his trial, the jury having disagreed last session, for the wilful murder of John Frederick Willmore, on the Thames Embankment; bet the evidence showed that he did not arrive on the scene until after the murder was committed, and the jury returned a verdict of not guilty. The Manchester Chamber of Commerce on Thursday morning received a letter from the India Office, stating that Lord Rartington had received a telegram from India to the effect that the remission of the Indian cotton duties came into force on the 10th inst. All cotton leaving after that date will be free of duty. A telegram from New York says :—Despatches, from the districts inundated by the overflow of the Mississippi con- tinue to report severe losses and great destitution awing the inhabitants. The Ralston cotton gin, in Tensas garish, Louisiana, has been swept away, 120 refugees perishing in the catastrophe. The gin was one of the largest in the State, and at the time of ahe occurrence was crowded with negroes.... • _ _

At Oldham, on Thursday, a serious charge was preferred against Richard Higham, formerly a police-constable. On the 11th Higham received from a woman named Marlon a gold necklet which had been taken from Mrs. Whittaker, landlady of the Dog and Partridge Inn. Mrs. Whittaker reported the loss, and the police were questioned, but all, including Higham, denied all knowledge of it. However, he subsequently said he received it I)ut forgot all about it. He was fined 20s. and costs.

A young lady named Minnie Darwell, daughter of John Damell, veterinary surgeon practicing at Leigh, poisoned herself by taking a dose of aconite on Thursday morning, it is believed through jealousy, having, it is said, seen her lover last night in company with two young ladies. De- ceased, who was eighteen years of age, was an accomplished girl, and much esteemed by a large circle of friends. On Thursday Mrs. Vernon, wife of Joseph Vernon, junr., farmer, Buerton, near Audlem, Cheshire, died from shocking injuries received on the previous night. The deceased lady was retiring to bed. when her night-dress caught fire from the candle, and she ran screaming downstairs. A waggoner happened to hear her cries and wrapped his coat round her, thus extinguishing the flames. Medical assistance was ob- tained, but the deceased never rallied from the shock to the system and the burns. A telegram from Athens says :—The budget for 1882 estimates the revenue at 66,841,560 drachmas, showing in increase of 17,790,500 drachmas over the previous year The expenditure is estimated at 67,854,786, the deficiency being, therefore, 1,013,328. As the government intend im- proving communications and increasing the navy, they con- template contracting on advantageous terms a loan of 60,000,000 drachmas. The Chamber of Deputies has com- menced the debate on the address.

A THIRD MunnEn IN IRELAND. A Tralee telegram states that as Mr. J. E. Herbert, of Killernherna, was pro- ceeding home from Castle Island he was shot dead. Mr. Herbert after attending the Castle Island Petty Sessions, left the town shortly before six. When half way to his home, which is two miles distant, be was shot by a rifle, one bullet lodging in his breast, and another passing through the hand. Sub-inspector Davies, who was following him, found the body, but life was extinct. THE LORDS' COMMITTEE ON THE LAND ACT. Mr. Litton, one of the members of the Irish Land Commission, was examined on Thursday before the Select Committee of the House of Lords on the Land Act. He gave evidence in favour of the extension of the purchase clauses, but de- clined, we believe, to answer questions bearing on the judicial administration of the fair rent clause. The com- mittee adjourned for the Easter recess until the 25th of April, when Mr. Justice O'Hagan will be examined. The report of the committee will, it is believed, be presented early in May.—Standard.

THE BRADLAUGH CASE.—The judges of the Queen's Bench Division on Thursday decided to issue judgment in the csse of Clarke v. Bradlaugh. The action, which was tried some months ago, was brought to recover a £5OO penalty tram the defendant for having sat and voted in the House of Commons without having taken the oath prescribed by law. A rule absolute for a new trial was subsequently obtained, but this was set aside by the Court of Appeal. Upon this the case reverted back to the Queen's Bench justices, who on Thursday directed the money to be paid into court within fourteen days. Mr. Bradlaugh will carry the case to the Lords; and, pending the decision there, the question of costs is reserved. An accident occurred to a hunting party on the Great Northern Railway near Ingestre on Thursday. The Meynell hunt was to have had its last run of the season, and was joined by a contingent of the North Staffordshire hunt on the occasion, a special train being chartered from Mickleover to Ingestre, to convey the party to the meet. Near the latter place the train ran off the line. Cnnsider- able damage was done to the rolling stock, several horse- boxes were turned over and smashed into splinters, three valuable horses being killed, and two members of the party were seriously injured and others much hurt.

LIBMIATIONISTS AND PENDING LEGISLATION.—A numer- ously attended meeting of Liberal members of Parliament favourable to religious equality was held on Wednesday afternoon in one of the committee-rooms of the House of Commons, Mr. H. Richards presiding, for the purpose of considering the many. bills upon ecclesiastical subjects now before Parliament, and generally the policy to be in future pursued in connection with such questions. After the meeting had considered a number of bills and the course to be taken in respect to them, it was resolved that intimation should be made to the Government that opposition would be offered to such measures as the Augmentation of Benefices Act Amendment Bill. It was decided that op- position to Mr. Stanhope's Patronage Bill should be con- tinued, and that Mr. Leatham's bill on the same subject should be supported. The Cemeteries Bill received the warm support of the meeting, and it was further agreed to appoint a standing committee to secure united party action on the part of the friends of religious equality in regard to ecclesiastical questions. The committee so appointed con- sists of Messrs. Dillwyn, Baxter, Illingworth, and E. A. Leathatn. A telegram says :—The division on the Closure was taken amidst a scene of great excitement. The Speaker put the question at 2-5, naming Lord Richard Grosvenor and Lord Kensington as Government tellers, and Mr. Marriott and Mr. Cowen tellers for the noes. The members im- mediately filed into the respective lobbies, and by 2-9 the House was cleared. Mr. Arthur Arnold was the first Liberal to re-enter the House, and Mr. Gibson the first Conserva- tive. As the Liberals came back they filled the benches on the right hand of the Speaker, and the majority was" told " in the unusually qnick time of nine minutes. The Conserva- tives were still coming through, and there was a faint hope on the part of the Opposition that they bad won. At 2-19 Mr. Gladstone was placed in possession of the numbers who had supported the Government, and Sir W. Harcourt almost im- mediately afterwards came from behind the Speaker's chair ' and informed him that the " noes " were 279. There was a smile of satisfaction on the Prime Minister's countenance as the news was told him. In another minute the clerks at the table were officially informed of the votes polled on each side, and amid deafening cheering Lord R. Grosvenor was given the papers. Loud and prolonged cheering went forth from the Liberal benches when it was found that the majority for the Government was 39, followed by the counter cheers, though less loud, from the Conservative benches. About 35 Home Rulers, including Mr. O'Connor Power and Mr. M'Coan, voted in the minority, and in the same lobby were Mr. Walton and Sir Edward Watkin. Mr. Storey, and Mr. Gourley voted with the Government, as well as the moderate Home Rulers and the Irish Liberals. An immense crowd in the Palace Yard cheered loudly as members emerged from the House. div.head: CAPTURE OF A NIHILIST LEADER.
div.p: CAPTURE OF A NIHILIST LEADER.

The Standard Berlin correspondent telegraphs: I learn from St. Petersburg that an important capture has been made by the police cf that city, though the news of the occurrence has up to the present been kept as secret as possible, and has not been pnblished in the Russian news- papers. The prisoner is one of the Nihilist leaders, and is affirmed to be the chief of the Executive Committee. He has been identified as one of the persons connected with the construction of the mine in Little Garden-strasse, through which street the late Czar was expected to pass on his return from a review to the Winter Palace. The project failed because the Emperor returned by a different.route.

ALLEGED FENIAN PLOTS IN LONDON. It is stated that information of an alariqing character has reached some of the authorities with reference to alleged Fenian designs in London. The police force at the docks has been increased to 600 men, who mount duty soon after dusk. All the entrances to the docks are specially guarded by picked reliable policemen, with the addition of mounted patrols. In addition to these precautions, the water-way and the shipping in the docks are watched by special police in galleys throughout the night. It is stated that the secret information which reached the authorities before the recent outbreak of fire, stating that some serious designs were con- templated at the docks, did not point to Messrs. Kirkaldy's engineering works as the place where the conflagration might be expected, but to Messrs, Bell, Burt, and Hayward's place for the pickling and dry,ing of railway sleepers. Had the conflagration occurred there, it is stated that the fire would have been most disastrous, and in all possibility the Volun- teers' Armoury, in the confusion which would have ensued, might have been easily rifled. Over this place, however, a special guard was kept that night, and this, it is believed, may have „prevented an incendiary fire at that spot. The authorities are reticent as to the full grounds for all the extra precautions, but it is stated among the officials that one of the chief parts in the plot, according to the information received, is that it was intended to blow the dock tunnel up with dynamite. If such a thing as this had been accom- plished, the loss of life and destruction of property must have been serious. The dock tunnel is about half a mile in length, through which the railway runs to North Woolwich. It branches off near to the Customs House Dock, and runs under the docks to Silvertovrn. The docks over the railway tunnel are 401 t. deep in water, and it is alleged that it was the Fenian intention to blow it up about midway. The voliime of water would have been terrific, and had such a plan been carried out, as the country lies low, thousands of families sleeping unconsciously in their beds must have been inun- dated and drowned.

div.head: RUSSIAN REVOLUTIONISTS IN LONDON.
div.p: RUSSIAN REVOLUTIONISTS IN LONDON.

An address" to the English people," signed "Vera Zas- soulitch," and " Peter Lavroff " was issued in London on Saturday. It opens thus: "The public prints have told you of political trials in Russia, and of the monstrous judg- ments daily pronounced in her courts. But they have told you nothing of the cruel sufferings of the condemned ; and the victims whose names are recorded by them are but a frac- tion of the crowds that go to their doom in darkness and silence. Before the vast and ever-widening discontent of the Russian people, authority in Russia is terror-stricken and amazed; and it lays hands by tens of thousands on our youth, and sends them, men and women alike, into hopeless banishment. The deserts in the north of the empire, from the dreary wastes round the White Sim to the frozen shores of Eastern Asia, are scattered over with bands of exiles, the flower of the Russian race. . . . They have to endure not only the moral tortures of isolation and inactivity, but the physical pangs of hunger and cold. There is scarcely a means of livelihood that is not denied them; and although to each the State allots a pittance for his support-12s. a month if he is nobly born, is. a month if he is not—there are of late so many of them that it is never paid until long overdue. Month after month goes by, and many an exile dies for lack of bread before he has received a single farthing." The address then states that " money alone is needed that much suffering may be spared and many suf- ferers may be saved," and it adds : " To raise it, and after- wards distribute it among our prisoners, we have formed a Red Cross Society of the People's Will. It bears no part whatever in our war against authority. Its relation to the revolutionary party is that of the Red Cross Society of Geneva to an army in the field. There is only one difference —that the Red Cross Society of the People's Will shares in each and every one of the dangers of the force it would succour and relieve.",

ST. HELENS BUTCHERS HEAVILY FINED. At the :st. Helens Police. Court, on Monday' before ! Meesrs. W. l'ilkii-gtou ae.l Willis, James Goes, butcher, Doka-et., NV:IS charged with ;eiying haef in his shop unfit for sale, and also with having beef in the back yard of his pre- mises in preparation for sale, the some being unfit for human food.—Defendant, who was represented by Mr. Thomas, pleaded guilty to the first charge and not guilty to the latter.—Mr. J. 0. Swift said he appeared on behalf of the Corporation of St. Helens to prosecute, under the 117th sec- tion of the Public Health Act. The 11,3 th also applied to the case, and said that any medical officer or inspector of nuisances nosy inspect any animal, carcase, or meat ex- posed for sale or deposited in any place, intended for the food of man. The meat in questio'n was destroyed under an order obtained on Tuesday last. The Act went on to say that the person who owned the meat was liable to a penalty not exceeding £2O for any piece of meat, flesh, or fish ; or, in default, not exceeding three months' imprisonment. On the 14th instant Mr. Thomas Coughtrey, the meat inspector, received a message from his wife when be came in from his rounds, and in consequence he went at once to the defen- dant's shop and found two pieces of meat and a cow's head —apparently from forty to fifty pounds of meat—on the front board, an ticketed the price of good ordinary beef- -101 a pound. The inspector saw it was unfit for food, and asked if there was any more meat of the same kind. Goss at that time was not in, but his wife was, and she said there was more in the back yard. He saw it, and then went for a cart. In the meantime Goss returned, when some conver- sation took place between them. The defendant then made admissions about the animal, and among other things said he at first was doubtful about the cow being good. He believed the circumstance that Coughtrey was sent for would be urged upon their worships in mitigation,. But Mr. Couelitrey was not obliged to go at the beck and ell' of all the butchers to see if, their meat was right; butchers were supposed to he practical men, and when the inspector was sent for Goss had committed the offence. It was admitted by Goss that the beef was bought by him and another butcher from a place at Parr, and if he had any doubts about it he ought to have sent for the inspector before it was dressed. Besides that Mr. Coughtrey noticed a few pieces in the shop, so that someone must have taken a few pounds away. He would call before them a slink butcher who dealt in very infeiior kind of meat, and he would say that he found the cow lying dead on a farm, in conclusion, he said that St. Helens a short time ago had a lot of bad meat in its midst, but action was taken against the offenders, and the town bad in consequence been comparatively free.. The present case was a bad one, and he asked for a heavy penalty.—Thomas Coughtrey, meat inspector, said that on the 14th instant, in consequence of what his wife told him he went down to Goss's shop and found on the front board a portion of the hind quarter ticketed!, 10d. a pound. There were two pieces in the shop and a head banging outside. The meat was soft and flabby and unfit for food. Mrs. Goss came into the shop, and he asked her if she had any more. She said there was a portion in the back yard. He found there the fore-quarter and a portion of the hind-quarter, and the offal. It was dressed for sale, and was unfit for food. He marked it and went away for a cart. When he got back Goss was in, and to Goss he expressed his surprise at his having such stuff in his shop. Goss replied that Hodson had told him that it was all right, and he (witness) said he ought to have known better. Goss then said he was doubt- • ful about it, but thought it might pass. He said they had given £4 for it. Witness then called his attention to the fact that a steak had been cut off.—Cross-examined by Mr. Thomas: Witness said he was sent for occasionally to go and look at meat. He had seen better meat with a worse liver.—James Lilley, butcher, Water-street, said that last Friday but two he was called out to Solomon Coates's farm at Parr. He there found a beast lying in the shippon. The owner said it had hung itself. It was stunk. He dragged it into a barn, took the hide off. but did not dress it for sale. It was in a very poor condition, and the lungs • were diseased. It tvas not fit for food.—Mr. Thomas: Have you been in gaol ?—Witness: Certainly. (Laughter.)— Witness said be had been a butcher 13 years, and had served his time at Crosby's shop. He had been in g .cd for having bad meat.—Dr. McNicoll and Win. Garton Dixon, veterinary surgeon, spoke to the meat being bad, and they said the beast had been suffering from what was commonly called "grape."—Mr. Thomas said defendant and Hodson went to Parr and bought the meat already dressed for sale, and they were told by Coates that it was good meat. Defen- dant, when he had it at home, thought it did not look so good. He immediately went for the inspector, who was not in; but he left a note for him. He went back home, and waited two hours for the inspector. He then went out, and while he was out his wife placed the meat on the board for sale. The defendant had been in St. Helens 30 years, and had had a shop 10 years; and many of his customers were the leading gentry of St. Helens. It had taken him 10 years to build up a business, and he bad been put to very serious loss indeed, some of his best customers having left him. Taking all the facts into consideration, he urged the magis- trates to be lenient with him.—The magistrates, before giving their decision, said they would hear the other case.— Thomas Hodson, College-street, was then charged with having beef on his premises, exposed for sale, such beef . being unfit for the food of man.—Mr. Swift prosecuted in this case, and Mr. Massey defended.—Mr. Swift said from what Goss told Ceughtrey be went to Hodson's place and found 20 pounds of the hind quarter exposed for sale in the window. Like Goss, Hodson admitted the facts; but what made this case worse was that he did not stop the remain- ing portion of the carcase. The inepector asked him where the carcase was, and Goss said it was at Coates's farm. The inspector went there as fast as he could, but it was not there, and Hodson afterwards said it had been removed in a rag and bone cart to Warrington. The Corporation tele- graphed to the inspector at Warrington to stop the beef, but the beef was not to be found, and probably it had gone into some country place and sold to the rustics, where they had not such an intelligent officer as Mr. Coughtrey.—Evidence having been given, Mr. Massey said his client pleaded guilty, and added that Hodson was so terrified at Mr. Coughtrey's entrance that he made false statements to him, for he had actually put the meat into the canal. He addressed the Bench on the fact that the evidence did not say that the meat would cause disease in those who might eat it, but that it was simply poor and wretched meat,which was not likely to give any nourishment.—The magistrates retired to consider their decision, and on returning fined each of the defendants £2O and costs, with the alternative of three months' imprisonment.—A month was allowed to pay the fine.

HIGHWAY OTFENCES.—Ann Rates was charged with allowing two cows to stray on the highway, at Appleton, on the 16t17 March, and she was fined 28. and Bs. costs.—For allowing four cows to stray, at Appleton, on the Bth instant, Wm. Hewitt was fined 4s. 6d. costs.—A carter named Wm. Ingham was summoned for driving a horse and cart without reins, at Latchford, on the 13th inst., and he was fisted 28. 61. and Bs. 6d. costs.—Win. Grounds was fined in the penalty of 2s. 6d. and Bs. 6d. costs for being asleep whilsb in charge of a horse and dray, at Moore, on the 20th inst.— On a similar charge, the offence having been committed at Acton Grange, on the 23rd inst., Matthew Bates was fined is. and 10s. "6d. costs.

DRUNKENNESS.—Mary Williams, an old woman, was charged with being drunk at Stockton Heath, on the 11th Inst., and she was tined 7s. 6. and lOs. 6d. costs, or, in de- fault, 14 days' imprisonment.—For being drunk in Seven Oaks, on the 27th January, Patrick Hansbury was fined ss. and costs.

REMOVING DISEISED ANIMALS.—Jas. Drinkwater, farmer, Little Legh, was charged with allowing four sheep suffering from sheep scab to be removed from his premises to Hart- ford; and George Barlow, farmer, Hartford, was charged with removing the same.—Drinkwater said the sheep were not his. and Barlow said he did not know the sheep were diseased when be removed them—P.S. Blair said that on the 14th January the defendant Drinkwater reported 20 sheep infected with sheep scab, and on the Ist inst., when passing the defendant's premises, he observed that there were only 16 animals in the field. On inquiry be was informed the sheep had died and been buried. The next day he again visited the field in company with a veterinary surgeon, and asked the defendant to point out the exact spot where the animals had been buried. Drinkwater then admitted the sheep had been removed to Hartford by Barlow.—Drink- water said the sheep were net his; and he was not aware that he could not allow them topbe removed. He admitted that he had had orders served upon him, but be had never read them (Laughter).—Drinkwater was fined 20s. and costs, total .£2 6s. 7d., and Barlow was fined 15s. and costs, total £2 Os. 7d.—A charge of allowing seven of the diseased sheep to stray on the highway, on the let inst., was then made against Drinkwater, and he was ordered to pay costs. A NntsxNcE.-Ann Taylor and Margaret Percival a ere sum- moned by Mr. Farrington, nuisance inspector to the Run- corn Rural Sanitary Authority, for an offensive nuisance on their property, at Appleton, and the Bench made an order for its removal.
