div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882.

THE discussion on the condition of Ireland which took place in the House of Commons on Tuesday evening will be read with painful interest. The hon. members for Cork, Tipperary, and Roscommon— Messrs. Parnell, Dillon, and O'Kelly—who, it is well known, are now confined in Kilmainham gaol as sus- pects under the provisions of the Coercion Act, had, in response to the expressed wish of their colleagues in Parliament, made application to the Chief- Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant to be released in order that they might attend at St. Stephens and vote upon the closure resolution. The application seems to us a most extraordinary one, even though sup- ported by the promise, as was the case, that the members would not speak on the question, but only vote, and that they would return to durance imme- diately after the division. This request was, on Tuesday, pressed upon the Government with all the gravity iraeginable by Mr. Sexton, and it was sup- ported by Sir J. M'Kenna; e The former urged that the demand was made because "we were on the eve of a Parlia:nentary struggle the most momentous that had distir, guished the century ;" and the imputation was thro, a out, without any apparent reason, that "if the r,.itiest were refused it would be because the Government were afraid that on a crucial question these three votes would be found in the Opposition lobby." We do not for a moment suppose that the suspects themselves, Mr. Sexton, or any of his friends believed that the request would be acceded to, but if they did the reply of the Premier was of the most conclusive na'ure. The right hon. gentleman admitted that the parole was safe, and that the sus-

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882.

Ipeets made an "enormous sacrifice" when they undertook not to speak; but, as Mr. Gladstone pointed out, if these gentlemen were to be released this week for a particular purpose there is no defensible reason why they should not be released another. A prece- dent-and the,House of Commons as has been often said s the slave of precedent—w 3 uld by acceding to the application be established, and it would be difficult to avoid following on its lines. With respect to the gravity of the division, it is idle to suppose it to have been more important than the one which took place a short time ago, when the Lords appointed a committee to inquire into the working of the Irish Land Act. It is unquestionable that but for that division the Peers would have made an unrestricted investigation into the operation of the measure, and done their utmost to damage it in the eyes of the public. The iefluence of the Committee was,however,nullified by the division before the Peers commenced their labours. But why should the suspects vote only on the first resolution I' If Mr. Marriott's amendment, for which it is presumed they would vote, is net carried, then it will be com- petent to submit the other amendments on the paper, and if the influence of the suspects is to be felt in the first division it ought also to be felt in the divisions on the other amendments, all of which have a bear- ing on the form which the closure is ultimately to as- sume. To our minds the suspects ask either too much or too little. The refusal of the Government to accede to the wishes of the suspects was not received very graciously by the Irish members present, several of whom indulged, it is to be regretted, in rather un- measured language, and the erratic member for Dungarvan, Mr. O'Donnell, was unnecessarily harsh in declaring that there was no son of Ireland who would not think night and day for the best means to avenge the English treatment of Ireland upon all who supported her Majesty's Government. Such language as this is the very thing calculated to lead to a repetition of the outrages which all right-think- ing people must deplore. We doubt not the Irish members are seriously anxious to have their friends in Kilmainham with them in the House; but it is open to question whether they ever seriously expected their last demand to be favourably entertained, much as we believe the Government would have liked to comply therewith if it could only have been shown that the adoption of such a course would have served any useful purpose and could have been followed with safety. An endeavour was made to show that because one or two of the suspects had been liberated for a period because of domestic bereavement, a con- cession ought to be made to the hon. members, but there is no analogy whatever between the two cases. Mr. O'Donnell intimated that the day on which these gentlemen were let out would begin a new era of in- creased difficulties between the British Administra- tion and the Irish race, and if that be so, a tem- porary release would doubtless be the signal for an outburst of feeling which it would not be wise to encourage and might lead to troublesome results. But the most important part of the discussion on Tnesday, and which will be perused with the greatest anxiety, is that which refers to the state of Ireland itself. It is satisfactory to hear from the lips of the Chief Secretary after so recent a visit to Dublin, that there are signs of improvement, though those outside ()facial circles and unacquainted with the facts on which the Chief Secretary's hopes are based must look in vain for such cheering news in the usual sources of information. According to the columns of the newspapers murders are committed as frequently as ever, outrages upon people whose only offence seems to have been that they have discharged their just obligations are not less prevalent, and intimidation and boycotting is resorted to on every hand. The prisons are filled with suspects, but the village tyrants whom it was thought the Coercion Acts would first reach—still continue their lawless conduct, the raids of the "Moonlighters" being still unsuppreesed. We are told that there shave been, and that there are in existence, secret societies whose object is murder; and it would seem that these have the countenance of men of "position and influence." So long as this is the case, improvement, however vigilant the authorities may be, must be slow; but it is not too much to hope that even with the enormous difficulties to be con- tended against the present coercive powers may be sufficient to meet every emergency without the appli- cation of anything more drastic. The "No rent" manifesto has failed of its object, and, as Mr. Forster says, though it has succeeded in being the cause of many a murder and many a mutilation, it has not succeeded in depriving the landlords of their rent. That of itself is a good omen. There is no disputing the fact that for the present unhappy state of Ireland many of tho Irish members are to a great extent responsible. The influence which they possess has not been exercised in a right direction. If the Land Leaguers have not—and we believe they have not—advocated violence, they have not on the other hand done much, if anything, to stay it. They were challenged on this very point on Tuesday by Mr. Brand, and the reply of Mr. Healy was of the very weakest character, for the reason that he was defend- ing a weak cause. Individual members of the League may have done something, but collectieely their actions have had a tendency to encourage resistance rather than obedience to the law. It is a pity that the power of the Executive should at such a time as the present be crippled even in the very smallest de- gree by the Opposition. 'Yet that will be the effect of such conduct as that of Mr. Gorst, who in his newly- born anxiety for the Irish members and their grievances repeated the imputation that the only ' reason the Government could have for refusing to liberate the Irish members on parole was their fear that three extra votes would he given against them. In certain Irish members such insinuations are par- donable, and their mistaken zeal in the cause they profess to have at heart may appear to them a justifi- able excuse, but it is unworthy of a member of Mn Gorst's reputation. The Government have a right to expect, too, at such a juncture as the present the sup- port of the responsible Leader of the Opposition, though on Tuesday he offered practically no assistan C 3 whatewer, for the obvious reason that there was the division on the closure looming in the distance. Mr Sexton did not press the question to a division, had he done so it would have been interesting to have noted in what lobby the Conservative leader and his fol- lowers would have been found. It is to be hoped there is no desire on the part of the Opposition to snatch a party victory out of the embarrassments of the Government, yet this is what the Conservatives May be fairly charged with doing if they do not give the Executive their cordial support in endeavouring to restore tranquility in Ireland.

THE Attorney-General this week obtained permis- sion to introduce into the House of Commons a bill to disfranchise certain cities and boroughs in which corrupt practices have recently prevailed and have been reported to the House, and to suspend the right of election in such places. The' present is, therefore, an opportune time for laying the demands of unen- franchised boroughs before the powers that be ; and we venture to think that the claims of the 'borough of St. Helens are such that they would in all probability be conceded. No harm can at any rate result from making these claims known, and if steps have not already been taken we cordially commend to the leaders of public opinion in St. Helens the necessity of at once bestirring themselves if they are desirous as we feel sure they are—of the borough taking its proper place in the county palatine. The cities and boroughs to be dealt with are eight in number, viz., Macclesfield, Chester, Boston, Oxford, Canterbury, Wigan, Sandwich, and Gloucester, each of which at one time had two representatives. In the first five mentioned places the writs in respect of both seats

are at present suspended, and in the latter three only one of the two seats normally belonging to the respective borough is vacant. It is worth while to point out that in the cases of Sandwich and Boston the population is actually undez 20,000, and that the registered electors in the latter place number only 3,043, while in Sandwich they number 2,207. The population of each of those two places is consequently considerably under a third of the population of the municipal borough of St. Helens, which has only a , portion of a representative, if the expression may be allowed. But coming nearer home, it may be noticed that of the boroughs to be dealt with Wigan has the highest population, 4,8196, and its regisiend electors number 5,937 ; yet the population of Wigan comes short of the population of St. Helens by several thou- sands. Notwithstanding this, Wigan enjoys, or enjoyed, two representatives in the House of Com- mons; and St. Helens per se is unrepresented there. So far as regards population, then, we think St. Helens has a fair claim to one, at least, of the seats to be disposed of; but there are other not less cogent reasons which may be urged. The borough, which is rapidly improving and extending, has now been in- corporated several years ; it has just had a separate commission of the peace granted to it; and we doubt not, that if the leading gentlemen in the town will only exert themselves it may have a Parliamentary representative as well, all to itself. We hope they will take the hint, and be up and doing in the matter.

I heritage of so many ages of wisdom and glory. The danger is terrible. The time is short. If this Bill should be re- jected, I pray to God that none of those who concur in rejecting it may ever remember their votes with unavailing remorse, amidst the wreck of laws, the confusion of ranks, the spoliation of property, and the dissolution of social order." FLACCUS.

WESLEYAN STINDAY SCHOOL SERMONS AT WIDNES.— On Sunday the Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, preached two sermons at the Albert-road Wesleyan Methodist chapel, on behalf of the Sunday school. The collections realised £26.

MEETING OF RATEPAYERS AT DOED.-0n the evening of the 24th ult., a meeting of ratepayers for the township of Bold, was held at the Griffin Inn, under the presidency of Mr. W. Tipping. Messrs. W. Johnson and John Newton, junr., were nominated overseers, and Mr. Thomas Whit- field was appointed way-warden.

CRONTON TOWNSHIP MEETING.— 011 Saturday even- ing, at the annual meeting of rate-payers, held at the National School-room, Mr. W. B. Longton, of Cronton Hall was nominated as Guardian in the place of Mr. Peter Long- ton, and Messrs. J. Cook and W. B. Longton were nom- inated overseers. Mr. J. Cook was elected way-warden. NELSON-STREET BAND /OF HOPE.—A very successful meeting of this Band of Hope was held in Nelson-street Mission Room on Monday evening, the room' being crowded. Xn interesting feature was the number of adults present. Addresses were delivered by the chairman and others. Some capital dialogues were given by several friends, and the usual recitations by the children. FORMATION OF A BRANCH OF THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY IN RUNCORN.—On Menday evening, a meeting was held in Regent Schoolroom, Runcorn, for the purpose of forming a branch of the Blue Ribbon Army in the town. A strong feeling in favour of the proposal was expressed by several of the prominent friends of the temperance cause, and a committee was constituted for the purpose of carrying out the arrangements. Mr. William Shaw was elected president, and Thomas Cooke and George Howard sectaries.. About 44 persons gave in their names as members. SERVICE OF SONG AT HALTON.-011 Wednesday evening ' Mr. Billingley's popular service of song, " The Basket of Flowers" (or the triumph of truth over falsehood) was rendered in the Wesleyan school-room, Halton, (kindly lent for the occasion), by the choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, assisted by a few friends. The service was given with precision and great spirit, and proved highly creditable to all concerned. We only regret there was not a larger audience. The Rev. J. Pickwell was the reader, and Mr. Billingsley the organist and conductor. We under- stand that although the work has not been before the public three months, yet the first edition of it (three thousand copies) was sold a fortn;ght ago. The publishers (Messrs. Hart and Co., London), are new issuing the second edition. They also state that a tonic-sol-fa edition is being prepared, which no doubt will further increase the sale.

TERRIBLY SUDDEN, DEATH OF A 'WIDNES CAPTAIN. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. C. E. Driffield, County Coroner, held an inquest at the Angel Inn, Mersey-road, Widnes, on the body of Samuel Radcliffe, of No. 83, in the same thoroughfare, captain of the flat Mary Foxley. The evi- dence showed that on Saturday, at about half-past ten in the morning, Radcliffe was steering the vessel which was mak- ing towards Widnes, in rough weather. Owing to this fact, deceased had to put forth considerable effort to keep the vessel in her course, and whilst doing so, he was seen to drop the tiller and fall. One of the bands, named George Ogden, ran to his assistance and found him frothing at the mouth, and unable to articulate a word. The poor fellow died shortly afterwards. For a number of years deceased had complained of a pain at his chest. His wife had treated Mm for wind, but it is supposed that he must have realty been a sufferer from heart disease, and that an attack had been brought on by the excitement caused by steering the vessel in very rough water. The jury returned a verdict of 'Died from natural causes."

1111,Tom MUTUAL IMPROVEM gxr SOCIETY. —Oa Mon- ' day evening, the closing lecture of the session was delivered in the Wesleyan schoolroom, by Mr. John Simpson, of Dunsdale, Frodsham. The subject Was " Contrasts; Eng- land, past and present." There was a good attendance. The Rev. J. Bateman Occupied the chair. The lecturer con- trasted the modes of travelling of 100 and of 50 years ago with those of the present time. Then, owing to the bad charac- ter of the roads; and the conveyances, it took almost as many days to travel any distance, as it now does hours. Mr. Simson described the vehicles used in his youth, and gave instances of his long journeys which he had himself performed when there were but few rail ways. He also corn- pared the dress of ladies.and gentlemen of former years with that of the present period, giving many laueliahle details ,and anecdotes. The oppressive taxes (such-, as those on glass, paper, tic.), and the difficulties of conlmunication by letter were mentioned and explained; also the use of the tinder box, and the origin of the word penknife. This word arose because the quill-pens were made by means of the knife. Owing to want of time the lecturer could not, as he would have liked, contrast former civil and religious liberty with the present. He expressed himself as being thankful that he was not born any earlier than he was. At the close of the lecture a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to him for his kind services, which were thoroughly appreciated by all present. The chairman also received the thanks of the meeting. T. IV. ROEERTSOW'S CASTE COMPANY IN Ilmeeoner.—The theatrical caste company, under the directioa of Mr. F. Faire, has visited Runcorn during the week; and performed at the Public Hall. On Monday " Caste " was given; on Tuesday "Ours ;" and on Wednesday evening "School." We might write a long critique upon the admirable manner in which each member of the company took his or her respective part, but it is not neceseaey we should do 80. Suffice it to say that the acting was, taken as a whole, pretty nearly perfection, and throughout each evening the company were exceedingly well received. But we suppose that there is a tide in the affairs of men which leads on to fortune so there is one in the history of histrionic companies; and certainly the visit can scarcely be said to have been fixed at a favourable date. Lent is now being pretty rigidly Observed in Runcorn, and the whole town has just been kirred to its depths by a religious movement in which many have taken part, who would scarcely feel at home at the present time listening to even J. IV. Robertson's plays. With the exception of here and there a somewhat too literal rendering of some conversation, the three plays are such as may be listened to by the west fastidious. We regeet that tile company will sustain a loss by their visit to the town, as it is not often that the lovers of the drama in Runcorn have an opportunity of seeing acting of so finished a character.

A HA.LTON COACHMAN ATTACKED BY A BULL-DOG.— During the last week, the principal topic amongst the in- habitants of the usually quiet village of Halton, has been a sad accident which happened on Friday week to John Grlf... fiths, aged about 30 years, the coachman to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., of Norton Priory. It appears that on the 24th ult.. rlriffiths was informed that a certain important note for the keeper of the kennels where the baronet's hunting dogs are kept, had not been delivered, and as the youngster who should have taken it was not at hand at the time, he volun- teered to go with it. Shortly before this a barred bull-bitch which was kept near the keeper's house, had broken loose from its chain, and as the coachman was going with the note, the dog sprang at his throat. Griffiths put up his left arm to save his neck, when the fierce animal tore his arm in a fearful manner. It next bit one of his legs, and tore a con- fiiderable piece of flesh away. The poor fellow's cries attracted the attention of the under-keeper, George Rigby, who ran to the spot, called the brute by name, and succeeded In seizing it as it was making a second spring at the man's leg. Griffiths was taken home, and put under the care of Dr. Carruthers. He is stated to be progressing favourably. The coachman is a general favourite in the village, and Much sympathy has been expressed for him. There is a general feeling that Sir Richard ought to have the dog shot. The animal is said to be related to a dog which some years ago worried a man so badly at Hale, that he died shortly afterwards

WIDNES PARISH Cnuncir SCHOOLS. On Tuesday evening, a sacred concert was given in the National School- room, Waterloo-road, on behalf of the class room fund. The Rev, J. Wright-Williams, vicar, presided, and the programme was entirely of a sacred character. The opening anthem was given by the glee class. Miss Fairley and Purver sang with commendable correctness " Hear my prayer ;" Mr. J. B. Limon the solo, "Take heed unto me," and Miss Brown contributed the recitative My heart is disquieted." Mrs. Fairley and Purver gave "Then I said ;" Miss Broad fol- lowed with Oh rest in the Lord." This lady possesses a contralto voice of considerable sweetness, which only re- quires more perfect training and constant practice to de- velop. Mr. F. W. Wilkinson gave " Nazareth," and was followed by Mrs. James White with "But Thou didst not leave," in the rendition of which she displayed vocal ability above the average. Mr. John Pownall sang "Thou shalt dash them." Miss Alice Purver gave "Angel of shanty" with sweetness and precision. Readings by Mr. Lewis diversified the programme; and they were not inap- propriately at such a time as the present, when the world of literature is mourning the death of Longfellow, the sweetest singer amongst the bards of Arucrica, taken from his poems, the first being the somewhat hackneyed "Psalm of life," and the second "The reaper," whose sickle keen," has now gathered the writer himself to the great majority. The glee class now gave the anthem " How beautiful upon the mountains," and Mr. F. W. Wilkinson "The shadow of the cross." Miss A. Purver and Mr. J. B. Imison sang the march from "Judas Maccabreus," and did full justice to one of the most magnificent passages from Handel's orato- rios. Mrs. James White was deservedly encored in her singing of " Oh, Lord, correct me." Mr. John Pownall rendered "With all your hearts ;" Miss Broad " Resigna- tion ;" and Mr. A. Purver "lie shall roll away the stone." The glee class having sung the chorus " Now pray we for our country," the proceedings were brought to a termination by the audience joining in the National Anthem. WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 9; children, 9; total, 18.

1.0.G.T.-STAR OF Wip.sns LODGE.—At the weekly meeting, on Wednesday evening, Bro. Rescorl in the chair, the secretary was instructed to communicate with the various temperance organisations in the town, with the view of a public meeting being brought abaut in support of the Sunday closing movement. WIDNES HASTE TO THE RESCUE LODGE.—This association of Good Templars met on ruesday evening, Bro. Bradshaw in the chair. An entertainment was held during the even- ing, when Bro. Thompson, W.C.L., of Liverpool, presided. Bros. Kinlier, Duckett, Thompson, and Sisters Golborne, Grey, and Molloy took part. RUNCORN AND TIFE UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.—On Monday evening, a meeting will be held in Bethesda school- room, Runcorn, under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance. Mr. J. R. Frith will preside, ann addresses will be delivered by Mr. C. H. Murray, of Preston, and Mr. J. White, of Manchester,

FARNWORTH COTTAGE LECTURES.—TiIiS series of lectures, which have been inaugurated by the Rev. J. Bond, vicar of Farnworth, fcr the benefit of the poorer classes, have not been so well attended as was expected. On Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. Holden was the lecturer, but the atten- dance was of a meagre character. RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.— MUSICAL AND ELOCUTIONARY ENTERTAINMENT. On Thursday evening, a musical and elocutionary entertain- ment was held in the Public Hall, Runcorn, under the auspices of the Young Men's Christian Association. The secretary (Mr. C. Nickson).' and the committee have worked very bard to make the matter a success, and in this they fairly succeeded, though if the reserved seats had not been so well filled, there is very little doubt that a different result would have had to be reported. Acting upon a very good suggestion, which we understand was made by Mr. George Bellamy, of The Examiner office, the committee kad applied to several frieads of the association, who kindly lent them a number of beautiful greenhouse plants, by the aid of which and a supply of crimson cloth and muslin, the otherwise somewhat uninviting platform, was made very attractive. Dr. Steele, the president of the association, occu- pied the chair. The concert was opened with Berger's "Night, IciVelr night," tie glee party being Miss Clark, Miss Littler, Mr. Joseph Littler, and Mr. Richard Morris ; and during the evening they also sang in a very pleasing manner the "Village blacksmith: and the "Fisherman's good night." Mr. Sansom, of Widnes, recited in fine style " Othello's address to the Senate," though in this, his first effort before a Runcorn audience, he was not heard to advan- tage, his voice being too thin, and a little husky. Miss Lambert, who is well known to Runcorn audiences, next sang "Some day," and was very well received, on which she gave as an encore " The three maids of Lee" which fairly brought down the house. Mr. J. Morrison, of Widnes, was heard to advantage in Cowen's "Children's home." Miss Ada Hindiey, of Liverpool gave "When the sparrows build" in a style distinguished by much sweetness, but her voice is scarcely powerful enough to be heard with any effect in so large a building as the Public Hall. Mr. E. Rhodes recited "The last days of Herculaneum." His, gestures were exceedingly appropriate, and though his voice wants cultivation, there is no doubt that in time he will take a high rank as an elocutionist. He won a hearty round of applause, to which he responded by giving the graphic piece entitled "John Maynard," in which he was not quite so effsctive, it being pretty evident that he had not bestowed the same careful study upon it that he had devoted to the one for which he was put down upon the programme. The second part of the concert opened with "The sailor Sighs," which was sung by Miss Lambert and Mr Morrison in a highly finished and captivating manner, which won them vehement applause, and they responded by a repetition of the last verse of the song. Mr. E. San- som then recited "As it fell upon a day " with marked ability, and received a very hearty encore. He next gave " Genevra " from Rogers "Italy" in magnificent style. His gestures were those of a finished actor; the tones of his voice were clear and under wonderful control and he chained the attention of the audience from the first word until the last. As he described the tragic fate of the lady depicted in the lovely composition the most perfect silence prevailed, and those present were worked up to a pitch of excitement as he told how the fair young bride was acci- dentally fastened in the old chest, in the noon-tide of her marriage day splendour, and when he pronounced, after a most dramatic pause, the words "For ever," an enthusiastic burst of applause rewarded his efforts. Truly Mr. Sansom has gifts which fit him for the career he has chosen—a theatrical one, and many present expressed a hope that in his new venture he may meet with some of those "friends indeed "of whom he spoke so pathetically in his recitation, "As it fell upon a day." During the evening Captain Hazlehurst sang "The old sacristian," Parker's " Close to the threshold," " Sailing, sailing," and " Thou art so near and yet so far." He seemed very popular with the audience, and the song "Sailing, sailing went very fairly, but there was a huskiness in his voice which marred the effect of his singing very much. Miss Hindley was applauded in "At the ferry," and M 913 Lambert sang "Angus Macdonald" very effectively. Miss Shaw was well received in the pianoforte solo "Auld Robin Gray." Miss Morrison's sing- ing of Campian's " Mignonette " was the gem of the even- ing. Mrs. Heal acted as accompanist, with the single ex- ception of Captain Hazlehurst's songs, in which he was ac- companied by his sister—very cleverly. Mrs. Heal is a pianist who has evidently a mastery of the key board. The proceedings were concluded with the singing of the National Anthem, in which tke audience joined. We may add to our report that when the proceedings were near their con- clusion, a scene took place in the bick seats of the body of the hall, which was full of mystery to the dignified occu- piers of the reserved seats. Certainly they heard a consi- derable amount of laughter going on, but this only caused them to turn round with astonishment at such a strange in- terruption to a concert in the town of Runcorn, the inhabi- tants of which are credited with a fair notion of the pro- prieties Of life. On enquiry, we find that the laughter, which occasionally burst forth in a .merry peal, arose from the fact that a somewhat notorious character in the town named Herringshaw, but who is known by the name Corfey, and who is understood to have to have what our friends across the borders call "a bee in his bonnet," was giving vent to his feelings as to the indig- nant treatment he had received from some prominent mem- ber of the committee of the Young Men's Christian Associa- tion. The worthy man, who occasionally gives vent to busts .of melody known by such titles as" Shall we meet beyond the river," in the public streets, and is rewarded with a stray copper for his pains, stated that the ground of i his complaint was that he had been asked to attend there in I order to "give a taste of his quality," and promised ten shillings for his labour. He appeared in all the glo:y of a whits waistcoat and, in fact, he was got up regardless of expense—according to his idea of things. He continued to pour foreh the tale of his woes in so loud a tone that one of his friends of the association at last seized him by the shoulders and ran him out of the building. Theepoor fellow left declaring that he would take proceedings in the County Court for the recOvery of the money he had been promised.

SUDDEN DEATH AT WARRINGTON.---Early last Satur- day morning, there died suddenly at his residence, 44, Hardy- street, Warrington, John Brookes, a clock cleaner, 54 years of age. Up to seven o'clock on that morning the deceased had enjoyed his usual health, but his. landlady observing he looked pale, inquired the cause. He said he did no:: feel well, and the woman gave him some warm water and brandy. As he became no better, she went to the Lev. M. Schonberg to obtain a " recommend " for the Infirmary, and whilst she was away he died. His landlady stated the deceased was very often drunk.—Mr. Diiffield, coroner, held an inquest on the body, on Tuesday, at the Old Crow, Fennel-street, and the jury returned a verdict that the deceased died from "natural cluses, and from the effects of long-continued in- temperate habits combined."

COCKUEDGE MISSION YOUNG MEN'S MUTUAL LIPROiTE- MENT SOCIETT.—A grand public tea party and. entertain- ment took place on Monday night last in connection V. iLh the above society, it being the closing meeting of the ses- sion. A very substantial tea was provided by the commit- tee, and a large number sat down to enjoy it. Upon enter- ing the Mission-room. the eye met a most beautiful and magnificent disdlay of flowers and rare plants kindly lent by Mr. Fell, of Springfield, Sankey-street, to whom tie society is greatly indebted, the display eliciting the admitation of all ptesent. After tea a public entertainment was given, pre- sided over by the Rev. John I onge. who was supported by the Revs. Thomas Rippon and E. Moore, when a most attrac- tive programme was admirably gone through to an appre- ciative audience. At the close Mr. Farrar proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be given to the Chairman, Revs. Rippon and Moore, and other friends for their presence and services, which was seconded by Mr. Peter Travis, and heartily responded to. Mr. Bridge next proposed that the best thanks of the meeting be given to Mr. liankinson for his kindness in procuring the flowers and plants, and for the labour which he had betowed in displaying them. This was seconded by Mr. John Willett, and dtily acknowledged. The meeting was brought to a close by singing the Doxo- logy.

The first statutory meeting of the creditors of George Clayton Hunt, of Culcheth, near Warrington, farmer, has been held at the offices of Messrs. Parker and Stocks, solicitors, Norfolk-street, Manchester. The state- ment of affairs showed liabilities to unseoured creditors £1,062; creditors fully secured, £12,000; and assets (less preferential claims) amounting to £1,900. Liquidation by arrangement was resolved upon. The principal creditors were represented by Messrs. Parker and Stocks, and Messrs. Rvlance and Son, solicitors, and Messrs. Trotter and Sclaol- fic:ld, accountants, all of Manchester.

FATAL ACCIDENT. TO A WALLINGTON CAMTET.-011 Thursday, Joseph Harrop, carter, in the employ of Mr James Warburton, farmer, Dallam, went with a horse and lorry laden with straw tc Manchester, and on the following day set out on his return journey with a load of manure. He stopped to rest his horses at Irlam, and then went on to Hollins Green, where he was seen sitting upon the front of his lurry. He was found about ten o'clock Iying dead on the road half a mile from Hollins Green, the wheels of the vehicle having passed over Dart of his neck, and the &de of his head. He was perfectly sober, and it is supposed he must have gone to sleep and fallen from ,his seat to the around. Deceased was a steady man, ani bore an excellent character. Ile was about a years of age, ard leaves a widow and three children.

Richard Kean, George Blackhurst, Alexander Mackie, and Matthew Bowden. • ~ 0 APPOEN= UNT Cr O!ZSEEVATIVE AGENT AT WAIL - RINGTON.—On Monday evening a meeting of the Council of the Warrington Conservative Association was held in the large billiard room at the club, Academy-street, for the pur- pose of appointing a Conservative agent for Warrington. Captain Reynolds presided, and about GO gentlemen were present. There were originally 153 applicants for the post, and the number was reduced to .14, the local candidates in- cluding the present agent, Mr. J. England, Mr. S. A. Tunks, and Mr. Fairhurst, Grappeuhall. The number was subse- quently further reduced to five, the Finance Committee strongly recommending the following gentlemen, namely, Mr. I3eeentson, of Whitehaven : Mr. George Atkinson, of Rochdale; and Mr. John Hampson, of Liverpool. The names of these gentlemen were, therefore, submitted to the meeting, and after a long discussion, Mr. Hampson was ap- pointed.

BEAMONT AND THE CICIETITIM SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the Chetham Society was held on Wed- nesday at Chetham's Hospital, Mr. James Crossley in the chair, when he read a letter from Mr. William Beamont, Warrington, resigning the positions of vice-president and member of the council. The letter was as follows :—" To James Crossley, E:quire, the President, and to the other members of the Chetham Society. Dear Mr. President,— It was agreed at the meeting of the society last year that at ' the end of the present year, when the society would have attained more than a second majority, there should be a pause, and a new series of its work should commence. In. revolving the agreement then come to, I have reluctantly arrived at the conclusion that it is my duty to resign my seat on the Council which I have so long held, and the high honour of being its vice-president, which I have held since the mantle of Canon Raines descended on me "licct in- dignus." Calling to mind his name, with those of Dr. Fleming, Dr. Parkinson, Mr. Corser, Mr. Langton, and many other noble workers in your literary field, I need not say that, regretting as I do their loss. I see that corporate bodies •only last long because their members are recruited by being continually renewed with new blood taking the place of the old. But for myself, I cannot plead as you can, sir, that literature is rejuvenescence; and I beg you to accept my resignation of the offices in the Chatham Council, which I have held with so much pleasure, and from which I have reaped so much that is valuable. Tendering to the Council wishes that the new series may attain the same success as for the kindness I have ever received,l wish to add my hearty my thanks for their forbearance with my short comings, and the old, and may in time occupy as conspicuous a place in the royal library at Windsor as I have sem the old filling there. Remembering what I shall neverforget, my pleasant intercourse with the saciety, I may truly hope and say, " et hxc olini nenzinr,sse juvabit."—l remain, dear Mr. PresiOent, yours truly, WILLIAM BEAMONT.—Orford Hall, Warrington, March 2.3.—The Chairman observed that he had not counted up the number of volumes they had received from 'llr. Beamont as editor, but they were very numerous and very val aable. He was one of the best and most indefatigable workers the Chetham Society had had, and he wished Mr. Beamont could have continued to wok longer for them.

div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOUS,
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOUS,

It is stated that the Finance Committee of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners have under consideration a pro- posal to reduce the district rate to is. 10d. in the pound. I wonder how the people of Widnes will bear such an an- nouncement as this. They are' only separated from Run- corn by the river Mersey, and yet their rates are more than double what they are in that town. Such a state of things must cause strangers to pause before they take up their residence in Widnes.

Mr. Sansom, the stationmaster to the London and North- Western at Widnes, has resigned his appointment, and vacates his situation this day. I believe your readers will heartily endorse the statement that whilst this gentleman has held the reins at the Widnes station, he has made many friends by his affability and attention to the wants of pas- sengers. I understand that he will be succeeded by Mr. Smith, who is at present night stationmaster to the com- pany at Warrington. Those tradesmen who are not much inclined to advertise their business ought to notice the manner in which Mr. Robinson Watson has conducted his late mission at Run- corn. No one can doubt that Mr. Watson has been wonder- fully successful in drawing crowded congregations. Indeed, on several occasions it was utterly impossible for a stranger to secure a seat at St. Paul's Chapel; and yet there are men who say that the general public have ceased to take an in- terest in the Bible and theological matters generally ! Would it not be well for these wiseacres to reconsider their decision ? Mr. Watson began his work in a business manner; in fact, he was not like many ministers who appear to imagine they can reap a rich harvest by simple prayer without any hard labour. Re had only been in the town a few days before 200 beautifully executed cards, about 20 inches in length and 12 inches in depth, were to be seen in every window, and an enormous number of large boards were placed its various prominent positions covered with placards drawing attention to the services in a very unpretentious manner. The result has been as I have above stated; and I would direct the attention of those who sneer at advertising to this fact. The services lasted about three weeks; and during this time nearly :NO was voluntarily contributed by the congre- gations. A newspaper is scarcely the place to dwell at any length upon the spiritual results of Mr. Watson's work, but I may add that they have been of the most encouraging character, and I have every reason to believe that his general conduct during his stay in the town has given every satis- faction, and made him many personal friends. A few days ago 106 people were summoned for non-pay- ment of poor rate in Runcorn. This does not say much for improvement in trade.

At the public meeting held to consider the adoption of the Free Libraries' Act in Runcorn, Mr. Robert Shaw certainly did not figure as a supporter of the proposal, but, judging from his speech, he threw the wet blanket upon it as liAr as his abilities enabled him. His observations included a good deal upon the matter of expense. It may interest your readers to know that the rateable value of Mr. Shaw's pro- perty is XDO 55., so that the immense sum which he will be called upon to pay yearly as his contribution to the Library Rate is about Ss. No sooner had the late Lord Beaconsfield drawn attention to the high prices which chemical manufac- turers were obtaining for their goods, than the value of them began to go down, and it has since constantly kept de- creasing. I, however, think Mr. Shaw will find but !ittle difficulty in meeting this immense call upon his finances ! Perhaps I ought in fairness to that gentleman to state that he now acknowledges himself a well wisher of the Tree Library, and that at the meetings of the Board of Commis- sioners he has expressed a hope that it will be made into one worthy of the town. Possiby this slight change of front may be accounted for on the ground that Mr. Shaw has reluctantly come to the conclusion that the Free Library movement is a popular one. Some short time ago the rateable Talue of this gentleman's property was only £7B 15s.

Widnes is in a state of great excitement in reference to the approaching Local Board election, and more money has been expended upon the present contest than upon any which has taken place of late years, if we may judge from the amount of mural literature with which the walls are covered. The war of words grows hotter day by day, and an attack has been made upon Major Cross, the present chairman of the Board, from which some of his friends have considered it right to 'defend him.

I read the speech of the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., on the opening of the new premises of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association, with a good deal of interest. The vicar is a fluent speaker, and though he can say with the Roman in the play of Julius Ctesar, "I am no orator, as Brutus is," yet he is possessed of a pleasant strain of talk. I have, however, 'yet to learn that the Rev. Canon Barclay is much of a politician. I observe that at the meeting re- ferred to he made use of the following remarks :—"All the great improvements of the present generation had come from the upper classes of society. Who was it that emancipated the slaves ? Was it not William Wilber- force, the member for the grand Yorkshire constitiencv ? Who was it that emancipated the factory workers from their thraldom of immense labour? Was it not Lord Shaftes- bury, who was then Lord Ashley? Let them even take the Reform Bill of 1832, which was the first extension of the Constitution, was it not brought forwardby a nobleman who was almost sobbing when he submitted it to the House, at the thought of the enormous change he was bringing about?" The vicar of Runcorn must have had a poor idea of the intellectual capacity of the audience if he really imagined they were prepared to swallow a statement that the members of the upper classes have been the givers of the various reforms enjoyed by the present generation. Take the case of the Reform Bill of 1832. Surely Canon Bare ' clay cannot have read the 114tory of the terrible struggle through which a free peoille had to pass before they obtained their just rights to a proper representation in their own house—the House of Commons. Has he never heard of how the agitation had to be carried or. with such determina- tion that the entire business of the country was for a time in a state of nearly perfect stagnation; and of how when the Bill was thrown out thousands of places of business were closed, and on the shutters were put placards on which were the words "The Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill." Has he forgotten the indignation caused by the Peterloo Massacre, when the people assembled in their thousands, and were dispersed by cavalry? The present generation can scarcely comprehend how a Government could dare to interfere with the right of free born English- men to meet together and discuss their political wrongs— men whose boast it is that they come "Of fathers brave and free."

Let the reverend gentleman read, if he has never yet done so, the marvellous speech de- livered by Mr. T. B. Macaulay (afterwards Lord Macaulay, the famous historian), when Lard John Russell moved the House of Commons for leave to bring in a Bill to amend the representation of the people in England and Wales, and he will then see how awful was the state of things in the country, and how peremptory was the demand which rung from the upper classes the electoral priyileges ,1 which had formerly been denied to hundreds of thousands. Listen to the concluding passage of that memor- able oration :—" Now, therefore, while everything at home and, abroad forebodes ruin to those who persist in the hope- less struggle against the spirit of the age, now, while the crash of the proudest throne of the continent is still resound- ' ing in our ears, now, while the roof of dm British palace affords an ignominious shelter to the exiled heirs of forty kings, now, while we see on every side ancient institutions Hsubwerted and great societies dissolved, now, while the heart of England is still sound, now, while o!d feelings and old associations retain a power and a charm which may too soon pass away, now, in this your accepted time, now, in this your day of salvation, take counsel, not of projudice, not of party sptrit, not of ignominious pride of a fatal consistercy, but of history, of reason, of ages which are past, of the signs of this most portentous time. * * * Renew the youth of State. Save property, divided against itself. Save the multitude, endangered by its own ungovernable passions. Save the aristocracy, endangered by its own un• popular power. Save the greatest, and fairest, and most highly civilised community that over existed, from calamities which may in a few days sweep away all the rich

div.head: SAD SUICIDE OF A GIRL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD SUICIDE OF A GIRL AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening the inhabitants of Higher Runcorn were thrown into a state of great excitement by the report that a girl named Charlotte Baths, aged 16, the, daughter of a labourer, living in what is known as the Holloway, had committed suicide by taking a quantity of arsenic. The police are at present making careful investigation into the particulars of the sad occurrence, and, of course, a certain amount of reticence has to be observed until the facts have been investigated by Mr. Ridgway, the County Coroner,: which makes it a not very easy matter to obtain very many details in respect to it. It appears that on the day named, between twelve and one o'clock, the mother of the unfortu- nate girl, who is married to Thomas Parry, labourer at the. Runcorn Bottom Locks, went with her husband's dinner, leaving her daughter alone in the house.: She was absent about aikhour, and when she returned she and the girl Bites sat downio their simple Meal, with which tea was supplied. They had not been at dinner many minutes before the' daughteecommeneed to vomit, and to complain of consider- able pain. Dr. McDougall was sent for but' was not at home, and instead of some other medical man being at once asked to attend, the mother waited for the re- turn of the doctor, probably labouring under the supposition that he might arrive at any moment. Unfortunately he did not do until about eight o'clock, and the poor girl died about Len. About four or five months ago, a quantity of arsenic was bought by the mother for the purpose of killing rats, and what was left of it was put into a can, which was bung up on a nail in the ceiling. About a teaspoonful of this was taken by the girl, and drunk in some tea.. We understatd that Bates had been keeping company with a young man, and that on Wednesday night she returned home so late that she was afraid to enter the house, and she took refuge in a neighbour's, and remained there until morning. It is stated that when she came home' on the following day, she was chastised by her mother. This may have had some effect in causing that despondency which has led her to take away her life.
The Coroner has, of course, been informed of the facts and the inquest has been fixed for Mginday morning, at the Railway Hotel, Lowland's-road, at eleven o'clock.

(The following was received too late for publication last 'week .:l THE LETTING OF CORPORATION CONTRACTS. Sir,—Allow us through the medium of your next issue of The Examiner to correct the statement made by " Attalus " in "Random Jottings" of last Saturday's issue in the matter of the contracts for police helmets. He states that we received 9s. Bd. per helmet, whereas we never re- ceived more than 9s. 31.; and instead of having a profit of nearly 23. per hat, the whole profit we received was is. per helmet and no more. As to the quality of the new helmet being superior to the ola one, there is a very great difference. The old helmet, after being in wear two winters, is superior in quality and material and more especially in colour than the new ones that have not yet been worn; and as the police generally wear caps in the summer, the new helmets are not likely to cerise in wear before next November, when the Mayor goes to church. Can your correspondent "Attains" inform us how it is that tradesmen who are 60 or 70 miles from this town have sufficient time given to enable them to furnish samples, when the local hatters of Warrington have two hours' notice only? We speak of hatters alone, as we have since learnt that due notice was given the several tailors of the town who usually tender for the clothing. We •may here state that the committee could have been well supplied with helmets of the same quality as those supplied from a strange town and at a lower price than what they have given, had we thought they would have accepted such a common quality. May I be so bold as to ask "Do you not think it rather hard that local contracts of this kind should be sent out of the town, when the tradesmen of the town are compelled to pay the heavy rates imposed upon them ?" We pay upon the small premises we occupy at Market Gate, the slim of 7s. in the £. Warrington I think, must be one of the heaviest rated boroughs in the United Kingdom.—. Remaining, yours respectfully, W. HALL & SON, Practical Hatters. Warrington, March 24, 1882.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Mr. P. Stubs. A DESERTER.—James Shaw, a young man, was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's 40th Regiment of Foot' stationed at Warrington. He pleaded guilty, and was handed over to the military authorities at the Bar- racks. ANOTHER ATTEMPT TO CHEAT THE RAILWAY COMPANY. —John Graham, a middle-aged man, was charged with riding in a third class carriage on the Cheshire Lines Rail- way from Stockport to Warrington, without having previ- ously paid his fare.—Mr. F. Simpson represented the com- pany. On the arrival at Warrington of the train due at 3-40 from Stockport, F. Risby, the ticket collector, observed the prisoner open a carriage ;door and jump on the platform before the train had stopped. He walked to the top end of the station, and the ticket collector followed and demanded his ticket. The prisoner protested he had not come by train, stating he had just come on the station from the town. He afterwards, however, admitted he had come from Stockport, and offered to pay the fare. This was refused.—The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, or a month's imprison- mmt.

Moernay.—atfore Major Cartwright and the Deputy Mayor (Coancillor Fairclough). BEGGens.—Bridget McCarty, of Foundry-street, was charged with begging in Bold-street, on Sataer.day. As this was the first time the prisoner had been before the Bench on any offence, she was discharged on payment of costs, 28. An old man, named John Jones, was charged with begging in Bold and Wilson-Patten streets at eleven o'clock on Sat- urday morning, and he was committed to gaol for 14 days. HUMAN PARASITES: DASTARDLY WIFE BEATERS.—A young man named John Clare living at School-brow, was charged under a warrant with assaulting his wife Ellen. The prosecutrix said that on Saturday night her husband went to where she lodged "fearfully drunk," and the land- lady and herself went to bed. The prisoner commenced to sing, and when told by the landlady to make less noise, as he would waken the children, he went upstairs. Without removing his clogs or clothing he got into bed and com- menced "kicking and thumping her all night." because she would not get up and get him something to eat. At eight o'clock next morning, prisoner told his wife she had better be quick and give him something to eat. She replied that she had enough to do to keep herself and two children, without finding food for him. He knocked her to the floor, and abused her "fearful." She picked up the poker to , defend herself, but he pulled it from her grasp, and with it struck her across the back. Bringing • his fist into use the prisoner struck his wife a blow on the nose, which bled profusely, and also kicked her.—ln reply to Councillor Fairclough, witness said the prisoner was a tanner by trade, but had never worked for six months, and she kept herself and children by "cutting." The prisoner during the day went to his mother's, house, and at night went to her lodg- gings to sleep, and she had had to find him many a meal. When he did earn a little money be spent it in drink.— The prisoner, in defence, said his wife had attempted to strike him with a knife, and had struck him on the head with the poker, and with a window shutter. He was unable to obtain work.—Mr. Fairclough said he ought to be ashamed to live on his wife in the manner he bad.—Major Cartwright said he richly deserved six months' imprison- ment.—The prisoner was sentenced to two months' imprison- ment.-Thomas Savage living at Cockhedge, was charged with assaulting his wife Hannah. The prisoner on Thursday afternoon, went home and demanded his tea, but as he had done no work for over a week, his wife had "nothing to put before him." He then gave her two blows on the face, blackening her eye. He had previously striick her many a blow.—Major Cartwright said he felt inclined to send the prisoner to gaol; but as his wife did not wish to press the case, the Bench bound him over to keep the peace for twelve months, or a month's imprisonment. How A "GAOL BIRD" TRAVELLED.—Mary Cox, a , woman of bad character, was charged with riding in a third- I class carriage from Liverpool to Warrington on the London I and North-Western Railway, on Saturday. It appeared I that on that day, the prisoner with three other women had I been released from gaol. Her companions had a pass to I Warrington given them by the gaol authorities, but as thel prisoner had 2s. 11-d. in her possession she did not receive one. The money was, however, spent in drink, and the pri- soner went the journey without a ticket.—She was fined 20s. and costs, with the alternative of a month's imprisonment. OUTRAGEOUS CONDUCT IN THE PARR—Thomas Lea, a young fellow, 0, Haydock-street, was brought up on a sum- mons charged with using obscene language in Bank Park Gardens, on Sunday, the 19th inst.—P.C. Bruen said the defendant with, several companions was near one of the greenhouses in the park making a great noise, and pointing to persons as they passed by. The witness, who was in plain clothes, told the defendant if he would not conduct himself properly he should be obliged to turn him from the gardens. He still shouted and laughed, and when two young women were passing made us of a very filthy expression which was not fit to be used in court.—Mr. Maguire confirmed this statement.—The Chief Constable said scarcely- a week passed but be had a complaint from the Watch Committee with regard to disorderly conduct in Bank Park on Sundays. The respectable portion of the community of Warrington did not visit the Park on Sundays on account of the rough boys and girls who frequented the place and acted improperly.—A youth named Thomas Stringer, of 105, Winwick-street, was called by the defendant, and stated he had used the had language.—Mr. Maguire' re-called, said he was watching the defendant's bad conduct for some time, and the officer said Stringer would also have been summoned but he ran away, and was unknown.—The Bench fined the defendant 203. and costs, the magistrates stating their determination to stop this lawless conduct in the Park. FURIOUS DRIVING.—Thomas Cermack, a hawker, was

charged- with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, and also with furious driving.—P.S. Bowen said about six o'clock on Saturday,. the 18th inst., he saw the defendant drive past Market Gate at a furious rate, and he was beating the pony drawing the cart as he went along. Prisoner was very drunk. For being drunk a fine of 53. and costs was imposed on the defendant, and for the furious driving he was fined 103. and costs. PROFANE LANGUAGF,.—WIIIiam BPtiley, a boy who walks with the aid of a crutch, and earns a living by selling mat Ches and newspapers, was charged with using profane language in the market on the 18th inst.—P.'l McLuen proved the case, and the ivy was fined 23 6d. and costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer, summoned 11. persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school. • Guilty" was pleaded in each case, and fines were inflicted as under : Joseph Fisher, salesman, King-street, ss. ; John Barnett moulder, 80, Cockhedge' 2s. 6d. in four cases; Wright Musl:ett, fustian cutter, Mill-yard, 55.; John Pemberton, chemical labourer, Latchford, ss. in two cases; John 3lannldn, fustian cutter, Mill-yard, 55.; P. Smith, fire- man, ss. in two cases ; William Sloane, joiner, Napier-street, 55.; *John Ryan, joiner, Lord Nelson-street, 55.; George Andrews, soap maker, James-street, ss. ; John Watson, joiner, Eardy-walk, ss. ; W. Farrington, fireman, Bank Quay, ss. in two cases. AN INCORRIGIBLE Yourn,—Thomas Chadwick,-of 35, Kerfoot-street, ahoy who had been five times before the Bench for felony, was charged with stealing 231bs. of scrap Iran' of the value of 61, from the Dallam siding of the L. and N.-W. Railway.—P.C. Seed when near the siding on Saturday night heard the sound of falling iron, and, pro- ceeding to the spot, found a, bag containing the iron, and saw the prisoner walking away. He took him int 3 custody. —P.C. Taylor proved the iron was the property of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles.—The Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for one, month, and then to a reformatory for five years. THE BLACK LIST.—The following persons were charged with drunk-ennes4, and a fine was imposed in each case : John Murphy, John McDay, Joseph Cartridge, John Don- nellan, Mary Rabbit, Saba McLotighlin, Bridget Fleming, Mary Gibbons, and Kate Maguire.—Jane Maynes, a bad character, was committed for three wceks' hard labour. • TCESDAY.—Before Major Cartwright. CHARGE OF STEALING A TUB.—TI3OMaS Hardman and Alfred Darbyshire, boys, residing with their parents in Orford-lane, were charged with stealing frcm the backyard of a chapel in Orford-lane, at seveli a.m. on Monday, the 27th March, a rain-water tub, value 58., the property of Mr. Edward Bolton.—They were remanded. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Councillor

Fairclough. AN AtvEuL NEIGIII3OrRHOOD.—Thom3s HArdman and Alfred Darbyshire, boys, were charged on remand with stealing a rain tub, value 55., the property of Mr. Bo!ton, from the back yard of Orford-lane chapel.—Mr. Bolton slid he wanted to be protected from the continual robbery of

property. Last year he suffered about £lOO worth of damage, on one occasion the rails round his field being pulled down.—Mr. Hunt said Orford-lane was a "fearful neighbourhood," an a house could not be empty a week without some damage being done or a robbery taking place. —The boys said they found the tub broken up, and, think- ing the tub was "nobody's," they took it away.—The Bench censured the parents of the boys for allowing the wood to be taken on their premises.—Hardmanwasfined 10s. and costs, and Darbyshire was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. ALLEGED FRAUDULENT BANICRUPTCY.—Edward Mackie, sen., was again brought up, but the charge had been altered from conspiring to defraud to fraudulently removing from the shop In Orford-street certain furniture and stock-in- trade, over.the value of £lO, within four months from the commencement e f proceedings for liquidation, with intent to defraud the creditors of the same. Edward Mackie, jun., and Eliza Mackie were charged with aiding and abetting.— Mr. Davies, who prosecuted, said he was not in a position to go forward with the case, and again asked for a remand.— Sufficient evidence to justify a remand was given, and the prisoners were remanded until Tuesday next. THURSDAY.—Before Captain Litton (chairman) and Alder-
man Webster.

A ROGUE AND VAGABOND.—A very old woman named Mary McHugh was charged with begging in Egypt-street on the previous afternoon; and also with being a rogue and vagabond, having been previously convicted of vagrancy.— P.C. Hitchmough proved the case, and the prisoner was com- mitted to gaol for 14 days. AN UNFOUNDED CHARGE.—Betsy Abrams, wife of Henry Abrams, draper and smallware dealer, living at Furness- street, Manchester, was charged in custody with stealing two pairs of boots of the value of Bs. 33., the property of Alfred Holliwell, shoe dealer, of Middleton, near Manchester.—The prosecutor and prisoner occupy stalls in the Warrington Market near to each other, and on the previous afternoon the prisoner purchased from the prosecutor a pair of boots, for which she paid 3s. 9d. It was alleged that the two pairs which were found upon her stall at night had not been pur- chased. The prosecutor was put into the box, and stated he had sold the prosecutor a pair of boots for 3s. 9d., and lent her the other two pairs for approval. The Bench immedi- ately discharged the prisoner, for whom Mr. Tucker ap- peared. FRIDAY. Before Capt. Reynolds (chairman), Mr. John White, and Mr. Ziba Armitage..

LICENSING PROSECUTION. Peter Knight, shopkeeper, Prince-street, Latchford, and who holds an off license to sell beer, was charged with selling liquor during prohibited hours. Matthew Heeson, Sparling-street, was charged with aiding and abetting.—Both defendants pleaded guilty.—ln consequence of instructions received from the Chief Constable Inspector Berry and P.S. Spinks went on Saturday night last, about 11.20 into the neighbourhood of the defendant's house. There are three entrances to the defendant's house, and after waiting some time, the officers saw a man go to the Fountain-street entrance, and confer with some person ' inside the house. He then walked about for a few minutes, when the officers again saw him go to the door and receive something. With his burden, the man passed down School- street, and the officers followed and captured him. The man was Heeson, and he was in possession of a stone bottle containing two quarts of beer, which he stated had been served to him by Mrs. Knight. This Mrs. Knight admitted. —Mr. Hunt said the reason he sent the officers to watch was because he had had complaints of the manner in which the defendant's house was conducted. He had always regarded Knight as a respectable man.—The Bench fined Knight 40s. and 10s. costs, and Heeson was fined 103. and Os. costs. CHEAP "LAW."—Katherine KAne, a respectable looking young woman, living at 16, Stamford-street, was summoned by Kate Higlaarn, a widow, of Oliver-street.—The complain- ant said the defendant went to her house on Saturday night, at six o'clock, and said she had poisoned her husband, and "struck at her." She (complainant) had in her hand a cup with which she struck defendant on the head, inflicting a cut. Defendant then got hold of her and struck her, and had not her brother been in the house she believed the de- fendant would have murdered hen—Many witnesses were called, and they all agreed that the defendant had received a severe blow with the cup, and was "teeming in blood."— Mr. Hunt remarked that the complainant had had a free summons.—Captain Reynolds said he was sorry for that. The defendant was more sinned against than sinning, and the case would be dismissed. The magistrates did not con- sider it a case for a free summons.—Mrs. Higham was then placed in the defendant's box to answer a charge of using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace to Mrs. I Cook' of 53, Haydock-street.—After hearing the evidence, the Bench dismissed the case, Captain Reynolds remarking that there was too much disturbance in the neighbourhood. QUARRELSOME WOMEN.—EIIen Shee, of Portland-street, was summoned for assaulting Ellen Carrol, of the same neighbourhood.—lt appeared that on Mondoy night the de- fendant went into the complainant's house and created a dis- turbance about a peg top and whipcord, and on leaving, .defendant struck the complainant twice on the face, blacking her eye.—A witness stated the defendant and complainant were quarrelling together, and the Bench dismissed the case on the payment of costs.
