div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE INTER-
NATIONA ELECTRIC EXHIBITION.

The following report of the deputation of the Gas Corn- I mittee of the Corporation on the International Electric Ex- hibition will be presented to the Council on Tuesday : Several members of the Gas Committee, together with the Manager, paid a visit to the Electrical Exhibition at the Crystal Palace on Tuesday, the 7th inst., and felt much in- terested in the visit. The onward march of human progress in the development of science and art has made great strides during the last decade, and in no branch of physics has this been more marked than in the division of electrical science as applied to telegraphy and artificial illumination. To these points electricians of all nations are directing their attention, with what ultimate result remains yet to be seen, bat the vast collection of apparatus exhibited on the main floor of the Palace was certainly marvellous and worthy of high commendation. The chief interest to the deputation was the different methods pursued in procuring the electric light. They do not offer any opinion as to which system is best, having no means of going into Lhese details. So far as they could judge from appearances, the effects in the case of the arc lights did not seem to differ in any perceptible degree with the various dynamo-machines used. All the arc lights are more or less subject to constant variation in intensity, and none seem to be exempted from this influence, whether at the Crystal Palace,Westrninster, Thames Embankment, or at the Mansion House. All seem to undulate to a greater or less extent, and in no case was a uniform light maintained for two consecutive minutes. The result of these irregulari- ties is not only disagreeable but painful to the eye, and may sooner or later lead to injury. This is undoubtedly the worst feature of the arc light, and one that will be difficult. if even possible, to remove, as the irregularity is in all pro- bability more influenced by difference in density of the electrodes than from any irregularity in, the transmission of the current; if so, the light cannot possibly be uniform so long as it depends upon the combustion of carbon. The in- candescent lights, which seem to be well adapted for domes- tic lighting beyond the limiPs of gas supply, form a distinguished feature in the Exhibition. They are exceed- ingly pleasing, effective, and beautiful. A charming example of these was given by the Brush Company with the Lane-Fox lights fitted to a handsome glass cbandlier, carry- ing about 100 lights, also to baskets of fruit and various other devices, in the Byzantine and Alhambra Courts. On the main floor of the building was a magnificent crystal candelabrum furnished with 92 maxi.n lights designed for the Government House in India, which had a very pleasing effect. In the Egyptian Court was a fine display of table glass in cups, goblets. vases, and other ornaments, in imita- tion of the ancient Venetian glass, amongst which were scattered a large number of maxim lights in cups, vases, cic., and also in jars of water, having a pleasant and pretty effect. About 200 of Swan's incandescent lights were placed in the picture gallery, the dining rooms south end of the building, and in Messrs. Elkington and Company's rooms. The most extensive display of the incandescent light was probably that of Edison, whose splendid lighting of the concert room and the large entertainment hall with something between five and six hundred lights may justly be regarded as a triumph. In this system of electrical lighting, the lights were steady, soft, and pleasant; they have not the spectre- like appearance, and are free from many of the irregularities and uncertainties of the arc lights. The only hitches ob- served were the occasional breaking of the glass bulbs con- taining the carbon film, and when in the splendid room of Elkington and Co., the Swan lights becamd instantly extin- guished and could not be relighted, so that the more dutiful and obedient agent, gas, had to take their place. To a casual observer, the conclusions arrived at would doubtless be favourable to the report circulated by its various promoters, that " the electric light is the light of the future." With- out pronouncing any decided opinion on such a hypothesis, there are many reasom which militate against it. Chief amongst these is the motive power required to drive the dynamo-machines, whieh, in this gigantic advertisement at the Crystal Palace and its approaches, cannot be estimated at lees than about 2,000 horse power, and which, divided amongst the numerous engines in and around the building, must be an enormous expense. Again, from the excessive velocities at which the dynamo-electrical machines are driven, varying at a speed of from 1,400 to 1,600 revolutions per minute, the wear and tear must be beyond calculation. Great speed involves great risk, and the probability of a breakdown is proportionately increased. The deputation could obtain no reliable information as to the cost in pro- ducing the respective classes of lights, but the expense of required skilled labour and attendance, outlay on machinery, wear and tear of plant, and the necessity of providing an ample reproduction fund, are elements which they consider as unfitted to bring it within the raugie of competition with gas at the present time. While holding these opinions, how- ever, the deputation have not only no wish to disparage the electric light, but would rather foster and encourage it, as a means of awakening attention on the part of the manufac- turers of gas to produce that article at the lowest possible cost, and thus extend its basis of consumption whether for domestic or public purposes, and either for lighting or heat- ing, for which last a great future for gas lies comparatively unexplored. March, 1882.
CHAS. J. HOLIES, Chairman.

CO-OPERATION PERFECTED.—In towns where the registra- tion of infectious disease is compulsory, and where the public co-operate with the medical officers of health. scarlet fever, imall-pox and measles will soon be things of the past. The simplest of all preventives (recommended by sanitary au` hori- ties) Is for heath of families to insis, that each resident in their house washes with Aright's Coal Tar Soap. It can be bouglat everywhere, but like all valuable remedies it is moat fraudu- lently imitated.—Advt.

AID TO PROVINCIAL MUSEUMS AND ART GALLERIES. The following report of the representatives of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee of the Corporation, on the deputation to the Lord President of the Privy Council to urge upon the Government the necessity of in- creased aid to provincial museums and art galleries, will be presented to the Council meeting on Tuesday.—Gentlemen, We have to report that on Wednesday last, the Bth inst., as the representatives of the institution, we attended the depu- tation to Earl Spencer and Mr. Mundella asking for increased aid to provincial museums and art galleries. The deputation was most influential and numerous, there being upwards of 40 members of Parliament present, besides a very large number of gentlemen from at least an equal num- ber of provincial towns and boroughs interested like our- selves in the success of these institutions. A preliminary meeting was first held, where the objects to be urged on the attention of the Department were freely discussed, and among other things it was definitely resolved not to ask for any money grants to the several institutions, as that might give the Government a right to interfere in their manage- ment, which it was considered would be most undesirable. Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., who presided at this meeting, subsequently introduced the deputation, and in a long and exhaustive address stated its ebject. In the course of his remarks he laid great stress on the general feeling and con- _ _

ductor), and to the children, for the very efficient manner in which they had given their very enjoyable entertainment. Several of the juveniles responded to the vote of thanks. An orange was presented to each of the chi:dren and they were _dismissed soon after nine o'clock, the basket being after- wards passed round to the adult members. A brother from the " Sandfoicl Example Lodge," Coventry, was present as a visitor, and, being out of employment, he was relieved. The attendance was good-44 adults and 23 juveniles, total 67. The lodge closed in usual form at 9-45 p.m.
viction throughout the country, that if we wishji to retain our manufacturing supremacy, more must be done for artistic and technical education than was the case at present,

really less.being done in England for that purpose than in any other European country; while to show the feeling of the country itself on the subject, he stated that very nearly £1,000,000 had been expended by local authorities in the establishment of free libraries, museums, and art galleries. In reply, Earl Spencer expressed the greatest willingness to assist in furthering the views of the deputation. He pointed out the great increase that had taken place of late in the number of objects lent from South Kensington to local institutions, and promised increased facilities in that direc- tion in the future. The Treasury, he said, had already agreed to give the Department an increased grant of money, to the amount of £3,750, which would enable them very materially to assist local institutions in the manner desired. A museum of casts from the antique was also being formed, which would be of the greatest val,ne, and would be so arranged at South Kensington as to enable the Department to send replicas, or reproductions, to such institutions as may desire them, at about half their cost. The metropolitan central museums were of the greatest value, and must be maintained ; at the same time he urged that no effort should be relaxed in the support of museums and art galleries by local assistance and contributions. Mr. Mundella also sympathized with the wishes of the deputation. Ha sail the' Department would be unsparing in its efforts to make the local museums and art galleries of the greatest possible use to the population surrounding them, and mentioned that owing to the transfer of the Indian Museum to the Depart- ment, an immense number of magnificent objects had been placed at their disposal, all of which would be available for circulation in the provinces, as soon as they could be re- ceived, unpacked, and arranged. In conclusion, we would state what we think the deputation was most successful, and that in the future, assistance will be willingly afforded by the Department to institutions desiring it ; by doing this, they will aid the spread of art education and in accom- plishing the objects we have in view. J. R. PICYMERE, Mayor. S. M. WEBSTBR. JOHN GRIIENING. March 10, 1882.

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY APRIL 1 1882 9 9 0 very efficient manner in EARLESTOWN VIADUCT INSTITUTE. 4)le entertainment. -- -f thanks. An ANNUAL SOIREE. were The distribution of the prizes to the successful students of the Earlestown Viaduct Institute Science and Art Classes, on Wednesday evening, was made the occasion ef a grand soiree which was held in the Viaduct Works of the London and North-Western Railway Company. A room called the "Lifting-room "had been cleared of its contents for the gathering, and across the middle of the room ran a curtain, which divided it in two portions. One portion was admi- rably fitted up for the tea party, and the other for the con- cert. The concert-room and tea-room had been most artisti- cally decorated and had a somewhat unique appearance. Round the walls of each room was a border of red, running the whole length of which were entwined ribbons of white and gr2en. Above were a large number of mottoes in blue and red lettering, tastefully interspersed with sprays of green leaves. The windows were draped with red and blun hangings and white curtains, and fixed in various parts of the rafters were a number of flags, which were very effec- tive. Among the mottoes may be quoted "May the indus- tries and commerce of the country continue to improve ;" "Success to the London and North-Western Railway Co. :” "Drive thy business or thy business will drive thee ; " " Get wealth honestly, use wealth generously ;" "May our Insti- tute develope and flourish ;" "Perseverance is the bridge by which difficulty is overcome ;" "Knowledge is no burden."
The decorations had been under the superintendence of Mr. F. Harwood, the chief foreman. It was estimated that between 1,500 an 1,600 persons were present at tea, but no . _ _ _ _

difficulty was experienced in seatingend providing for this large number at one time, so excellent were the arrange- ments which had been made. That bustle which is so usual an accompaniment of tea parties, was here totally absent, for when the people had satisfied their inner wants, they had simply to leisurely walk into the concert-room, which was capable of holding a much larger humber. The room in its entirety would comfortably hold upwards of three thousand people. Mr. Richard Moon, chairman of the London and North-Western Railway Co., presided over the concert, and he was supported by Lieut.-Col. McCorquodale, Mr. Shaw, district superintendent, Liverpool; Mr. Taylor, goods manager, Liverpool; the RevsaT. Matthews, vicar of Earlestown; J. Whitley, vicar of Wargrave ; R. Crozier, Wesleyan, Earlestown; and S. Weaver, Dr. Handysides, and Messrs. Emmett, P. M. Campbell, E. Braide, C. Ashton, secretary of the institute, and R. King, secretary to the science classes. Mr. C. Amnon', the secretary, read the 12th annual report as follows : In accordance with the usual practice the Institute Com- mittee have very great pleasure in making known the pro- gress of the various departments of the Institute for the year ending June 1881, and they are glad in being able to an- nounce the very satisfactory state in which the various de- partments stand. The financial year began with a balance of £3B 15s. 11c1., and the receipts comprised: subscriptions from the members £224 15s. 111 d., donation by John Hick, Esq., £5, sale of papers £24 17s. 3d., sale of grass and profit of excursion £43 19s. 4d., hire of hall £lB 10s., bowl- ing green, lectures, ,irc. £3O 7s. 10d, total £386 is. 9d. Dis- bursements: newspapers £9l 18s. Llscl., wages £lO4 Os. 5d., new books £34 Os. 10i-d., tea cans and ware £3O 4s. 7d., shrubs, plants, Jz.c. £33 7s. 2d., lectures, arc. £ll us., print- ing, ground rent, science teachers' fees, and sundries £65 Os. balance £l5 6s. 70, total £386 Is. 9d. At the end of the year there were 2,208 volumes in circulation from the library, including 140 new books which were added during the year. The issue for the 12 months was 6,368 volumes, being considerably above the average. The Com- mittee desire to record their gratification in seeing the library so well patronised, and to state that it is their endeavour by a choice selection of works to disseminate literature of an elevating and good moral character. The reading room has probably not been so well appreciated as the library, but, nevertheless, maintains its position, and the Committee believe it is productive of much good. The green and the grounds adjoining the Institute have met with a good share of the Committee's attention and great improvements have been made in the appearance of the place. The science and art classes have been established since 1876, during which time they have been carried on with varying degrees of suc- cess, the passes in proportion to the number of the students sitting for examination being as follows:—In session 1876-7 the per centage of successful students was 33; 1877-8, 72; 1878-9, 53; 187980, 63. The number of individual students who attended the classes last session, 1880-1, was 65. Twenty-three entries were made for the study of art and 57 for science. Fifty students sat for examination and 31 certificates were gained, being at the rate of 62 per cent. of success. Four Queen's prizes were also gained for first class certificates, and 7 students entitled to prizes from the In- stitute Committee. These latter prizes are given to those who have made progress since the previous session. There are also prizes to the value of £4 4s. and Ll is. respectively, given by Lieut.-Col. McCorquodale for the two students who stand highest on the list in both science and art sub- jects. The total amount of fees received last session was £9 145., and the total payment on the result of the class examinations was £26. The allowance by the Science and Art Department for the works sent up to South Kensington for examination was £4 75., making a total of £4O is., which has been paid over to the teachers in the usual way. The classes were up to the present session conducted by one teacher only, but the Institute Committee, believing that it would be greatly' to the advantage of the students, have en- gaged the services of two thoroughly competent instructors in the various branches of science and art taught here, and the new arrangement seems to be doing well. When it is taken into consideration that last year the standard of ex- amination questions was considerably raised, we may fully say that the classes are on the whole working satisfactorily, and the committee hope that by continued attention they may have a still further improvement to report next year. The CHAIRMAN, who was heartily greeted, traced the origin of the Viaduct Works at Earlestown. At one time there was a wagon works for the northern and southern divi- sion of the line, but he came to the conclusion that there ought only to be one, and he, in his ignorance as it turned out, thought of placing it near Birmingham. It was found that the company had 12 acres of land at Earlestown, and eventually the works as they now saw them were constructed. Though at present they were too large for the work, it was expected they would not be so in a few years. It was con- sidered best to provide for the future. He referred to the improYements which had been made in wagons, and said in such matters there was no finality, and he had no doubt they should still see great improvements in wagons, under the able management of Mr. Emmett. He did not believe in competitive examinations. He did not think a few extra marks in Latin, Greek, or mathematics would make a man. The man in whom he believed was a man who could cope with difficulty, as that man—and he hoped there were many such present—would become one of the leading men of the country. There was no position in this country which was not open to every one who had the requisite qualifications. It was said in America that when a man arrived in Boston in search of employment, the question asked him was, •‘ What do you know ? " in New York, "What are you worth ? " and in Chicago, "What can you do ? " But in England they had to combine all these things. A man must have knowledge and self-denial, and instead of having value represented only by dollars, he must have worth in good conduct and capacity to overcome any difficulties which en- countered him in his career. He hoped those who were to receive prizes would not think that they had done all that was to be done in the world. There was no limit to knowledge, for as soon as they mounted one hill there was another beyond. He also trusted those who had not succeeded in obtaining prizes would still continue in their search after knowledge, taking perseverance for their motto. They must bear in mind that the great object of our nature was to obtain happiness. Happiness was a thing which was required more than any other. The main anxiety of the poor man was to be in continual employment, and then with health and his family around him he was happy. (Hear, hear.) He wished them all happiness and prosperity, and ti usted they might always be able to have sufficient employment to keep themselves and their families in happiness. (Applause.) The Chairman then presented the prizes to the students. The following is the list :—Machine drawing, 2nd E, Thos. Owen, William Austin, William Mitchell, Joseph Wood, Frederick A. Galloway, Charles Singleton ; Alfred Caldwell, 2nd E, building construction • John Lindsay and Thomas Sutton, 2nd E, practical pane and solid geometry, and machine drawing; Thomas Kent, 2nd E, prac- tical plane and solid geometry„ and Ist E, building construction; William J. Bradshaw, 2nd A, machine drawing; Edward Eckersley, 2nd E, machine draw- ing, and certificate for model drawing; Thomas and James Seedon' 2nd E, steam, and committee's prin ; Waiter Blair, 2nd F 2, building construction, and committee's prize; Frederick J. Emmett, 2nd E, machine drawing and aim- mittee's prize; Scott Forrester, 2nd E, practical plane and solid geometry, 2nd E machine drawing, and committee's prize; Obadiah Wheeler, 2nd E thearetical mechanics, and Ist E steam and Queen's prize; William A. Sims, lst E, theoretical mechanics, and Ist A building con- struction and Queen's prize; Henry Bunting, 2nd E, building construction, certificate for freehand drawing, Colonel McCorquodale's 2nd prize, and committee's prize; Thomas Teece Massey, certificate for model freehand diaw- ing, Colonel McCorquodale's let prize, and committee's prize. The Rev. J. WHITLEY said his heart was with them all, and they knew from their long experience of him, whilst living amongst them, how very sincerely he wished all health and prosperity to them, especially to that noble com- pany—the London and North-Western Railway—over which their worthy chairman presided. (Hear, hear.) Lieut.-Colonel MCCORQUODALE, who was loudly cheered, said he could assure them he had great pleasure in being permitted to come amongst them once more on their annual gathering. He had listened with great pleasure and interest to the chairman's speech of the origin of the works, of which he (the chairman) perhaps knew more than any other man. And when they understood the chairman's acquaintance with the method and system of the numerous works of the com- pany, they were—at least he was, reminded of what was reccaded on the monument of Sir Christopher Wren at Westminster. No doubt they were all familiar with it. It runs thus : "If you want to see the monument of Sir Christopher Wren look around you." And so it was there with regard to the chairman. He thoroughly endorsed the chairman's senti- ment as to young men coping with difficulty, and gave a short account of some of the difficulties surmounted by one of the prolirietors of Ch,antbers' Journgl. He concluded by expressing the hope that the chairman would long continue to enjoy good health, and occupy the position he had held for to long with such benefit to others. The Rev. RICHARD CROSIER remarked that having been nearly three years in Earlestown and knowing how much of its prosperity depended upon, that \auks, it was quite

div.head: F RODS fall,
div.p: F RODS fall,

SECOND CON'CEET OF THE FRODSHAM MUSICAL SOCIETY. —On Wednesday evening the Frousham Musical Society gave their second concert of the season in the Town Hall, Frodsham, to an appreciative audience, although the hall was not so crowded as when the Messiah was given, which first introduced the society to the favourable notice of the public. The first part of the programme consisted of F. H. Cowen's cantata, "The Rose Maiden," the argument of which is as follows :—"The Queen of the Flower Fairies, weary of a life of unbroken calm, prays of the newly- returned Spring that he will bestow upon her also the gift lof love that he bestows upon man. He warns her of the risk I she runs, but finally yields to her entreaties, by changing I her, while she sleeps, into the form of a beautiful girl. Under the name of Roseblossom she wanders through the world to find the love that she seeks, and meets with a girl who, having been betrayed and deserted by her lover, loses her senses and dies broken-hearted. But, undeterred from her search, Roseblossom becomes the wife of a forester, with whom she lives for a time in such perfect happiness that she canno imrviva his death." The cantata is admir- ably set to music, and the fairy tale, with its romantic ideal, -has enabled the composer to make it exceedingly interest- ing; the introductinn is an instrumental piece for the piano and harmonium, which in the ,hands of Mr. Heywood and Mr. Argent was rendered with precision, and effects were produced which few but a Mr. Argent could accomplish on the harmonium. The choruses were given by about sixty voices, who did their work well, but a considerable amount of indecision was noticeable, particularly in the chorus "Mid the waving rosetrees." The trebles seemed somewhat weak, but this may be accounted for by several of their number being absent. The second part of the programme conerksted of the following, viz. :

Duet (piano and harmonium) "Weber." Farvarger Mrs. H. E. Heywood and Mr. W. I. Argent. Part song "You stole my love." Macfarren Bong "Angus McDonald." Roeckel Miss Janet Ilerpoint. Chorus "Charity." song "There is a green hill." Gounod Mr. J. R. Alsop. Cavatina "I'll follow thee." Farmer Miss Madeline Roe. Part song "On the sea." Mendelssohn Song "Mignonette." Champion Mr. J. Morrison. ....

Chorus The soldiers" (Faust) Gounod God save the Queen. The duet for piano and harmonium was given in masterly style, and was repeated, encores being afterwards demanded for most of the items on the programme. Miss Pierpoint was very successful in "Angus Mc l'onald," the accompani- ment by Mr. Argent being highly realistic of the national 'instrument of Scotland. Miss Madeline Roe was awarded hearty plaudits for "I'll follow thee," which contains some difficnit vocalisation. Mr. Morrison has a sweet tenor voice and sings with expression and naturalness, which is very pleasing. Mr. Alsop is a baritone of high merit, and Gounod's sublime composition received full justice. The chorus appeared to better advantage in the second part of the programme, the catchy piece, entitled "You stole my love," being well balanced and was given in correct time. The gem of the evening was, however, Rossini's chorus, " Charity " in which the female voices only took part ; and here was observed the excellence of the treble and alto voices, whose efforts were highly creditable, and the natural result was an enthusiastic encore. The concert would have been more highly appreciated and better enjoyed if given for two even- ings, as the cantata was entirely strange to the audience, and the thread el the story would have been more clearly panderstood if the words of the poem had been given on the excellently arranged programme, in the style of which con- siderable pains had been taken. The vicar took the oppor- tunity of thanking all who had contributed to the success of the society, and particularly to Mr, and Mrs. Rigby, of Bellemonte, who had liberally provided refreshments for the members at each of the concerts.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

TOWNSHIP MEETING.—On Friday evening, March 24th, the annual meeting of ratepayers was held in Mr. Brewis's school. The attendance was not large, owing to it being so little known amongst the ratepayers. The Rev. C. T. Quirk, Rector of Golborne, presided. Mr. Mather, assistant over- seer, and Mr. Bennie, surveyor, were called upon to read the accounts for the past year. Both accounts were passed as read. A highway rate of Bd. in the pound was moved and carried for the ensuing year. Mr. Bennie was again elected surveyor for the year, and the following gentlemen were elected members of the Parochial Committee :—Messrs. Brewis, W. Mitchell, T. Mitchell, T. Pierpoint, J. Unsworth, sen., J. Unsworth, jun., W. Garton, A. Jackson, J. Fearns, J. Low, WI H. Arnott, aad R. Fairhurst. LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The members of the above Asso- ciation met on Monday evening last, in the large room of the Association, to hear Mr. Jackson submit the rules for the guidance of the members of the Debating Society which is being formed in connection with the Association. BREACH OF THE INLAND REVENUE LAWS.—At Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Dr. Worsley, of Golborne and Lowton, was charged with not signing and delivering a declaration as required by the laws of the Inland Revenue. —lt was stated that it had come to the knowledge of the local officer of the Inland Revenue for Newton district that the defendant employed a boy in such capatity as rendered him liable to pay the dues required by the revenue keepers of men iervants The usual form had been sent to defendant in order for him to fill it up and return, but he neglected to do so. A special form prescribed for such cases was then sent, but to this also no heed was paid,and the present course was then entered on.—The defendant stated that he had not returned the papers through inadvertence, and he had been under the impression that no license was required for a lad under 15. This he had since found was a mistake, and he was willing to take out a license.—A fine of 255. and costs was imposed.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

MEETING OF CREDITORS,—On Saturday morning a meet- ing of the creditors of Jonathan Ellison, Dog and Patridge Inn, New Springs, Aspull, joiner and beerseller, was held at the office of Mr. Lees, solicitor, King-street. The liabilities amounted to £156 10s. 5d., and the assets to £67 125. 6d. The meeting resolved that the estate be wound up in liquidation. Mr. J. Hill was ppointed trustee, with Messrs. G. J. Healey, T. Kenyon, and J. McLoughlan as a com- mittee of inspection. The debtor was granted his dischargef and the registration of the resolutions was entrusted to Mr. Lees.

FIRE IN GREENOUGH-STREET.—At one o'clock on Tues- day morning, a fire was discovered in the lock-up shop of James Ward, toy and provision dealer, 66, Greenough- street. An alarm was raised, and the police were promptly on the scene with the fire appliances from the Scholes police office. The hose was connected with the water main, and in the course of about forty minutes the fire was effectually got under. Upon a subsequent examinaticn it was found that it had broken out behind the counter, but from what cause could not be ascertained. Considerable damage was done to the stock in the shop, which is for- tunately covered by insurance. NOXIOuS VAPOURS PROM A CHEMICAL MANUFACTORY.— On Wednesday, at the Wigan County Court, before Mr. W. W. Ffoulkes, judge, Robert Gill, farmer, sued the Crook Chemical Company for £lB, the amount of damage to his crops by the emissioa of noxious vapours from the defen- dant company's works. It appeared that the complainant occupied a field adjoining the works, which he planted with potatoes in 1379 and 1880, and sowed with wheat in 1881. In all those years it was alleged that the crops had been damaged by noxious vapours coming from the works, the leaves of the potato plants being burnt off or rendered of a brown colour, and the wheat ears were also of the same colour. His Honour gave a verdict for damages of £l6.

div.head: ST. HELFNS (CORPORATION) WATER
div.p: ST. HELFNS (CORPORATION) WATER

BILL. • The petitions of the Corporation of Liverpool and the London and North-Western Railway Company against the bill were considered on Thursday by the Court of Referees. It is proposed in the bill to make and maintain additional waterworks and to borrow .£95,000. Mr. Pemberton, M.P., presided. Mr. O'Hara, on behalf of the Liverpool Corpora- tion, stated that an agreement was made in 1880 between the Corporations of St. Helens and Liverpool by which the latter was to snpply 2,000,000 gallons of water per day to the former on demand at the rate of Gd. per 1,000 gallons. This was the price at which the Liverpool Corporation got rid of the opposition of the St. Helens Corporation. ' Now the St. Helens Corporation came to Parliament ?or powers to supply thunselves with water, after putting the Liver- pool Corporation to the expense of so constructing their waterworks as to be able to comply with their obligation. The Corpozation of Liverpool, after the passing of the bill, would still be under this obligation of supplying the water, while they would have nothing to remunerate them for their outlay.—The court refused to grant the locus standi. Mr. Pope contended that the London and North-Western Rail- way Company had a locus standi against the bill, but his claim was disallowed.

At a special meeting of the Prescot School Board on Monday evening, it. was resolved to make a call upon the overseers for £240 for the next half-year. In the House of Commons on Tuesday a petition was presanted in favour of the new rules of procedure, from Pvscot,_by Lord Hartington.
Both Houses of Congress at Washington, have finally passed the bill granting Mrs. Garfield an annual pension of 55,000.

iHR PARCELS POST.—The Globe states that unexpected difficulties have arisen with respect to the proposed parcels post. The negotiations with the railway companies, which at one time were progressing rapidly, have been almost en- tirely suspended, in consequence of the exorbitant demands which have lately been made by the directors of several leadin a companies.

div.head: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.
div.p: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.

The Northwich Local Board have made arrangements with Mr. Jos. Lamb, jun., for the removal of house refuse, &c., during the ensuing twelve months. The ceremony of cutting the first sod in connection with the erection of a new church in Springfield, Sale, took place on Saturday, Mrs. Clegg, of Holly Bank, officiating. The church will be oblong in shape, containing nave and side aisles, and will seat 850 worshippers. It is to be erected at a cost of £7,000, of which £3,500 has been collected and promised. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A CHESHIRE SALTWORKS.—A horrible accident occurred on Saturday morning at Messrs. Verdin's saltworks, Marston. A man named Thomas Lamb, aged 27, Wilton-street, Northwich, was engaged filling rock into the grinding mill, and whilst standing over the aperture into which the rock is put his foot slipped and he fell into the machine and was literally ground to pieces, his body passing through wheels with teeth an inch and a half long. Deceased leaves a wife and three children. WORKING A HORSE IN AN ' UNFIT STATE. At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Henry Nield, Middle- wich, was .summoned for working a horse in an unfit condi- tion at Over on the 25th ult. P.C. Dunning said he saw the defendant in charge of a horse at High-street, Over, and ' en examining the animal he found a raw wound about the size of a five shilling piece on one of the shoulders, and a smaller wound on the other.—Police-sergeant Leather gave corroborative evidence, and defendant, who stated that the wounds were the consequence of a badly fitting collar, was ordered to pay the costs.—Jas. Woodward, who was sum- moned for causing the horse to be worked, was fined 103. and costs. PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE NANTIVICH WORKHOUSE. —At the meeting of the Nantwich Guardians, on Saturday, Mr. Bebbington said that from time to time when visiting the workhouse he had noticed that there was great insuffi- ciency of accommodation for the little children, and he thought the time had now come that an alteration should be made. He thought those who had gone through the house would agree with him that the old hospital was not only in- adequate for the requirements of the house, but also that the rooms for the accommodation of little children were too small. He thought they ought to form a committee to go into the matter, and seeing that Dr. Munroe was in the room he would like to ask his opinion of the subject.—The Chair- man thought it would be inexpedient to appoint the com- mittee that day, because the existence of the present Board was coming to a close.—Mr. Bebbington said the matter had been shelved from time to time, and he did not agree that it should be put off any longer.—Dr. Munro gave testimony as to the inferior accommodation both for hospital cases and little children. He had reported many times that it was sadly deficient. —Mr. Pearce supported Mr. Bebbing- ton's view, and MP. Byrd referred to the necessity for being careful in their expenditure of money.—After several other members had expressed their views, the matter was, on the suggestion of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, left over until the meeting of the new Board. SAD DEATH OF A FARMER'S WIFE.—An accident of a very melancholy nature occurred last week on the highway between Middlewich and Whatcroft. It appears that Mr. John Hesketh, of Whatcroft Farm, who is a waywarden for the township of Whatcroft, attended the meeting of the Northwich Highway Board, which was held at Sandbach on Thursday, the 16th inst., and drove towards home in the evening accompanied by his wife, Sarah Hesketh. On the road between Middlewich and Whatcroft he met a dog-cart owned by Mr. W. Jones, who was driving to Middlewich. Mr. Hesketh had no lamps, and it was very dark at the time. ' It would seem that the lights which were carried by Mr. Jones's vehicle somewhat baffled the horse, and it imme- diately began to be restive and shied, the consequence being that the trap was upset in the ditch on the roadside. Hear- ing a noise Mr. Jones returned to the spot and found both Mr. and Mrs. Hesketh beneath the overturned conveyance. with some difficulty he removed Mrs. Hesketh, but failed to extricate her husband until he had got assistance. Mrs. Hesketh appeared to be very seriously injured. They were both conveyed to Whatcroft Farm, and Dr. Moore' of Middlewich, was sent for and promptly arrived. Mr. Hesketh soon recovered, but Mrs. Hesketh suffered severely from the shock to the system. She, however appeared to be progressing favourably, and strong hopes were entertained of her ultimate recovery, but on Saturday symptoms of a grave character set iu, and she expired between three and four o'clock on Sunday morning. The deceased, who was 41 years of age, was well known in the district, and much sympathy is felt for her bereaved husband and family. Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquest on the body at What- croft Farm, Whatcroft, near Middlewich, when the jury- re- turned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

The annual Sunday school sermons were preached at the Congregational Church on Sunday last by the Rev. Hugh Campbell, of Wigan; and an address was given in the afternoon to the scholars by Mr. John McClure, 8.A., of Wigan. Collections amounting to £lB.los. were made. CRICKET EOM BOWLING CLon.—The annual general meet- ing of the Newton Cricket and Bowling Club was held on Thursday evening, at the Pied Bull Inn, Newton. Mr. Jas. Fairclough was appointed president, in the place of Mr. J. H. Bailey, deceased; and Mr. Pardey, Mr. Robert Stone, and Mr. Thos. Stone were appointed vice-presidents. The question of introducing the games of lawn tennis rnd quoits was discussed, but no decision was made. The club is in a satisfactory financial position, and there is a good list of matches arranged for next season. I.O.G.T.—HOpeI OF EARLESTOWN LODGE—The usual weekly entertainment was held in the Lodge Room? 15' Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Saturday evening last, Bro. George Clarke presiding, when it very good programme was gone through, sengs being given by Bros. Broomhall, Geo. ll.4ward, A. Allison, and a duet by Sisters A. Howard and M. J. Howarth ; readings by Bros. George Clarke and John Taylor; and a Lancashire sketch by Bro. John Warburton, L.O. Sister M. Clarke gave a recitation "Bus,' your own cherries." There was a very fair attendance of members and friends, who heartily enjoyed the meeting, which closed about D-30 p.m.—On Monday evening, at the usual weekly session, one candidate was initiated, after which a recess was called to admit the members of the Juvenile Temple, who, according to the programme, were to entertain the Adult Lodge. Bro. B. Preston, V.S.J.T., of Huyton, presided, and gave a very encouraging address, bearing chiefly on the work amongst the children, and the groat need for earnest efforts in trying to remove some of the great temptations which are so numerous around us, and which go so far to undo the good we may be able to accomplish. He asked that the children might be encouraged and assisted in 'their work, as they would have to take the places of those who would in a while be passing away to meet :their rewards ; and in order to fight the battle successfully it was necessary that they should be thoroughly trained for it. An excellent programme of melodies, songs, recitations, lex., was gone through in a most creditable manner indeed; and at the close of the entertainment votes of thanks were passed to Bro. Preston for his visit and address, to Bro. Edward New- man (Temple superintendent), Bro. George Clarke (cor..

pleasing to see Mr. Moon in the chair. (Hear, hear.) He spoke of the labour which could be accomplisht'd by per- severance, instancing the lives of George Stephenh'on, and Lord Eldon, the greatest Lord Chancellor the world ha,l ever seen. He believed that ordinary men, or men very ttl e above the ordinary, had done far more than men of genit:s by their perseverance, and they would overcome all diffi- culties if they would take for their motto, what Colonel McCorquodale called " Gladstone's motto." (Applause.) It was" Strive in the days of your youth to estimate aright I the precious hours and the precious opportunities that are I offered you." (Applause.) Addresses were afterwards delivered by Mr. Henry Stone, aid the Rev. T. R. Mathews.

The musical entertainment was given by the following well-known artistes :—Madame Laura Haworth, Miss H. Edwards, of Liverpool; Mr. Seymour Jackson, of Manches- ter; Mr. Geo. Wright, of Earlestown; The Liverpool Orpheus Glee Union: Alto, Mr. Child ; first tenor, Mr. Austin; second tenor, Mr. Lewis ;bass, Mr. Shimmin. The various items of the programme, as was to be expected with such a strong company, were given in good style, and the audience honoured Madame L. Haworth, Miss Edwards, and Mr. Geo. Wright with an encore. By the conclusion of the concert, the tea tables had been cleared away, and a ball was held in that part of the building. Dancing was kept up until a late hour next morning.

div.head: SHOCKING MURDER AND SUICIDE
div.p: SHOCKING MURDER AND SUICIDE
AT ST. HELENS.

A terrible tragedy has this week sent a shock through the inhabitants of St. Helens, more particularly the district of Sutton, where the tragedy was perpetrated. On Tuesday night, about half-past six o'clock, a shocking discovery was made in a house at Mill-brow, Sutton, occupied by Mr. Alfred Rawlinson, manager of the Lancashire Agricultural Chemical Company, Limited, whose works are at a short dis- tance from the St. Helens Junction, and midway from there and Mr. Rawlinson's residence. The house in which Mr. Rawlinson resides is at the summit of a brow, and is one of four new houses directly opposite the residence of Mr. Geo. Parr, who is the owner of them. That portion of Sutton is not thickly populated, being in the suburbs. The Rev. Mr. Vallancey's residence is in close proximity to the scene of the sad event. Mr. Rawlinson's family consisted of his wife (whose maiden name was Mary Ellen Arnold), 27 years of age, who was the daughter of an extensive boiler manufacturer of that name at Barnsley, and a child named Arnold Rawlinson. The couple had been married about two years, and it is stated they lived very comfortably together. On Tuesday morning, at breakfast time, Mr. Rawlinson, who is the son of a Congregational minister in Manchester, left home for business at the manure works, and his wife, who had the child in her arms, accompanied him to the garden gate, and took leave of him in her accustomed affectionate manner. In the course of the forenoon she was engaged assisting the servant in various household duties, and the two were in fre- quent communication. Between eleven and twelve o'clock in the forenoon she went upstairs informing the servant that she was going to lie down with the child, and about noon she went downstairs for the child's dinner, but partook of none herself, having told the servant to get her own dinner and not to prepare any for her. The girl did not consider this as unusual, and after dinner went about her work. During the afternoon, however, she saw 1 nothing of her mistress and did not communicate with her until six o'clock in the evening when she prepared tea. Tea , being , ready, she went upstairs, knocked at the bedroom 1 door, and announced that tea was ready. There was no res- ponse, and she repeated her call, at which Mrs. Rawlinson said "All right, I'll be down in a minute." The girl noticed that the door was loosely fastened by a small chain. About this time Mr. Rawlinson arrived home from business and his wife not coming down he went upstairs but found that the door of the room was fastened by a chain so that he could not open easily. He called to his wife several times, but receiving no answer, he then put his back to the door and burst it open. He was horrified at the sight which pre- sented itself to him. On the floor lay his wife with a dread- ful, gash in her throat, and by her side lay a razor with which it had been matte. She was in the midst of a pool of blood, and close beside her was a basin partly filled. From the position in which Mrs. Rawlinson was found it was evi- dent that she had in the first instance knelt over the basin and inflicted the wound from which she intended that the blood should run into the vessel. Through weakness she would be unable to remain in this position for any length of time, and would then fall into the position in which she was I found by her husband. The wound was very deep and long, I and Dr. Twyford gave his opinion that death must have re- sulted almost immediately after the infliction of the wound. Mr. Rawlinson then looked into the cradle, which was close ,to the bed, and he there found the child quite dead. No I marks of violence were found upon the child, and for some time the affair had a most mysterious laspect. The condition of Mr. Rawlinson, on making these discoveries, can be well imagined. He at once ran out and acquainted Mr. George Parr of the facts, and that gentleman forthwith visited the place and des• patched a messenger to St. Helens for Dr. Twyford. The room was examined, and it was noticed that the bed upon which the deceased lady would have lain, had she carried out her promise of lying down with the child, was quite straight as though it had been unused. If she had used it she must have made the bed again. In due time Dr. Twy- ford arrived, but said he could not account for the death or the child until a post mortent examination had been made. The sad occurrence has caused a great sensation throughout the district, the family being held in great respect. No reason can be assigned on the part of the deceased lady why she should have committed the rash act, unless it arose from the illness of a brother whom she regarded with great affec- tion. Mr. Rawlinson has only resided in the district about ten months, and during that time she has received letters from her family at Barnsley. These letters contained news of trouble and sickness in the family, arid it was noticed they had a dispiriting effect upon her. Recently she visited her home in Barnsley. Mrs. Rawlinson was not naturally of a melancholy disposition and was not regarded -as a likely person to commit so rash an act. On the contrary she is spoken of by the neighbours as a cheerful person, and kindly disposi- tioned. She was a member of the Plymouth Brethren, and was always looked upon as an earnest and sincere Christian. She was in the habit of distributing tracts of a religious character amongst the people of Sutton, and regu- larly walked three miles to her place of worship in St. Helens. On Tuesday morning, the day on which the deed was committed, she sang some sacred hymns, and played the pianoforte. There is nothing to lead one to suppose that the occurrence was due to any change in her husband's cir- cumstances. On Wednesday 4vening a letter was found ; behind a picture in the bedroom, which throws light on the I child's death. The letter was in the handwriting of Mrs. ' Rawlinson, and addressed to her husband. She attaches no blame to anyone, but says that she has had the kindest of husbands. The letter further stated that she could not live any longer, and that she could not pass away without taking the child with her. THE INQUEST YESTERDAY MORNING.
The inquest on the bodies of deceased woman and child was held yesterday morning at the Mill Brow public-house, by Mr. Driffield, coroner. Mr. Oppenheim represented Mr. Rawlinson and relatives.

Eliza Walton said she had been with Mrs. Rawlinson as servant for the last ten months. They had only one child. Mr. Rawlinson on Tuesday left home at nine o'clock, and• was not expected to return till night. Mrs: Rawlinson was as usual in her talk, but very quiet. Witness remarked nothing curious about her. She was singing in the morning. Mrs. Rawlinson generally prepared the dinner, but on that day she told witness to get her own dinner, and not to prepare any for her. It was not an unusual thing to be without • dinner on Tuesdays, as Mr. Rawlinson was generally away. Mrs. Rawlinson and the child were up stairs the greater part of the forenoon. Between eleven and twelve o'clock she came down and took the child's dinner up stairs between one and two. Witness was not to wait for deceased to come down stairs to fold the clothes as she was going to Vy down with the child. Wit- ness had no more communication with her until ten minutes to six in the evening, when she went up to the bedroom door and told her that it was nearly six o'clock, and that tea was ready. She answered that she would be down in a minute. Witness then went down stairs and Mr. Rawlin son came in. He told witness to go up stairs to tell her to come down. She went up, found the door fastened by a chain as before, but could not make her hear. Mr. Rawlinson then went up, broke the chain, and entered the room. He called for witness to come up to look at de- ceased lying on the floor. Witness went up and saw the deceased lying in a pool of blood. She was quite dead, but warm. The baby was in the cradle laid straight out on his back, and was quite cold and dead. There was no blood about the baby, nor was there anything tied round its throat. Mr. Rawlinson went across for Mr. Parr, with whom he returned, and they went up stairs together. They then sent for the police, and the sergeant came down. Wit- ness did not see any paper in the room, nor the razor, but Mr. Rawlinson saw the latter. Witness had not known the , deceased to talk wildly, but during the two or three days [ previous to Tuesday she was rather quiet, but talked [ rationally. Witness had not the least suspicion about the state of her mind, and she was very good and fond of the child. There was nothing wrong between her aed her hus- band. He was always kind to her. Deceased had been very much put about in regard to her brother's illness, and she was often talking abont him, and about her halter being I ill. Witness knew of no other trouble. I Police-sergeant Banks deposed : I got there between " seven and eight, shortly after hearing. Dr. Twyford had just reached. I found the two deceased, the elder was lying on the floor on her right side, with her throat cul, and dead. She was quite warm, the razor produaed was open on the floor and close by her right hanl. The letter pro- duced I found behind a frame of photographs over the chimney-piece. It was addressed "A. J. Rawliason, Mill Brow, Sutton." As Mr. Rawlinson had gone to Man- chester, I left it there until the following day. I went in company with P.C. Middlebrook, and saw Mr. Rawlinson and asked him if he had found any letter. He said " No," and I theta told him I would find him one. Rawlinson got hold of the letter, and before he opened it said it was her writing. He then opened it and commenced crying. Pr. LECTURE AT ST. HELENS ON "DICK WHITTINGTON." The Rev. W. G. Pascoe, on Monday night, delivered a Ilecture on " Dick Whittington, the famous Lord Mayor of London," in the Nutgrove Wesleyan Chapel. There was a good attendance. The lecturer. in the introductory portion of his lecture, dissented from any and all who would for a moment prefer any preceding age to that in which we live. This was as it should be. It would be a monstrous shame if we were not better and wiser than our forefathers. We had their experience, and wisdom and example to guide us in forming our judgment and shaping our actions and we had our own brains withal; and if our age was not better than any preceding age it was a grave reflection on us. England five centuries ago was a very different spot. There were only about 21 millions of inhabitants (little more than half as many as the London of to-day), though 25 years before there were probably as many as four millions, but pestilence and "Black death" had carried away more than a third of the inhabitants. Astrology was practised by medical men, towns were un- drained, and all parts of the kingdom were infested with highwaymen. It was the age of the rise of the labourers from the serfdom of the past, and it was the age when the English language became the language of the court and of the bar. It appeared a hopeless task to discover the family of a magi who came to London as a boy in the 14th century, who lived there all his life, and whose records ror centuries had passed into oblivion. But one fact about Whittington furnished an enthusiastic antiquary with a clue, and that was his coat of arms which was presented to him by the King. According to the will of Robert Whittington (1424), Pauntley, in Gloucestershire, wis the burial place of the family. In the ordinary legend of Whittington he was re- presented as of obscure oLigin, and utterly friendless. Pro- bably it added to the romance of his career. But his father was a knight and country squire, and his mother belonged to the Manse's, a Devonshire family of some rank. In 1350 the head of the family was Sir Wm.Whittington, who was outlawed in 1358, for what offence it was not known. Dr. Lvson's conjectures were because he married the widow of Sir Ihomasde Berke ley without the royal consent. The famous " Dick" was the yougest son, and his birth must have been about the year 1358. After describing the difficulty experienced in those days in getting the sons of wealthy families on in the world, the lecturer described "Dick's" journey to London ia the hope of there becoming a printer. Then, only the sons of good families could be admitted to the seven years' apprenticeship of the divers callings in city life, hence many of the traders of London boasted of their noble descent. Having described some of the principal features of London, a city then occupying a smaller area than Hyde Park, Mr. Pascoe traced Whittington's career, and spoke of his be- coming master of the honourable Company of Mercers in 1398, 1407, and 1420, as many times as he held the highest civic dignity in the city. The lecturer exposed some por- tions of the legend and corroborated others. The cat story was rejected by some who fully accepted the truth of the great success of the man. But the story was so interwoven with the name of Whittington that it could not without great violence be thrown overboard. There was not much doubt that the foundations .of his fortune lay in the sale of his cat. That in early times cats were very valuable there was no manner or doubt. He showed that the cat was held in great estimation in those times, and pointed out that there used to exist in the Mercer's Hall his portrait, dated 1536, having a black and white cat on his left hand. That picture was lost, but another portrait, the lecturer said, exists in which " Dick " was re- presented in the robes of Mayor, his hand resting on a cat. In the house in Gloucester which was once occupied by the Whittingtons whilst some repairs were being executed in 1862, there was dug up a stone,probibly part of a chimney, on which in bass relief was represented the figure of a boy carrying a cat. But though the truth of the story seemed established there was no need to accept all the sentimental nonsense with which it had been associated. It was quite enough to suppose that Sir John Fitz-Warren permitted his 'prentices, when his ships went to sea, to make their own little ventures. It was commonly done by owners of vessels even to-day. There Whittington would very probably hear from the sailors of the pest of rats and mice in certain places they visited, and of the value of a cat in such places. What more natural than that the aspiring 'prentice boy would go out and purchase a cat and send it out as his venture to fetch as much as could be got for it. It may have been a jewel which proved of considerable value. At any rate it was the foundation of his success. He gradually and steadily advanced in wealth. After speaking of-' Dick's " wooing and winning his master's daughter, after he himself bad started in business, Mr. Pascoe briefly traced his official acts as mayor and member of Parliament. He spoke of his religious life. It could not be asserted that Whittington necame a Lollard, though it appeared certain he favoured the doctrines of Wiclif. In conclusion he said that as they looked back through 500 years of strangely chequered Eng- lish life, they found that the same principles which uplifted society now operated then. They saw that However men might be deluded by the catchwords" luck "and " chance," diligence was the only sure path to success; that virtue was the quality which men most loved to honour, and still the grand truth was pressed upon everyone that a good man's life was an inspiration to all
