div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
21011DAI.—Before Messrs. James Brundrit (chairman) and Alfred Thomas. _

OVER SEERS' APPOINTMENT—The following were ap- pointed overseers by the magistrates for the various town- ships named :—Aston Grange: George Percival and Wm. Wilkinson. Aston-by-Sutton: George Percival and William Wilkinson. Clifton: Messrs. William Baker and Joseph Stokes. Halton: Messrs. Thomas Wright and Hugh Rowe. Norton: Messrs. Thomas Percival and Thomas Acton. Runcorn: William Handley and William Whittaker. Stock- ham: Joseph Wallworth Baguley and Daniel Tinsley Baguley. Sutton: Wiliam Fowles and Thomas Rigby. Weston: Richard Clarke and John Poole. THE SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN CONTRACTOR. DEFENDANT ORDERED TO PAY £2O.
Mr. Thonaas Cliffe, street cleansing _contractor to the

Runcorn Board of Commissioners, and who lives in Ross- street, was charged with having on the 16th ult., assaulted and beaten his wife Mrs. Hannah Cliffe.—Mr. Burton appeared for complainant, and Mr. W. H. Linaker repre- sented defeniant.—The court was crowded. Mr. Burton, in opening the case, said he shoald call certain evidence in support of the charge, and then he should ask the magistrates to adjudge the defendant to have been guilty of an assault within the meaning of the 24th and 25th Vic., cap. 100, sec. 43. If the Bench so decided, he should then ask that, in addition to any punishment which they might think the defendant deserved, to make an order that complainant should not be any longer obliged to cohabit with him, or, in other words, that they should grant her an order of judicial separation under section 43, which was as follows, "If a husband shall be convicted summarily or otherwise, of an aggravated assault, within the meaning of the above section upon his wife, the court, or magistrate before whom he shall be so convicted, may, if satisfied that the future safety of the wife is in peril, order that the wife shall be no longer bound to cohabit with her husband; and such order shall have tha force and effect in all respects of a decree of judicial separation on the ground of cruelty." The complainant and defendant had been married some 20 years. Mr. Cliffe was a contractor very well known in Runcorn. There was one child by his marriage with com- plainant—a daughter, 16 years of age. For some years the couple appeared to have lived unhappily together; in fact, for the last four or five years defendant had treated his wife with systematic cruelty. Sometimes it bad been his pleasure to turn her out of doors at all hours of the night, whilst at others he had kicked her, and struck her in the face and other parts of the body. On four or five different occasions the violence defendant had inflicted had caused his wife to put herself under medical treatment. Mr. Linaker contended that the line of remark pursued by Mr. Burton was calculated to prejudice the case for the defence.

The Chairman said the magistrates would be guided in their decision by the evidence produced, and not by the speech made by the solicitor. Mr. Ashton (magistrates' clerk) remarked that Mr. Burton was entitled to lay before the court anything which was material for the purpose of showing that the safety of his client was emperilled. Mr. Burton went on to say that in November, 1880, defen- dant was brought before the court, but the proceedings wike withdrawn. However, since that time his conduct had been no better, and on the evening of the 16th ult., he, withoat any adequate provocation, chased his wife into the field at the back of his own house, and then threw after her the spade produced, which was a very ugly weapon indeed. The spade hit her on the forehead, and caused a very,serious wound. She afterwards went to Dr. Motzrita, who dressed the wound. Defendant next went out, and on his return again attacked complainant, striking her in the mouth with his fist. Before retiring to rest Mr. Cliffe, as he went from room to room in the house, said that if he could get hold of his wife he would murder her. As to the question of defendant's means, he believed he was in possession of an income of £4OO or £5OO a year, and possessed of a freehold house in Greenway- road.

Mr. Linaker contended that the statement as to defendant's income was altogetleer inaccurate; and the question of the terms on which a judicial separation should be agreed to might easily be decided by a private negotiation between the two persons interested, without any undue exposure of Mr. Cliff e's affairs. Complainant was then called, and said she had been married 20 years to defendant. For some years their married life had been very unhappy. The difficulty commenced about six years ago, through the defendant being concerned in a certain divorce case. He had abused her night and day, and had struck her with walking sticks, and, in fact, _ _

nearly all sorts of weapons. She had had to see Dr. McDougall and Dr. Mouritz half-a-dozen times. On one occasion she went to the doctor and it was found she was suffering from pleurisy through defendant's striking her. She had also had her ribs "staved in," on both sides of her body, through defendant's conduct. She had frequently been afraid to go to bed, and had had sometimes to sit up all night through fear of his violence. She had been kept out of the house all night many times by him. In Novem- ber, 1880, she took proceedings in that court against defen- dant owing to being abused about the head and face by him. She went to the doctor about the matter, but Mr. Linaker withdrew the legal proceedings. On the night of the 16th ultimo defendant came home, and she handed him a letter containing a bill for attending 'upon his mother. Defendant said the account would not have been sent but for her. A few words took place between them, and he ran her into the yard. She went into the adjoining field, and he threw over the wall a spade, which struck her on the head. She screamed, on which defendant came, and took her into the yard, and locked the door. The wound caused by the spade bled very badly. Defendant's aunt wished to fetch a doctor, and she agreed she should do so. They afterwards, however, went to one, who attended to her wounds. When she returned home defendant came in, and remarked "I think you will have had enough soon." She answered "I think you will soon, but you will have to pay for this." Defendant then came out of the sitting-room, struck her in the face, and next put her mother into the field, and fastened the house windows. After she had gone out, defendant followed, and, as she was talking to her sister-in-law in the field, he said to the latter "You can take her to your house and keep her." The sister replied that she should not, as he (defendant) was more able to do so than she was. Defendant then struck her (complainant) on the mouth, making it bleed. She afterwards went into the house, and her sister gh her a cup of tea. Later on in the night her husband came home tipsy. She followed him, as he went from room to room in the house, stating that he would murder her if he caught her. Her sister-in-law said she should not stay in the house after what had taken place. She then left, and did not see her husband until last Monday, when he appeared in court. She dared not go back to live with him, as she was in danger of her life both night and day. Frequently when defendant had abused her at night, on the following morning he had assailed her with a pillow, and struck her about the head with it until she was not able to stand upon her feet. She had often been attacked by him in the night, and had risen and screamed "Murder," until the neighbours at the next house had rapped at the wall, requesting quietness. Cross-examined by Mr. Linaker : Is defendant the only one to blame for this sort of thing takin,, place? Well,l may certainly have had a few little faults myself.--On the morning of the 16th March had you anything to drink? I had neither seen nor tasted any.—ls it a fact, or not, that you are accus- tomed to taking drink to excess? No, it is not.—ls it a fact that you are in the habit of taking drink to the extent that it makes you tipsy? No, I am not. My husband does not trust me with the housekeeping money. He has been very mean in providing for the house lately.—Has he alleged that you spent the money in drink? He has said so, but it is not true .that I have spent it in that manner.— _ _ _

You admit that on the Saturday when your sister-in-law was 1 at the house, he gave you a sovereign. Now, how much of • that went in drink? Perhaps about a shilling.—lsit not a fact that you are in the habit of following him about the house, cursing him? No; it is not true. Certainly I have some times cursed him in the house, but I have been forced to it.—ls it not a fact that you are in the habit of pawning things he gives you? No, it is not; It is my daughter who does that,—Ha 3 Margaret Barlow ever pawned anything for you? No, she has not. Re-examined by Mr. Burton: Defendant had frequently- gone out on a morning in the early part of the week, and commenced drinking, and continued to do so until nearly the end of it, leaving us in the house without tea, sugar, or butter.

Mrs. Griffiths, wife. of Thomas Griffiths, stonemason, Heath-road, said that on the night of the 16th ult. she was crossing the field near defendant's house. She saw Mr. Cliffe push his wife out of the door, and when she had got into the field, look over the wall, and, after finding where she was standing, throw the spade at her. Mrs. Whitlow, wife of Peter Whitlow, Ross-street, stated that she heard the quarrelling, but did not see the spade thrown. She had,however, seen defendant run his wife out of the house on another occasion, and then throw a tile after her.

Dr. Mouritz said he had known complainant since he came to Runcorn, and had attended her on several Occasions for assaults, when he found her body black and blue in various parts. At one visit, be found her eyes "banged up," and both of them were black. When she visited him on the last oce.,.:fion but one, she was suffering from pleurisy, and scarcely able to draw her breath. He found her side all black, and she attributed her condition to the defendant's violence. On the 16th ult. she came to him, and he dressed the wound (upon her forehead) which was about 21: inches long, and the upper part of it was exposed to the bone. The wound was a dangerous one, and he did not consider complainant out of danger from erysipelas yet. She was formerly a woman who had robust health, but was now delicite, and the treat- ment she bad received wou!d have a tendency to injure her health. For the defence, Thomas Prohin, carter, was the first wit- ness called. He said he had on several occasions heard i complainant make ass of bad language n her husband's house, when in liquor. Mr. Cliff) had several times asked him to come into the house and hive a look at the sort of helpmeet he had. On these occasions, he saw complainant lying on the floor in a drunken sleep, and there was no fire in the grate. He had seen her in that condition several times recently. On the evening of the 15th ult. he had to go into the house for the purpose of stating what work he bad done, and he saw Mrs. Cliffs run her husband out of the door, and use very bad language to him. One day he (witness) aund her selling a man some tools for fourpence, and "he made her put them back again." Cross-examined by Mr. Burton: You never saw defendant do these sort of things? No.-1 suppose Mr. Cliffe is a sober, ! upright sort of a man? (Laughter). I have not often seen him worse for liquor.—Speak up and let us hear what you haye

to say on this part of the matter. You are a big man, and can surely speak a little louder. Ncw, have you seen defen- dant tipsy continuously? Well. I have seen him drunk several times, but I have not seen him abusing his wife.— What time do you leave your work at his place? About half-past five in the afternoon. The Chairman (to witness) : Which of them have you seen drunk the oftener? I could not tell, sir.

• The Chairman, who expressed his dissatisfaction with the manner in which the witness replied to the questions in cross-examiimation, said he supposed it was a case of six of one and half a dozen of the other, as far as the drunkenness was concerned. (Laughter). Joseph Aldridge, a horse driver in the employ of the de- fendant, said the habits of Mrs. Cliffe were drunken, and she wag given to using bad language frequently. A man named Walker said that on the 16th ult. he was at the yard belonging to Mr. Cliffe, and heard his wife use language of a most irritating character. Samuel Lee, carter, Frodsharn, stated that on the 16th ult. he was on defendant's premises, and heard a violent quarrel going on in the house. Complainant called her husband a whoremonger, and remarked' that his character was well known in Runcorn, and she would make it equally well known in Frodsham. _

Mrs. Mary Hewitt, a respectable looking woman, sister to defendant, said she had been at Mr. Cliffe's house for about five weeks, owing to the illness of her mother. On the Saturday before the assault, complainant told her husband that if he would give her the wages for the week "she would be as right as she ought to be." The money was handed to her, and complainant conducted herself all right until five o'clock in the afternoon, when defendant brought in some fish for her to cook. Complainant went into the kitchen for this purpos2, and on defendant going there, she hit him across the mouth with the fish, and then walked into the yard, where she commenced pulling faces at him, and using language of a terrible des- cription. Complainant was "fanatic drunk" at the time. She was positive that defendant did not give her provoca- tion. After defendant had gone upstairs, she said to. Mrs. Cliffe, "You might be quiet, as mother is so ill." Her reply to this request was "I won't; I will make him either hang for me, or I will hang for him." During most of the five weeks complainant had been under the influence of drink. Mr. Linaker, in addressing the Bench for the defence, said he would at once admit, on behalf of his client, that he did, after great provocation, put complainant out of the house into the yard, and also throw over the wall at her the shovel produced in court. He was not present, personally, to apologise for Mr. Cliffs, or to excuse his conduct, but he trusted the Bench would take into consideration that all the blame was not on one side. Whatever might have been the cause of disagreement between the parties—and it had been hinted at by Mr. Burton—that could be no justification of the course of conduct complainant had been pursuing for the last three or four years. He was instructed that during the time named Mrs. Cliffe had given way to habits of drunkenness, and neglected her household duties. Fre- quently when defendant had come home, he had found her drunk in the house, the fires out, and no food cooked for his meals. Such a course of conduct as that was not one calcu- lated to induce a man to treat his wife with that kindness which she ought to receive. When Mrs. Cliffe was under the influence named, she had been in the habit of using language of a very provoking and tantalising character, which no doubt had reference to a certain event in their married life. Men were but human, and complainant had so irritated and excited defendant, that he on some occasions used violence which he ought not to have done. On .behalf of Mr. Cliffe, he should raise no objection to the proposal for a judicial separation, for as matters now were, he was satis- fied that he could not live with his wife in any comfort and safety. If the Bench made such an order, he (the speaker) was quite prepared to confer with Mr. Burton as to the pay- ment of a weekly sum which would be satisfactory to both parties. The Chairman said the magistrates had carefully con- sidered the case, which was really a very serious and grave one, as defendant must himself be aware. This sort of thing had been going on for a period of some years and it was a question with the magistrates, whether Mr. years, had not really brought it on by his own conduct in the past, for his wife was not always a drunkard, even if it was really a fact that she was one now. Another point arose for considera- tion, and that was whether defendant was not really as bad as his wife, as he had for a long time been in the habit of drinking. However' under no circumstances had Mr. Cliffe any right to assault his wife in the manner in which he had. The evidence of the doctor showed that the case might have been a far more serious one, and it was fortunate for defend- ant that he did not stand there arraigned upon the capital charge. Whatever complainant had done, defendant had no right to throw a spade over a wall at her. Such an act was not manly, and it was not such as* Mr. Cliffe ought to have been guilty of to a man, much less to a woman whom he had promised to love and cherish. The only difficulty with which the Bench had had to contend in coming to a decision was whether they ought not to commit defendant to gaol without the option of a fine; but they had come to the decision not to do this but to give him another chance. He would, however, have inflicted upon him the highest penalty which the justices had the power to impose, viz., £2O, or, in default of payment, two months' imprisonment. The costs, which were £0 45., would be included in the £2O. _ _

Mr. Burton said he must now apply for an •order of judicial separation on the part of complainant. He asked that Mr. Cliffs might be called upon topay Li per week. Some discussion took place upon the matter, and even the offer of 153. per week was opposed by Mr. Linaker, as being more than defendant could afford. The Chairman said the magistrates were surprised there should have been any difficulty when so small a sum was asked. They should have thought defendant would have been only too glad to accept it. An order would be made upon him to pay 15s. per week. Mr. Linaker : I am instructed to ask if you will allow him until to-morrow in which to pay the £2O. Mr. Brundrit : I have nothing to do with that. It is in the hands of the court. Defendant ultimately found the money, and was dis- charged from custody.

FIGHTING IN TILE STREET.—Henry Reynolds and John Rowbottom were summoned for causing a breach of the peace. —P.C. Clarke said that on the 19th ult., he was on duty in Norfolk-street in plain clothes and saw the two defendants fighting. He separated them and made them go home. Er ch defendant was ordered to enter into recognizances of £lO each to keep the peace six months, and pay 7s. 6d. costs.

FOURTEEN DAYS' IMPRISONMENT FOR A" JOKE."—Robert Henry Barker, a young man described as a stonemason, was charged with stealing three handkerchiefs, the property of Wm. Dutton, a watchmaker in the employ of Mr. Imison, dawnbroker, Widnes.—Prosecutor said he visited Runcorn on Saturday night, and met the prisoner at Coffey's lodging- house. They agreed to visit certain public-houses, and amongst others, went to the Royal. They next called at Mr. Unsworth's, where prosecutor purchased three hand- kerchiefs. Whilst walking to the lodging-house, he felt the prisoner's hand in his pocket, and as soon as he bad taken it out, missed the articles. He said nothing until they entered the house, when he told Coffey. Barker then struck him (witness) thrae times, and he afterwards gave information to P.C. Clarke, who took the prisoner into custody, and found the handkerchiefs near where he had been sitting.—Prisoner, who said the handkerchiefs were taken in a joke, was sent to gaol 14 days, with hard labour. LICENSING MATTERS.—Mrs. Lee was granted permission to sell at the Clarendon Hotel, Church-street, under her late husband's license.
YESTERBAY.—Before Messrs. Charles Reynolds (chairman
and C. W. Hazlehurst.

A SON ROBBING HIS FATHER.—John Henry Turner, a young man, was charged with stealing a pair of boots, value 95., the property of his father, Henry Turner, Granville- street.—The prisoner works at a Widnes chemical manufac- tory, and it was stated that he took the boots from the house and pledged them at Mr. Imison's through a woman named Grimes. Prisoner, who had been "on the spree," was apprehended on Thursday morning, in a house in Mill- street. The father did not wish to press the case, and the prisoner was discharged.

div.head: WHITECROSS WIRE AND IRON COMPANY, MUTED, V. SAVILLE AND OTHERS.
div.p: THE WHITECROSS WIRE AND IRON COMPANY, MUTED, V. SAVILLE AND OTHERS.

In the Court of Appeal at Westminster, on Monday, before Lord Coleridge and Lords Justices Holker and Brett, the case of the Whitecross Wire and Iron Co., Limited, v. Saville and others was part heard, and concluded on Tues- day. This was an action brought by the plaintiffs, who are wire manufacturers, carrying on business at Warrington. On the 7th October, 1876, they shipped from London in the Himalaya, a sailing vessel belonging to the defendants, 50 coils of fence wire of the value of £l6O for a customer at Wellington, in New Zealand. They took the precaution to have the cargo insured with the New Zealand Insurance Company. The Himalaya arrived safely at Wellington on the 25th January, 1877, and got alongside the wharf to dis- charge her cargo. On the 16th of February a fire broke out in the hold of the vessel, and, in order to extinguish it, water was poured upon that portion of the cargo that was undis- charged. The plaintiff's goods were at the bottom of the ship, and they were damaged by water to the extent of £56 is. Bd. A claim was sent in to the underwriters, who objected to pay on the ground that the damage done was in order to extinguish a fire in the hold of the vessel, and that the loss should be compensated for on a general average. In the end the underwriters paid the damage claimed by the plaintiffs on the understanding that- they should be at liberty to sue the owners of the vessel. The underwriters accordingly took proceedings against the owners, and the case was tried before Baron Pollock, in London, when he gave judgment in favour of the underwriters, be being of opinion that the loss should be compensated for on the general average contribution. Against this judgment the defendants now appealed. Sir H. Giffard, Q.C., and Mr. Pollard were counsel for the appellants • and Mr. Cohen, Q.C., and Mr. F. Hollansl. For the appellants it was con- tended that the pouring of the water on the cargo was un- necessary, and that the vessel being iron she would not have been destroyed, and she was never in danger of des- truction. Lord 'Justice Brett supposed that she had got decks of wood, masts' and other wood fittins.—The court confirmed Baron Pollock's judgment, and the appeal was dismissed with costs.
Habits are soon assumed, but when wa strive to strip them off 'tis being flayed alive.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 1, 1882

SAD CHARGE AGAINST A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER.— Margaret Sullivan, an elderly woman, ani her daughter, Mary Sullivan, about 22 years of age, were charged with stealing a pair of boots and several yards of flannel, the property of Mr. Samuel Reed, draper, Albert-road.--Prosecu- tor said that the younger prisoner was in his employ as domestic servant, up to the 23rd ult. She had no authority to pledge the boots or take the flannel, which, together,were worth 7s. sd.—John Ward, pawnbroker, Victoria- street, said the elder prisoner brought the boots to • his shop to pledge. She said they were her daughters, who had only had them on once. He gave her 35. upon them.--Sergeant Strickland took the prisoners into custody. The daughter said the boots had been given to,her by Mr. Reed, who told her to pawn them and anything which she obtained upon them above 35., them, might have for herself. At the house of the mother, in Leigh-street, he (witness) found the stolen flannel in a cupboard in the front room. Mrs. Sullivan said her daughter had brought the flannel home on the previous night, and obtained it upon credit from the prosecutor. The daughter afterwards said she had given laid. per yard for it, and also stoutly denied stealing the boots. Both priso- ners wept bitterly at the end of the case.—From the state- ment of Superintendent Barker, it appeared they bad been before the Bench previously on minor chorges.—Each of them was sent to gaol 14 days with hard labour. A LIVELY NHIGHBouRHOOD.—Mary Power and Kate Cannon, two young women, were charged with unlawfully wounding Johanna Kerwan, an old woman living in Water- street.—Complainant's head was bandaged; she sat in a chair ,a hilst giving her evidence, and altogether appeared de- termined to make the most of whatever injury she had sus- tained. She allegod that on the previous Tuesday night the two women set upon her with pieces of "slag," and after they had used up their supply of this kind of ammunition, one gathered more of it, whilst the other continued the cannonade. She alleged that her head wak very badly cut by one of the pieces of "slag," and she was covered with blood, so that she had to visit a medical man who advised her to see Dr. Cooper "as the case was too serious for him to undertake." Another piece of "slag" cut a lump of flesh out of her right arm.—A woman was called who stated she saw the assault committed —Superin- tendent Barker reminded the Bench,that the complainant had that day been fined for having been drunk.—P.C. Laing was put in the witness box, and said that the row, of which he believed the assault to be a part, had been kept up be- tween a number of people for an entire fortnight. He had visited the neighbourhood a number of times with the object of securing some of the disturbers, but they had always decamped upon seeing him in the distance.—Power was fined 10s. and costs, and the other defendant ss. and costs. _ _

ANOTHER CASE OF UNLAWFULLY WOUNDlNG.—Catherine Brennan was charged with unlawfully wounding Catherine McCormick, on the 27th ult.— Superintendent Barker said the complainant was unable to appear, and upon his appli- cation, the magistrates adjourned the hearing of the case until Wednesday next.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WEDNBGDAY.—Before Me;srs. A. Fletcher (chairman) and

R. Pilkington. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT ifYouti.—A number of people were summoned by the Widnes School Board, who were repre- sented by Mr. O. H. Danby, their clerk. The cases were proved by school attendance officers Davies, Wood, and Joynson, and the following were each ordered to pay 55., including costs :—John Houghton, John Smith, and Eliza- beth Ireland. An attendance order was made upon Jabez Rostrance, in the case of a child named Mary Whitfield. The hearing of a summons against Dennis Murphy was adjourned for one month. A FIERCE WOMAN.—Catherine Carey was charged with making a row in the street, and assaulting P.C. Barker.— The officer said that on Saturday night he found the prisoner in Waterloo-road, fighting with another woman. He asked her to go away several times, but she declined. He then took hold of her to take her to the police station, on which she bit him on both hands.—Superintendent Barker said that the prisoner had only just come out of gaol, wiaere she had been undergoing three months' imprisonment, and she had been frequently convicted.—Prisoner gave a brief sketch of her history for some time past to the Bench, and observed that up to the last two years no one could say anything against her. She commenced her difficulties at the date named, when her bad husband put her in gaol. When her tbrm of imprisonment terminated, she came out to find her husband dead and buried. This man was so tender hearted that he left her in such straits that she had to go into the workhouse to be confined.—The Chairman said the prisoner would not be dealt with for the case of breach of the peace, but in the other she would have to pay a fine of 203. and costs, or in default, go to gaol one month. A FORMER SURVEYOR TO THE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD IN COURT.—Charles Allcard, who formerly was surveyor to the Widnes Local Board, and some two years ago took a very prominent part in connection with the Ratepayers' Association, was summoned for having been drunk on the morning of the 17th ult.—P.C. Ross said he found defendant lying druok and incapable near to his own house at Crow- wood. Allcard was so inebriated that he could not rise. Defendant's wife came out, and he then saw him safe in his own yard, informing him at the same time that he would be summoned.—Defendant cross-examined the officer as to the exact spot where his house was, and put in a document which was understood to be a plan of the locus in quo.—He was informed by the Bench that his questions had not the slightest relevancy to the matter under censideration.—De- fendant : Well, I will pass that point over, but I want you to bear it in mind. I also state distinctly that the officer was not there at the time he states. Defendant said that on the night referred to he had been to Runcorn, which place he left at about five minutes to eleven. Before he arrived at his own house, he must, therefore, have walked a distance of about four miles, and gone past several dangerous places about Crow-wood, so that if he had not been sober he would, in all probability, have met with some accident. It was quite true that he stumbled when near his own house owing to the effect of suddenly coming upon the light from the window. The reason why be did not get up immediately he was seen by the police constable, was that if he had at- tempted to do so he would have torn his clotheswith the briars. He was on his own ground at the time.—The son of defen- dant, a young man, stated that it was the custom of the family to put a light in the house window, so as to show the way down the walk, and they had often to take out a candle to let persons who were coming to the house see the path. On hearing defendant coming down the lane, Ma said, "There is pa coming, and he has walked into the hedge in- stead of through the gateway." Pa next shouted "Ma, I have fallen into the hedge; you had better give me your hand.' Defendant was perfectly sober, and he (witness) was with him taking instructions for the next day for one hour and a half after he returned.—Superintendent Barker: How often have you been convicted? Twice ?—Witness: That has nothing to do with this case.—The Chairman: Yes it has.—Witness then admitted be had been convicted in that court for felony.il—Defendant denied that he was other than perfectly sober on the occasion referred to. In reply to the Superintendent, he said he had two glasses of sherry whilst the business was going on at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn. After further questioning, he replied that he also had a small Irish whiskey and a glass of beer at the house. This was all he had, "as near as he could tell." He would swear that he had not a score of glasses. He also called at Mr. Hayes beerhouse, Ashridge-street, Runcorn, that night, and asked for a glass of ginger ale. He would not swear he had not also a glass of ale at the same house.—Defendant • was fined ss. and Bs. 6d. costs. _ _ _ _ _ _

• A QUEEN-STREET DlSTURBER.—Catherine Matthews was convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Laing, of having been , guilty of causing a great disturbance in Queen-street, on the 18th ult.—Superintendent Barker said this was defendant's 25th appearance, and in January of the present year she was sent to goal two months in default of finding sureties.— Defendant was ordered to find sureties to keep the peace for three months, herself in £lO and two in £5 each.--Mary Robinson was summoned for a similar offence in West-street. —An officer stated that on the 18th tilt., the defendant col- lected a crowd of about 200 people in the street, and declined to go into her house, though requested several times.—Two witnesses were examined in the case, awl the Bench dis- missed the summons on Robinson paying 7s. 6d. costs. YourrtFut, GAMBLERS.—Richard Grace and John Tobin, two lads, were each fined 6d. and 7s. 6d. costs, for playing at pitch and toss in Sankey-street, on the 19th inst. OBSTRUCTING TRH FocerPs.TH.—Andrew Gallagher was summoned for wheeling a barrow upon the public footpath, in Waterloo-road, on the 22nd ult.—Defendant said he did not know he was doing wrong, and on Superintendent Barker stating he had no wish to press the case, the sum- mons was withdrawn. VANDALISM AT WIDNES. John Howard...and Thomas

Ris'ca'n—were summoned for stealing, on the 15th ult., some timber from a house in charge of Mr. Lightburn, secretary to the Lancashire and Cheshire Building Society, Runcorn.— John Maloyne, an old man, said he saw the lad Howard on the roof of the house stealing the timber and the other on the ground ready to receive it.—Mr. Lightbnrn said he should not have pressed the ca* had it not been for the wholesale deStruction of property which took place in Widnes. In fact, there did not appear to be any protection for property in the town. It frequently happened that a landlord prepared a house for a tenant, and though he might enter it immediately afterwards he found it a scene of devastation and wanton destruction.—Superintend- ent Barker remarked that on the very day when the offence was committed one of the defendants was brought up and dealt with at that court for wilful damage.—Risban was sentenced to receive six and Howard nine strokes with the birch rod. ALLEGED VIOLENT ASSAULT AT DrrroN.—Frederick Lowe, William Blundell, and Robert Beasley were charged with assaulting John Clare, at Ditton, on the 25th ult.— Complainant said that whilst walking home from the Ham- mer and Pincers public-house, and near Ditton bank, he met the defendants, and Lowe began a conversation of a rather insulting character. Complainant then told him he was quite as good a man as he, on which the three fellows set upon him, knocked him down, and kicked him, so that he took refuge in a yard belonging to a Mr. Barlow, to whom he cried for assistance. Defendants, however, fol- lowed him into the yard, and again assaulted him.—The defendants, Robert Beasley, and a man named Edward Hut- chinson, were also charged with assaulting James Kelly, a Ditton labourer. Complainant said he heard the defendants in the last case assaulting care, whilst in the Brown Cow public•house. He afterwards went out on hearing Clare's cries for help, and saw two of the men illuse him in a most cowardly manner. He (witness) said, "For shame; don't murder the poor man." He then pulled Beasley off Clare. Beasley next said he would do the same to him, and knocked him down. Hutchinson also set upon him, on which "se came to the conclusion that he had got into a hot shop " (laughter)—and ran off.—Each defendant was fined lOs and costs.

THEFT OF ROPE FROM A MARINE STORE DEALER'S.— I James Highland was charged with stealing *cwt. of rope, I the property of Mr. Frederick Bibby, marine store dealer,' on the 18th January.—Prosecutor said his shop was in Mersey-road, and on the 18th January he bought *wt. of Italian flax rope from the Widnes Alkali Company, and on the evening of the next day 21cwt. of Manilla rope belonging to a flat. On the 23e1 of the same month, on making the rope into coils, he found it was 4cwt. short. During the course of enquiries he afterwards made, he met the prisoner on the Old Marsh with a large amount of rope on his back. He asked him where he had obtained it, and he said from one of Cooper's flats, lying in the basin. He told Highland nat the rope belonged to him, on which he became Indio.- nant, and ealet he would feteh the captain frona whom lie purchased it. Ve went away, bat did not return, and was afterwards apprehended by Sergeant Clarkson.—The Super- intendent of Police said the prisoner was sent to gaol seven days last November for stealing coal.—He was committed one month with hard labour. A FITTER'S NIGHT ADVENTURE—Sarah Thornton, a good looking and respectably dressed woman, who formerly lived in Church-street, and has lately suffered six months' imprisonmeet for stealing a considerable sum from the person, 11,33 charged with robbing William Dedd, a fitter, about 40 years of age, of 81—Prosecutor, who appeared rather ashamed of the position he occupied, said he lived in Waterloo-road, and on Monday evening he met the prisoner, with whom he had formerly been acquainted, and asked her to go with him to the George Hotel, Waterloo-road He paid for a small whiskey for her, and had a glass of beer himself. At this time he had. .£2 fis. in his right trousers pocket. They remained at the George quarter of an hour, ard then went to the Arch Hotel, West Bank. On the way Thornton asked him if be would lend her some money to take her to Manchester, but be said he would not. He again paid for a glass of whiskey, and one of beer, and handed four shillings to a man from whom he had borrowed some money. They next 'adjourned to a private house, where he paid for a qaart of ale, and at Tansey's beerhouse they had each a glass of ale. lie then stood with the prisoner about twenty minutes in a passage in Hutchinsen-street, and whilst there put a sovereign into his waistcoat pocket, and immediately missed the Bs., which he charged her with stealing. She denied the charge, and he gave her into custody in Wellington-street. —Thornton, who has evidently been fairly educated, cross- examined the prosecutor at great length. He admitted that when the prisoner was tried upon the last occasion, he ad- vanced a friend of tier's named Heyes, money with which to pay the charges of a Liverpool solicitor or barrister. He denied having told her to never mind thinking of paying him back, as he supposed he should never receive what he had put down.—P.C. Worthington said that he apprehended the prisoner, and upon her being searched at the station Ss. lid. wee found upon her.—She was committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. J. PAUL RYLANDS.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. J. PAUL RYLANDS.

At the parish church of St. Mary, West Derby, near Liverpool, there was a large and fashionable assembly of the fairer portion of the residents of that pretty suburban village, on Thursday, to witness the marriage of Mr. John Paul Rylands, of the Middle Temple, elder son of Mr. Thos. Glazebrook Rylands, The Highfields, Thelwall, to Miss Mary Isabel Glazebrook, second daughter of Mr. Nicholas Smith Ulazebrook, Hayman's Green, West Derby, surgeon. The wedding party commenced to assemble at eleven o'clock, but long before that hour the edifice was filled with friends and neighbours. About a quarter-past eleven the bride entered the church with her father, and accompanied by her six bridesmaids—Miss Glazebrook, Miss F. E. Glasebrook, Miss A. Glazebrook (sisters of the bride), Miss Rylands and Miss M. G. Rylands (sisters of the bridegroom), and Miss M. Tetley (cousin of the bride), the organ, at which Mr. Arnold Cleaver presided, pealing forth Mendelssohn's "I waited for the Lord." The bride was met by the bridegroom, who had previously entered the church accompanied by his brother, Mr. W. Harry Rylands (who acted as best man), Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Mr. C. T. Gatty, Mr. H. Greenall, Mr. W. C. Jones, jun., Mr. J. Claude Morris, and Mr. J. R. Thomson. The choir having sung the hymn, "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," the ceremony was proceeded with. The marriage was celebrated by the Rev. Canon Stewart, rector of the pArish, and the bride was given away by her father. The bride was attired in a lovely ivory satin dress, trimmed with orange blossoms, and wore a tulle veil and wreath of orange blossoms. The bridesmaids wore dresses of pale blue nun's cloth, trimmed with cream coloured lace, and large straw hats trimmed with cream lace and harebells, and carried baskets containing tea roses, 'Meg of the valley, harebells, dm. By the friends of the bride, the chancel had been most tastefully decorated. The alter rail standards were exquisitely adorned with camelias, a variety of delicate ferns, and primroses ; while the pulpit, reading desk, and ends of the choir stalls were ornamented with daffodils, hyacinths, and wallflowers, the floral decorations being executed in such a manner as to evoke frequent expressions of admiration. While the marriage was being registered Mr. Arnold Cleaver played Mendelssohn's "Wedding march," and as the party left the church he played " The march of the priests," from " Eli." Breakfast was provided at the residence of the bride's father, and besides the above named there were also present the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Stewart, Mr. and Mrs. T. G. Rylands, Mr. and Mrs. T. Wilkinson Tetley, Miss M. J. Tetley., Miss C. Tetley, Miss M. Tetley, Mr. T. Lownds, Miss Lownds, Miss M. Lownds, Mr. and Miss Springman, Pro- fessor Rendall, Mr. Arnold J. Cleaver, Mr. Edward P. Busch, Mr. R. 'l'. Glazebrook, Mr. F. K. Glazebrook, and Mr. W. R. Glazebrook. In the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. J. Paul Rylands left Liverpool by the four o'clock train, en route for the Riviera, for their wediltng tour. The esteem in which the newly wedded pair are held by their friends was testified by the 120 elegant and costly presents which they had received; and numerous flags were displayed in various parts of the village in honour of the event. Mr. Bolloud, of Chester, supplied the wedding cake.

div.head: WARRINGTON ORCHESTRAL
div.p: WARRINGTON ORCHESTRAL
SOCIETY. REPORT AND FINANCIAL STATEMENT.

Under the presidency of Mr. L. W. Reynolds, 'a general meeting of the members of the Warrington Orchestral Society was held on Monday evening, in Cairo-street school- room. The SECRETARY read the report, which, after referring to the two recent concerts and stating that there had been a loss by the second of about £lO5, proceeded: "The finan- cial position of the satiety is not at all satisfactory, this season being the first in which two concerts have been given. The committee considered last season that, in order to fully develope the society, it was necessary to extend its opera- tions, and anticipated that, by so doing, taking into account the favourable impression created by the society's former concerts, they would obtain a much larger subscription list. This hope proved fallacious, and the committee found that, with an expenditure nearly doubled, they had only an increase of upwards of £2O in the subscriptions. The result of this was, that alter defraying the expenses of the first concert and carrying forward half the subscriptions to the second concert, there was a loss of about £l3. The loss on the second concert was about £2O, and these added toge- ther, plus the deficiency from last season, make a total deficiency of about £4O. The committee regret to have to report a very considerable falling off in the band, both in the number of the band and the interest shown in it. The orchestral portion of the concerts this season have not been at all up to the standard of last season's performances, and Dr. Hiles complained that the band was very inefficient at the Musical Society's concert on December 13th, 1881. All through the season there has been a great want of interest in the society by many members, and the attendance has been very poor, the average at each practice being only 10 out of a total number of 18, six of whom reside out of War- rington. As the season advanced the attendance became smaller and smaller, till it culminatsd in the last two prac- tices, which were held to work up the music for the Musical Society's concert on April 13th, when only four and six members turned up, and of these only one at the second practice, and none at the first were residents in War- rington. In the face of this, the committee thought it best to discontinue the practices, and to call a general meeting to consider the advisability of winding up the society, the want Qf interest and epathy of Warrington instrumentalists being such as to leave little or no hope of getting and keep- ing together an amateur band that would be of any real service either to the Orchestral or Musical Society. Btate- meet of Accounts :-Receipts: To donation, J. Marson, Esq., £2; subscription, £62 25.; subscription unpaid, £1 83; sale of tickets, November 14th, £9 55.; sale of programmes, November 14th, £1 155.; sale of tickets, January 25th, £46 6s. 3d.; sale of programmes, January 25th, £3 Os. 6d.; music (returned), 4s. 7d.; amount owing for tickets, Iss. 6d.; balance, £39 168. 11M.; total, £166 13s. 91d. Expenditure : By balance for season 1880-1, £6 17s. 53/4d•; professional assistance, Nov. 14th, £23 14s. 61; ditto, ditto, Jan. 25th, £73 16s. ; cencert expenses, November 14th, £7 ; ditto, ditto, Jan. 25th, £7 12s. 6d.; printing and, ad- vertising. £2O 13s. 6d.; conductor (Mr. L. Veerman)% £l5 Os; music. £5 2.4. 211. ; deficiency on special train, £1 14s. 3d.; postage, £3 ss. 9d.; stationery, 9s. ed.; sundries, 18s. 7d.; total, £166 13s. nel. The CHAIRMAN called attention to that portion of the re- port relating to the band, and showed that it appeared im- possible to keep the society in existence, owing to the great falling off in the band and the great want of interest shown in it, and stated that in consequence it had become neces- sary to call a general meeting to consider the advisability of winding up the society. After a long discussion the following resolution was carried," That there appearing no reasonable prospect of keeping together an amateur band in Warringtr,n that would be of any real service, the society be wound .up, and the secretary authorised to dispose of the property, and to apply the money so raised towards reducing the deficiency." 'rho proceedings terminated with votes of thanks to the president (Mr. James Marson) for the active interest he has taken in the society, and to the secretary and librarian for their services.

LATEST NEWS.
The German Admiralty has suddenly ordered six torpedo boats from a Bremen shipyard, to be finished within four months.
The International University sports took place at Willie Bridge yesterday and resulted in gambridge winning five events to Oxford four.
Yesterday a prize fight occurred between Jim Hill, town crier of Wolverhampton, and a man named Lane for £l.O a side. After a t9ugh battle the former won before the police arrived.

The weavers employed at the extensive works of Messrs. William Hartley and Sons, Heywood, have struck for an advance of *d. per lb. all round. There are about 80 on strike, which has lasted for a week. The firm have offered to pay an advance on two kinds of clop. Mr. Mayer, F.G.S., the eminent silversmith, late of Liverpool, a native of Neweastle-under-Lyne, Staffordshire, has intimated his intention to present about 100 valuable pictures to the borough of Newcastle. The gift is intended as the Rueleus of a public art gallery and museum, which Mr Mayer long since notified he should like to see estab- lished in his native town.

M. Maovin. the special Russian correspondent of the Newcastle Chronicle, informs that journal that he can obtain no information in St. Petersburg respecting the Czar's reported reprimand of General Skobeleff, but his own impression is that General Skobeleff stands higher in the Emperor's favour than ever before. James Robinson, 25 years of ago, was apprehended on Thursday and brought before the Clitheroe magistrates for assaulting his wife. On Tuesday prisoner locked the door and brutally assaulted his wife. He threw her down, kicked her, and when she got up knocked her head against a wall, causing a severe wound. They had only been married three years, and he had repeatedly abused her. He was committed to prison for three months without the option of a fine. COTTON " ADULTERATION " EXTRAODINARY.

A neat little pistol, a breechloader, charged with ball, has just been found inside a bale of American cotton opened at Springhill Mill, Royten. The weapon, which is in beautiful condition, was apparently made in Massachusetts. On being fired the ball penetrated a thick board, and was after- wards picked up. The pistol, which has been exhibited, is much admired, and would find many willing purchasers. SALVATION ARMY RIOTS AT CHESTER.

div.head: THREATENING TO MURDER THE MAYOR.
div.p: THREATENING TO MURDER THE MAYOR.

On Friday morning the police-court, Chester, was crowded to overflowing, when some 20 prisoners were placed in the dock charged with riotously attacking the Salvation Army in Boughton, the Irish district of Chester, on Sunday. There was a f nil bench of magistrates, and on Sir Thomas Gibbons Frost, the mayor, taking the chair, he said: I have this morning received this letter, addressed to me, and signed "Revenge and Death " :—" Chester, March 30th, 1882. Sir Thomas Frost,—We, the Secret Brotherhood of Chester,' hear you will occupy the chair to-morrow in the hearing of the attack on the Salvation Army, and we, the Secret Brotherhood undersigned, that is, Revenge and Death.' solemnly vow And swear that if you pronounce one or any of the prisoners guilty, you and all your brother magistrates will answer with your lives." Cries of " Shame" from all parts of the court greeted the reading of this epistle.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. To insure insertion it is necessary that all items of news intended for publication should reach this Qffice as early in the week as possible. ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS. T.W., Robson-street, Warrington.—We should say that you must give a week's notice at least. Q.E.C., Warrington —The " Upper Ten" is synonymous with "the aristocracy." The term was first used by Mr. N. P. Willis, in speaking of the fashionables of New York, who at that time were supposed to Ibe not more than 10,000 in number. ATHEIST. Latchford.—Tne oath of allegiance which members of the House of Commons are required to take under the statute 31st and 32nd Victoria, cap. 72 (1568), is as follows :—" I do swear that I will bc faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Victoria, her heirs and successors, according to law, so help me God." A.P.S., Nantwich.—No property qualification is now necessary for members of the House of Commons. All that is required is that the candidate shall be a born or naturalised subject of the Queen, of full age and sound mind, and that he shall not be a peer, a clergyman, a pensioner under the Crown, the holder of a disquallfying office, a Government contractor (with certain exceptions), Or a person who has forfeited his right by his own misconduct. Warrington.—Mr. Bradlaugh has neither taken the oath nor declined to take it. He at first claimed the right t , affirm, and, this being disallowed, he expressed his readiness to take the oath, but was also refused permission to go through that ceremony. Since then, he has over and over again presented himself to be sworn, but always with the same result, except that the majority against him has dwindled from over half a hundred to 15. E.P., Knutsford.—The Stewardship of the Chiltern Hundreds is an office of emolument under the Cr own, which in the old days, when the Chiltern Hills were invested with robbers, had duties attached to it, but which is now, and has been for years past, a sinecure. It is only by accepting an office of emolument under the Crown that a member of the House of Commons can voluntarily vacate his seat. When, therefore. a member wales to resign, he applies for and receives the appointment of Steward of the Chiltern Hundreds, which he subsequently gives up, and so leaves it available for any other member who may wish to follow his example.
